Approximate Lowest Astronomical Tide: An approximate level, usually within 0.3 metres from that of lowest astronomical tide.
Approximate Mean Lower Low Water: An approximate level, usually within 0.3 metres from that of mean lower low water.
Approximate Mean Low Water: An approximate level, usually within 0.3 metres from that of mean low water.
Approximate Mean Low Water Springs: An approximate level, usually within 0.3 metres from that of mean low water springs.
Approximate Mean Sea Level: An approximate level, usually within 0.3 metres from that of mean sea level.
Equinoctial Spring Low Water: The level of low water springs near the time of an equinox.

Ground Level: A continuous surface over dry land and non-tidal waters (for example: lakes). [desc] In the case of non-tidal waters it is necessary to specify hydrologic conditions in order to ensure a precise reference surface specification. Over extensive areas it is often defined by a digital elevation model (for example: a matrix of elevation values or a Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN)). Over tidal waters (for example: oceans) it is usually considered to be extended to cover the remainder of the world based on a Mean Sea Level (MSL) surface.
Higher High Water: The highest of the high waters (or single high water) of any specified tidal day due to the declination A1 effects of the moon and sun.
Higher High Water Large Tide: The average of the highest high waters, one from each of 19 years of observations.
Highest Astronomical Tide: The highest tidal level, which can be predicted to occur under average meteorological conditions and under any combination of astronomical conditions.
Highest High Water: The highest water level observed at a location.

High Water: The highest level reached at a location by the water surface in one tidal cycle. [desc] When used on inland waters it is generally defined as a level that the daily mean water level exceeds less than 5 percent of the time.
High Water Springs: An arbitrary level, approximating that of mean high water springs.
International Great Lakes Datum 1985: A vertical reference system with its zero based on the mean water level at Rimouski/Pointe-au-Père, Quebec, over the period 1970 to 1988.

Indian Spring High Water: A tidal surface datum approximating the level of the mean of the higher high water at spring tides. [desc] This tidal datum approximates the highest water level observed at a location and is usually above that of the higher high water at spring tides.

Indian Spring Low Water: A tidal surface datum approximating the level of the mean of the lower low water at spring tides. [desc] This tidal datum approximates the lowest water level observed at a location and is usually below that of the lower low water at spring tides.
Lower Low Water: The lowest of the low waters (or single low water) of any specified tidal day due to the declination A1 effects of the moon and sun.
Lower Low Water Large Tide: The average of the lowest low waters, one from each of 19 years of observations.
Lowest Astronomical Tide: The lowest tide level that can be predicted to occur under average meteorological conditions and under any combination of astronomical conditions.
Lowest Low Water: An arbitrary level conforming to the lowest tide observed at a location, or somewhat lower.
Lowest Low Water Springs: An arbitrary level conforming to the lowest water level observed at a location at spring tides during a period shorter than 19 years.

Low Water: An approximation of mean low water adopted as the reference level for a limited region, irrespective of better determinations later. [desc] Used mostly in harbour and river engineering. Used in inland waters. It is generally defined as a level which the daily mean water level would fall below less than 5 percent of the time and by no more than 0.2 metres during the navigation season. A single level surface is usually chosen as the low water datum for a whole lake. On a river, low water datum is a sloping surface, which approximates the surface of the river at a low state.
Low Water Springs: A level approximating that of mean low water springs.
Mean Higher High Water: The average height of higher high waters at a location over a 19-year period.
Mean Higher High Water Springs: The average height of higher high water at spring tides at a location.
Mean High Water: The average height of all high waters at a location over a 19-year period.
Mean High Water Neaps: The average height of the high waters of the neap tide.
Mean High Water Springs: The average height of the high waters of spring tides.
Mean Lower Low Water: The average height of the lower low waters at a location over a 19-year period.
Mean Lower Low Water Springs: The average height of lower low water at spring tides at a location.
Mean Low Water: The average height of all low waters at a location over a 19-year period.
Mean Low Water Neaps: The average height of the low waters of the neap tide.
Mean Low Water Springs: The average height of the low waters of spring tides.
Mean Sea Level (MSL): A continuous surface over the oceans (or its hypothetical extension under the land masses) defined by the mean of sea level surfaces approximated and observed over 19 years.
Mean Tide Level: The arithmetic mean of mean high water and mean low water.
Mean Water Level: The average of all hourly water levels over the available period of record.

North American Vertical Datum (NAVD) 1988: A fixed reference for elevations derived from a general adjustment of the first-order terrestrial levelling nets of the United States, Canada, and Mexico. [desc] In the adjustment, only the height of the primary tidal bench mark, referenced to the International Great Lakes Datum of 1985 local mean sea level height value, at Pointe-au-Pere, Quebec, on the Gulf of St. Lawrence was held fixed, thus providing minimum constraint.

Neap Tide: A tide of decreased range (or tidal currents of decreased speed) occurring semi-monthly as the result of the moon being in quadrature. [desc] The neap range of the tide is the average range occurring at the time of neap tides and is most conveniently computed from the harmonic constants. It is smaller than the mean range where the type of tide is either semi-diurnal or mixed and is of no practical significance where the type of tide is predominantly diurnal.
Nearly Highest High Water: An arbitrary level approximating the highest water level observed at a location, usually equivalent to the high water springs.
Nearly Lowest Low Water: A level approximating the lowest water level observed at a location, usually equivalent to Indian spring low water.

National Geodetic Vertical Datum (NGVD) 1929: A fixed reference for elevations derived from a general adjustment in 1929 of the first-order leveling nets of both the United States and Canada. [desc] In the adjustment, mean sea level was held fixed as observed at 21 tide stations in the United States and 5 in Canada.

Spring Tide: A tide of increased range (or tidal water currents of increased speed) occurring semi-monthly as the result of the moon being new or full. [desc] The spring range of tide is the average range occurring at the time of spring tides and is most conveniently computed from the harmonic constants. It is larger than the mean range where the type of tide is either semi-diurnal or mixed, and is of no practical significance where the type of tide is predominantly diurnal.

Water Level: A locally observed level of the water surface. [desc] In the case of non-tidal waters (for example: lakes or rivers) it is necessary to specify hydrologic conditions in order to ensure a precise reference surface specification. Over tidal waters (for example: oceans) it is necessary to specify tidal conditions in order to ensure a precise reference surface specification.
WGS 84 EGM08 Geoid: The geopotential surface defined by the World Geodetic System (WGS) 1984 EGM08 Earth Gravity Model that is closely associated with the mean ocean surface.
WGS 84 EGM96 Geoid: The geopotential surface defined by the World Geodetic System (WGS) 1984 EGM96 Earth Gravity Model that is closely associated with the mean ocean surface.
WGS 84 Ellipsoid: The oblate ellipsoidal figure of the Earth defined by the World Geodetic System (WGS) 1984.

Confirmed. Confirmed by other sources. If it can be stated with certainty that the reported information originates from another source than the already existing information on the same subject, it is classified as "confirmed by other sources" and is rated 1.

Probable. Probably true. If the independence of the source of any item of information cannot be guaranteed, but if, from the quantity and quality of previous reports its likelihood is nevertheless regarded as sufficiently established, then the information should be classified as "probably true" and given a rating of 2.

Possible. Possibly true. If, despite there being insufficient confirmation to establish any higher degree of likelihood, a freshly reported item of information does not conflict with the previously reported behavior pattern of the target, the item may be classified as "possibly true" and given a rating of 3.

Doubtful. An item of information which tends to conflict with the previously reported or established behavior pattern of an intelligence target should be classified as "doubtful" and given a rating of 4.

Improbable. An item of information which positively contradicts previously reported information or conflicts with the established behavior pattern of an intelligence target in a marked degree should be classified as "improbable" and given a rating of 5.

Truth Cannot Be Judged. Any freshly reported item of information which provides no basis for comparison with any known behavior pattern of a target must be classified as "truth cannot be judged" and given a rating of 6. Such a rating should be given only when the accurate use of a higher rating is impossible.
Bottom Bounce. Sound travels from source to receiver via bottom bounce.
Convergence Zone. Sound travels from source to receiver via convergence zone.

Add. Adds specified items to a message/report.

Aerial Refueling. An airborne tanker and another aircraft conducting refueling operations.
Aerial Combat Maneuvers. The aerial maneuvers used to effectively employ fighter aircraft against hostile or simulated hostile aircraft.
Acquisition/Weapons Procurement. The process or act of obtaining a weapon or weapons.
Aircraft Recover. The phase of a mission which involves the return to a base.
Aircraft Refueling. The process of replenishing an aircraft with fuel.
Active Measure. Covert or overt actions that affect another nations policies and actions; includes a wide variety of activities such as assassination.
ADA, Engaging Aircraft. ADA site engaging enemy aircraft.
Antisubmarine Warfare, Air. Aerial operations conducted with the intention of denying the enemy the effective use of his submarines.
Aircraft Airborne. A term applied to an aircraft from the instant it becomes entirely sustained by air.
Interdiction. To isolate or seal off an area by any means, i.e., to deny use of a route or approach.
Air Sampling. An operation in which specifically equipped aircraft collect samples of air in the atmosphere.
Antiresettlement. Refers to one ethnic group resisting the settlement of another ethnic group in a specific area.
Aircraft Arrival. The arrival or landing of an aircraft.
Assassination. An assassination or attempted assassination on military or civilian leaders.
Assault. An unlawful threat or attempt to injure another physically or verbally.
Barrier Combat Air Patrol. One or more divisions or elements of fighter aircraft employed between a force and an objective area as a barrier across the probable direction of enemy attack.
Bid. An attempt to obtain something, usually with money.
Biological Attack. Warfare involving biological weapons or disease producing microorganisms.
Bombing. A term for air operations when using air to ground ordnance to destroy or neutralize enemy forces or installations.
Briefing. Process of giving or receiving information.

Combat Air Patrol. An aircraft patrol provided over an objective area, over the force protected, over the critical area of a combat zone, or over an air defense area, for the purpose of intercepting and destroying hostile aircraft before they reach their target.
Cargo Transport. Air movement of military supplies and equipment.

Close Air Support. Air attacks against hostile targets which are in close proximity to friendly forces and which require detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of these forces.
Contracting. Act of obtaining services, materials, or personnel from a civilian organization.
Compromise. Situation when protected material is exposed, such as information concerning a human collector, source, or operation.
Contact. In air intercept, a term meaning unit has an unevaluated target.
Cooperative R&D. Collective action in the field of research and development.

Defensive Counterair. A term for air operations conducted to attain and maintain a desired degree of air superiority by the destruction or neutralization of enemy forces, conducted near to or over friendly territory and generally reactive to the initiative of the enemy air forces.
EPW Death. The death of an enemy prisoner of war.
Debriefing. To question, discuss events, or solicit input with the goal of obtaining information from a cooperative source.
Defense Suppression. An air suppression mission, e.g., Wild Weasel mission.
Delegation. A person or group representing another person or group.
Demarche. A civil statement or protest addressed to the public authorities.
Aircraft Deployments. The relocation of aircraft to desired areas of operation.
Detected. The discovery of the existence of an object or phenomenon.
Displaced Persons or Refugees. Displaced persons or refugees; civilian who is involuntarily outside the boundaries of their country or is outside their area or region within their country.
Election. The action of selecting someone by vote for office.
Enemy Prisoner of War Escape. Escape by an enemy prisoner of war.
Escort. In air operations, aircraft assigned to protect other aircraft during a mission.

Espionage. The act of obtaining, delivering, transmitting, or receiving information about the national defense, with the intent of using the information to injure the U.S. or to give an advantage to U.S. adversaries.
Enemy Training. An activity related to the training of enemy forces.

Electronic Warfare. Military action involving the use of electromagnetic energy to determine, exploit, reduce, or prevent hostile use of the electromagnetic spectrum and action which retains friendly use of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Exercise. A non-real world event conducted to practice an activity.
Expulsion. The act or state of driving out by force or by right.
Freedom of Movement. The right to unrestricted movement across ethnic boundaries or borders.

Ground Alert. That status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time (usually 15 minutes) after receipt of a mission order.
Gravesite. Location where dead bodies are buried.
Harassment. To annoy or torment repeatedly.
Hijacking, Aircraft. To seize control of an aircraft.
Hijacking, Maritime Vessel. To seize control of a maritime vessel.
Intercepted. The identification and/or engagement of an airborne object.
Intel Collection. Act of obtaining and reporting information from all sources to satisfy requirements.
Intel Operation. A variety of tasks that generally refer to collection, processing, exploitation, and reporting of information.
Joint Venture. Action or operation involving more than one agency or organization.
Killed in Action. A casualty category applicable to persons killed outright or who died from wounds before reaching a medical facility.
Major Civil Crime. A major civil type crime.
Major Accident. An accident that results in the loss of life or substantial damage to property.

Missing in Action. A casualty status defined by United States code as military members not present at his or her duty location due to apparent involuntary reasons and whose location is unknown.  Excluded are personnel who are in an absent without leave, deserter, or dropped from rolls status.  Additional categories excluded from the MIA category are individuals beleaguered, besieged, captured, detained, or interned.
Military Event. Action or activity conducted by the armed forces.
Minelaying, Air. The process of placing mines in a minefield by aerial means.
Minesweeping. The technique of searching for, or clearing mines using mechanical or explosion gear, which physically removes or destroys the mine.
Mine Clearing, Engineering. The process of detecting and/or removing mines by manual or mechanical means.
Main Supply Route Critical Points Security.
Movement Activity. An activity related to the movement of forces.
Negotiations. To come to terms or an agreement with another.
ADA, Normal Operations. ADA site conducting normal operations.
Observed. Identification based on an observation.

Offensive Counterair. A term for air operations conducted to attain and maintain a desired degree of air superiority by the destruction or neutralization of enemy forces, conducted throughout enemy territory and generally conducted at the initiative of friendly forces.
Offload. In air operations, to remove cargo and/or equipment from an aircraft.
Offer. Something presented for acceptance, such as a proposal, invitation, or suggestion.
Onload. In air operations, to place cargo and/or equipment in an aircraft.
Opinion, Position Expressed. A belief or idea communicated by an individual or group.
Orbiting. In air intercept, means circling or circle and search.

Order and Discipline. Maintenance of unit wide obedience to prescribed practices and directives.  Refers to the smooth operation of an organization.  Rooted in an individual's respect for the legal authority for superiors, respect for their leadership examples, and commitment to comrades in arms.
Other. Explain the use of other in subsequent free-text set.
Photo Reconnaissance. Aerial photography for use in intelligence.
Polygraph. An instrument that simultaneously records variations in such physiological processes as heartbeat, blood pressure, and respiration, often used as a lie detector.
Positioned. In place, e.g., "equipment positioned on a hill."
Property Destruction. Destruction of property of major value.
Proliferation. Process in which items such as weapons spread to other groups or nations.
Project Related. Connected to a specific assignment.
Provocation. Act of challenging or provoking.
Passive Countermeasures. Employment of techniques or actions with the intention of impairing enemy actions without being detected.

Raid. An operation, usually small scale, involving a swift penetration of hostile territory to secure information, confuse the enemy, or to destroy equipment or installations. Typically ends with a planned withdrawal after completed mission.
Ranged. The process that established target distance such as echo, manual, navigational, optical, etc.

Reconnaissance. A mission undertaken to obtain, by visual observations or other detection methods, information about the activities and resources of an enemy or potential enemy. A visual observation or detection by other means with the goal of securing data.
Recruitment. The action of persuading individuals to participate in a specific activity, or the action of enrolling individuals into the armed forces.

R&S. Reconnaissance and Surveillance (R&S) are operations to obtain data or information regarding a specific target through systematic observation by various methods including technical application of electronic sensors or human examination.
Redeploying. The transferring of a unit, an individual, or supplies deployed in one area to another area, or to another location within the area.
Remains Disposal. Area where human remains are found or activity to illegally destroy human remains.
Reported. Repeated as something heard or said.
Research and Development. Activity that involves the discovery of new technologies and translating those discoveries into products.
Riot/Disturbance. A riot or disturbance of such magnitude that affects the command or the civil populace.

Recruitment in Place. Establishment of a controlling relationship over an agent by a case officer for the purpose of obtaining data or information from a specific target area.  Agent remains in the employment of the adversary.
Search and Rescue. The use of aircraft, surface craft, submarine, specialized rescue teams and equipment to search for and rescue personnel in distress on land or at sea.
Personnel Shuttling. Repetitive, frequent movements of personnel between two or more locations.
Special Inquiry or Investigation. Sophisticated, unique, or exceptional actions taken to obtain evidence to be used in a legal proceeding, such as in a security violation.
Special Operations. Secondary or supporting operations which may be adjuncts to various other operations and for which no one service is assigned primary responsibility.
Subversion. Action designed to undermine the military, economic, psychological, or political strength or morale of a regime.
Supply. Replenish/refuel to a location ashore.
Aircraft Takeoff. The takeoff or departure of an aircraft.
Tactical Airlift. The use of transport aircraft in direct support of airborne assaults, tactical air supply, evacuation of casualties from forward areas, and clandestine operations.
Target Antisubmarine Patrol. The systematic and continuing investigation of an area or along a line to detect or hamper submarines.
Technical Transfer, No Export. The act of providing sensitive or controlled technological information or equipment to another organization.
TeleCommunications. Any transmission, emission, or reception of signs, signals, writings, images, sounds, or information of any nature by wire, radio, visual, or other electromagnetic systems.
Terrorist Attack. An attack by terrorists.
Targeting. The detection, identification, and location of a target.
Transshipment. To transfer from one vessel or vehicle to another for further transit.
Transport, General. The movement of non-specific personnel and/or cargo.
Political, Military Treaty. A document in which a formal agreement is laid down.
Trial, Judicial Proceedings. Legal process involving examination of evidence to determine the guilt or innocence, and potential punishment of an individual based on specific charges or claims.
Travel Advisory, Alert. Warning issued to avoid traveling to a specific country due to dangerous or potentially dangerous conditions.

Technical Surveillance Countermeasures. Includes techniques and measures to detect and neutralize a wide variety of hostile penetration technologies used to obtain unauthorized access to classified and sensitive information.
United Nations Violation. Act which breaks international laws or basic human rights as defined by the international organization of countries referred to as the United Nations.

Unexploded Ordnance. Explosive ordnance which was primed, fused, armed, or otherwise prepared for action, and was fired, dropped, launched, projected, or placed in such a manner as to constitute a hazard to operations, installations, personnel, or material and remains unexploded either by malfunction or design or for any other cause.
War Crime. A crime committed against military or civilian personnel in a wartime environment that is contrary to the rules of land-warfare.
Wounded in Action. A casualty category encompassing all kinds of wounds and injuries incurred in action to an external agent or source.
Weapons Storage Site. Facility where approved military equipment including arms and ammunition may be legally stored in accordance with procedures established by a signed treaty.
Weather Collection. The collection of meteorological information.

Area Fire. Indicates that the mission will be fired as an area mission rather than a precision mission.

Danger Close. Indicates the target is less than 750 meters from friendly elements, when using 5-inch naval guns, and less than 1000 meters from friendly elements when using 6-inch naval guns or larger.
Destruction. Engagement of the target for the purpose of destroying it.
Mark. Indicates rounds fired to orient observer.
Registration. Indicates that the mission will be a registration mission.
Aerial Refueling. Refueling aircraft in flight, which extends presence, increases range, and serves as a force multiplier. May include bladder drop and refuel operations.
Anti-Air Warfare. Measures taken to defend a maritime force against attacks by airborne weapons launched from aircraft, ships, submarines, and land-based sites.

Airborne Command and Control Center. An aerial mission depending on an aircraft equipped with communications, data link, and display equipment; it may be employed as an airborne command post or a communications and intelligence relay facility.
Administrative Lift. An aerial airlift normally provided by specifically identifiable aircraft assigned to organizations or commands for internal administration.
Air Drop. Delivery of personnel or cargo from aircraft in flight.

Airborne Early Warning. Air surveillance and control provided by airborne early warning aircraft which are equipped with search and height finding radar and communication equipment for controlling weapon systems.
Attack Helicopter. A helicopter specifically designed to employ various weapons to attack and destroy enemy targets.

Air Interdiction. Air operations conducted to destroy, neutralize, or delay the enemy's military potential before it can be brought to bear effectively against friendly forces at such distance from friendly forces that detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of friendly forces is not required.  Does not include battlefield interdiction for this usage.
Aeromedical Evacuation. The movement of patients under medical supervision to and between medical treatment facilities by air transportation.
Air Landed. Moved by air and disembarked or unloaded after the aircraft has landed or while a helicopter is hovering.
Air Logistic Support Operations. An air operation, excluding an airborne operation, conducted within a theater to distribute personnel, equipment, and supplies.

Airborne Mission Commander. An aerial mission in which the Commander serves as an airborne extension of the executing component's Rescue Coordination Center (RCC) and coordinates the Combat Search and Rescue (CSAR) effort between the Combat Search and Rescue Task Force (CSARTF) and the RCC (or joint search and rescue center) by monitoring the status of all CSARTF elements, requesting additional assets when needed, and ensuring the recovery and supporting forces arrive at their designated areas to accomplish the CSAR mission.
Armed Reconnaissance (Maritime). An aerial mission with the primary purpose of locating and attacking enemy maritime targets of opportunity.

Armed Reconnaissance. An aerial mission flown with the primary purpose of locating and attacking targets of opportunity, i.e., enemy materiel, personnel, and facilities, in assigned general areas or along assigned ground communications routes, and not for the purpose of attacking specific briefed targets.

Advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar System. An aerial mission type which focuses of the use of a multimode real-time, high-resolution reconnaissance system carried on the U-2 with all-weather, day-night, and long-range mapping capabilities. ASARS detects and accurately locates stationary and moving ground targets to satisfy the mission goal.
Anti-Surface Warfare/Anti-Surface Vessel Operations. Air operations conducted with the intention of denying the enemy the effective use of maritime surface assets.
Anti-Submarine Warfare. Operations conducted with the intention of denying the enemy the effective use of submarines.
Attack. Any aerial mission meant to disrupt, neutralize, or destroy enemy forces.

Barrier Combat Air Patrol. An aerial mission which use of one or more divisions or elements of fighter aircraft between a force and an objective area as a barrier across the probable direction of enemy attack. It is used as far from the force as control conditions permit, giving added protection against raids that use the most direct routes of approach.

Combat Air Patrol. An aircraft patrol provided over an objective area, the force protected, the critical area of a combat zone, or in an air defense area, for the purpose of intercepting and destroying hostile aircraft before they reach their targets.

Close Air Support. Air action against hostile targets which are in close proximity to friendly forces and which require detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of those forces.
Container Delivery System. An aerial mission, which focuses on the use of a system where containers are airdropped into a forward operating location.

Chaff. Strips of frequency-cut metal foil, wire, or metallized glass fiber used to reflect electromagnetic energy, usually dropped from aircraft or expelled from shells or rockets as a radar countermeasure.
Communication, Intelligence, Collection. An aerial mission which focuses on gathering communication intelligence in order to meet current operational requirements.

Command and Control. An aerial mission in which a properly designated commander exercises authority and direction over assigned and attached forces in the accomplishment of the task, command, and control functions are performed through an arrangement of personnel, equipment, communications, facilities, and procedures employed by a commander in planning, directing, coordinating, and controlling forces and operations in the accomplishment of the mission.

Contingency. An aerial emergency mission involving military force caused by natural disasters, terrorists, subversives, or by required military operations. Due to the uncertainty of the situation, contingencies require plans, rapid response, and special procedures to ensure the safety and readiness of personnel, installations, and equipment.
Communications Relay. Airborne operations where aircraft serve as a communications relay extending existing capabilities.

Combat Search and Rescue. The detection, location, identification, and rescue of downed aircrew in hostile territory in time of crisis or war and, when appropriate, isolated military personnel in distress, who are trained and equipped to receive combat search and rescue support.
Courier Flight. An aerial mission conducted to carry mail, information, or supplies.

Defensive Counterair. An aerial mission, which focuses on all defensive measures designed to detect, identify, intercept, and destroy or negate enemy forces attempting to attack or penetrate the friendly air environment.
Destruction Enemy Air Defenses (DEAD). An aerial mission that destroys surface-based enemy air defenses by any means.
Distinguished Visitor Support. Air operations where military aircraft are used to transport distinguished visitors.

Electronic Attack. An aerial mission conducted by a division of electronic warfare involving the use of electromagnetic energy, directed energy, or anti-radiation weapons to attack personnel, facilities, or equipment with the intent of degrading, neutralizing, or destroying enemy combat capability and is considered a form of fires.
Electronic. An aerial mission, which is primarily for the purpose of collecting data on electronic emitters.
Electro-Optical. An aerial mission which focuses on the use of imaging sensors that collect imagery in or just beyond the visible spectrum.

Electronic Support. An aerial mission, which provides information, required for decisions involving electronic warfare operations and other tactical actions such as threat avoidance, targeting, and homing.
Escort. Aircraft assigned to protect other aircraft during a mission.

Electronic Warfare. Military action to exploit the electromagnetic spectrum encompassing: the search for, interception, and identification of electromagnetic emissions, the employment of electromagnetic energy, included directed energy, to reduce or prevent hostile use of the electromagnetic spectrum, and actions to ensure its effective use by friendly forces.

Electronic Warfare Support (ES). An aerial mission conducted by a division of electronic warfare involving actions tasked by, or under direct control of, an operational commander to search for, intercept, identify, and locate or localize sources of intentional and unintentional radiated electromagnetic energy for the purpose of immediate threat recognition, targeting, planning, and conduct of future operations. Thus, electronic warfare support provides information required for decisions involving electronic warfare operations and other tactical actions such as threat avoidance, targeting, and homing.  Electronic warfare support data can be used to produce signals intelligence, provide targeting for electronic or destructive attack, and produce measurement and signature intelligence.

Exercise. A military maneuver or simulated wartime operation involving planning, preparation, and execution. It is carried out for the purpose of training and evaluation. It may be a combined, joint, or single-service exercise, depending on participating organizations.
Forward Air Controller. A qualified individual who, from a forward position on the or in the air, directs the action of combat aircraft engaged in close air support of land forces.
Force Protection CAP. An aerial mission, which focuses on the use of aircraft patrol, provided over an objective area containing friendly forces.
Functional Check Flight. A flight conducted to confirm operational readiness of the flight crew or aircraft.

Forward Looking Infrared. An aerial mission, which focuses on an airborne, electro-optical thermal imaging device that detects far-infrared energy, converts the energy into an electronic signal, and provides a visible image for day or night viewing.

Ground Alert Anti-Air Warfare. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform anti-air operations.

Ground Alert Airborne Command and Control Center. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform command and control operations.

Ground Alert Airborne Early Warning. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform early warning operations.

Ground Alert Attack Helicopter. The status in which rotary-wing aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform attack operations.

Ground Alert Aeromedical Evacuation. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform aeromedical evacuation operations.

Ground Alert Troop/Cargo Helicopter Operation. The status in which helicopter aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform transportation operations for troops or cargo.

Ground Alert Aerial Refueling. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform aerial refueling operations.

Ground Alert Anti-Submarine Warfare. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform anti-submarine operations.

Ground Alert Attack. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and are ready to employ various weapons to destroy enemy targets.

Ground Alert Battlefield Air Interdiction. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and to bring airpower to bear on those enemy forces not yet engaged but positioned to directly affect the land battle.

Ground Alert Barrier Combat Air Patrol. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform barrier combat air patrol operations.

Ground Alert Combat Air Patrol. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform combat air patrol operations.

Ground Alert Close Air Support. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform close air support operations. See close air support.

Ground Alert Communications Relay. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform airborne operations where aircraft serve as a communications relay extending existing capabilities.

Ground Alert. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order.

Ground Alert Defensive Counterair. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform defensive counterair operations.

Ground Alert Destruction of Enemy Air Defenses. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform a DEAD mission.

Ground Alert Escort. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform escort operations.

Ground Alert Electronic Warfare. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform electronic warfare operations. See electronic warfare.

Ground Alert Forward Air Controller. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform forward air control operations.

Ground Alert Flare Illumination. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform battlefield illumination by airdropping high-powered flares.

Ground Alert Interdiction. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform interdiction operations.

Ground Alert Joint Airborne Communications Control/Command Post. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform joint command and control operations.

Ground Alert Minelaying. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform airdrops of encased explosive over ground or in water and that are set to explode when disturbed.

Ground Alert Minesweeping. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and once airborne will locate minefields and neutralize them by dropping ordnance over the area.

Ground Alert Offensive Air Support. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform offensive air operations in order to disrupt enemy operations.

Ground Alert Offensive Counterair. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform offensive counterair operations. See offensive counterair.

Ground Alert Personnel Recovery. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform a personnel recovery mission.

Ground Alert Reconnaissance. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform reconnaissance operations. See reconnaissance.

Ground Alert Strategic Attack. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform any long range air operation meant to strike an enemy at the sources of its military, economic, or political power.

Ground Alert Strategic Airlift. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform strategic airlift operations. See strategic airlift.

Ground Alert Search and Rescue. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform search and rescue operations. See search and rescue.

Ground Alert Reconnaissance Strike Control and Reconnaissance (SCAR). The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and conduct reconnaissance strike control and reconnaissance operations.

Ground Alert Surface Combat Air Patrol (SUCAP). The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform a combat air patrol in support of surface vessels conducting maritime operations.

Ground Alert Suppression Enemy Air Defense (SEAD). The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform SEAD operations.

Ground Alert Security. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform security operations. See security.

Ground Alert Special Operations Forces. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform special operations. See special operation forces.

Ground Alert Support Mission. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform air missions that include movement of personnel or equipment other than via tactical airlift.

Ground Alert Sensor Implant. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, airdrop sensors.

Ground Alert Defense Suppression. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform SEAD operations that will attempt to neutralize, destroy, or temporarily degrade surface-based enemy air defenses by destructive and/or disruptive means.

Ground Alert Theater Airlift. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform theater airlift operations. See theater airlift.
Troop/Cargo Helicopter Operation. Helicopter transportation operations airlifting troops or cargo.
Heavy Equipment Airdrop. An aerial mission to unload heavy equipment from an aircraft in flight.
Ingress Combat Air Patrol (CAP). Combat air patrol flown in support of friendly aircraft as the aircraft ingress into enemy territory.

Image Intel Collection. An aerial mission which focuses on the intelligence collection by visual photography, infrared sensors, lasers, electro-optics, and radar sensors such as synthetic aperture radar wherein images of objects are reproduced optically or electronically on film, electronic display devices, or other media.
Flare Illumination. An aerial mission which focuses on battlefield illumination by airdropping high-powered flares.
Imagery. Collectively, the representations of objects reproduced electronically or by optical means on film, electronic display devices, or other media.

Intelligence Collection. An aerial mission, which focuses on the gathering of information from all available sources to meet an intelligence requirement. Specifically, a logical plan for transforming the essential elements of information into orders or requests to sources within a required time limit.

Interdiction. Operations conducted to destroy, neutralize, or delay the enemy's military potential before it can be brought to bear effectively against friendly forces at such distance from friendly forces that detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of friendly forces is not required.

Intelligence. An aerial mission that's product results from the collection, processing, integration, analysis, evaluation, and interpretation of available information concerning foreign countries or areas or information and knowledge about an adversary obtained through observation, investigation, analysis, or understanding.

Joint Airborne Air Transportability Training. Training operations or exercises involving airborne and appropriate troop carrier units. This training includes: a. air delivery of personnel and equipment; b. assault operations by airborne troops and/or air transportable units; c. loading exercises and local orientation fights of short duration; and d. maneuvers and/or exercises as agreed upon by services concerned and/or as authorized by the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Joint Airborne Communications Center/Command Post (JACC/CP). A suitably equipped aircraft used by the commander for conduct of operations.

Joint Surveillance Target Attack Radar System. An aerial mission which focuses on the use of a long-range, air-to-ground surveillance system designed to locate, classify, and track ground targets in all weather conditions.

Low Altitude Parachute Extraction System. An aerial mission which focuses on the use of self-contained system capable of a low-level delivering, heavy loads into an area where air landing is not feasible from an optimum aircraft wheel altitude of 5 to 10 feet above ground level. One or more platforms may be dropped.

Mapping. An aerial mission which permits to create a graphic representation, usually on a plane surface and at an established scale, of natural or artificial features on the surface of a part or the whole of the earth or other planetary body. The features are positioned relative to a coordinate reference system.
Medical Evacuation. The movement of patients under medical supervision to and between medical treatment facilities by any means necessary.
Minelaying. An aerial mission which permits airdrops of encased explosive over ground or in water that are set to explode when disturbed.

Minesweeping. The technique of searching for, or clearing mines using mechanical or explosion gear, which physically removes or destroys the mine, or produces, in the area, the influence fields necessary to actuate it.
Observation Flight. The airborne surveillance of aerospace, surface, or subsurface areas, places, persons, or things, by visual, aural, electronic, photographic, or other means.

Offensive Counterair. Offensive operations to destroy, disrupt, or neutralize enemy aircraft, missiles, launch platforms, and their supporting structures and systems both before and after launch, but as close to their source as possible. Offensive counterair operations range throughout enemy territory and are generally conducted at the initiative of friendly forces. These operations include attack operations, fighter sweep, escort, and suppression of enemy air defenses.
Other. Indicates the mission is something other than any of the missions listed. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.

Peacetime Aerial Reconnaissance. An aerial mission flown during peacetime meant to obtain, by visual observation or other detection methods, information about the activities and resources of a potential enemy, or to secure data concerning the meteorological, hydrographic, or geographic characteristics of a particular area.
Point CAP. Combat air patrol flown in support of a rendezvous or a break-up point.
Personnel Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on the delivery of personnel from an aircraft in flight.
Helicopter Mission (Plane Guard). An aerial mission, which focuses on the use of helicopter maintaining station in vicinity of carrier for potential SAR during flight operations.
Photo. An aerial mission which focuses on the representations of objects reproduced by optical means on film, electronic display devices, or other media.

Pararescue Jumper Combat Rescue Exfiltration. The removal of personnel from areas under enemy control by specially trained personnel qualified to penetrate to the site of an incident by land or parachute, render medical aid, accomplish survival methods, and rescue survivors.

Pararescue Jumper Combat Rescue Infiltration. The movement through or into an area or territory occupied by either friendly or enemy troops or organizations specially trained personnel qualified to penetrate to the site of an incident by land or parachute, render medical aid, accomplish survival methods, and rescue survivors.

Personnel Recovery. The combat rescue coverage capable of recovering personnel wherever and whenever it is necessary to ensure commanders can pursue national interests with negligible political or military risk from the possibility of isolated or captured personnel.
Psychological Operations. Planned psychological activities designed to influence attitudes and behavior affecting the achievement of political and military objectives.
Reconnaissance Attack Interface. An aerial mission, which serves as an interface between recce missions prior to attack.
Armed Road Recce. An aerial mission with the primary purpose of locating and attacking targets of opportunity such as enemy troop movements along lines of communication.

Reconnaissance. A mission undertaken to obtain, by visual observation or other detection methods, information about the activities and resources of an enemy or potential enemy, or to secure data concerning the meteorological, hydrographic, or geographic characteristics of a particular area.
Air Reconnaissance. The collection of information of intelligence interest either by visual observation from the air or through the use of airborne sensors.
Reconnaissance, DoD Theater. Reconnaissance conducted by aircraft assets belonging to theater or Joint Force Commanders.
Reconnaissance, National. Reconnaissance conducted by overhead satellites.
Reserve. A force held to counter unforeseen situations or to impact on future events.
Rescue. The use of aircraft, surface craft (land or water), submarines, specialized rescue teams, and equipment to rescue personnel in distress on land or at sea.

Rescue Combat Air Patrol. An aircraft patrol provided over a combat search and rescue objective area for the purpose of intercepting and destroying hostile aircraft. Its primary mission is to protect the search and rescue task forces during recovery operations.
Radar Scope. An aerial mission, which focuses on conducting surveillance operations using radar scopes to collect information.
Strategic Attack. Any long range air operation meant to strike an enemy at the sources of its military, economic, or political power.

Special Assignment Airlift Mission. An aerial mission which focuses on specific airlift requirements, that requires special consideration due to the number of passengers involved, weight or size of cargo, urgency of movement, sensitivity, or other valid factors that preclude the use of channel airlift.
Strategic Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on long range airdrop operations, meant to strike an enemy at the sources of its military, economic, or political power.

Strategic Aeromedical Evacuation. The phase of evacuation which provides airlift for patients from overseas areas or from a theater of active operations to the home base, to other countries or to a temporary safe area.
Strategic Airlift. The carriage of passengers and cargo between theatres by means of: a. scheduled service; b. special flight; c. air logistic support; d. aeromedical evacuation.
Special Air Operation. An operation, conducted at any level of conflict, in support of unconventional warfare and clandestine, covert, and psychological activities.
Search and Rescue. The use of aircraft, surface craft (land or water), submarines, specialized rescue teams, and equipment to search for and rescue personnel in distress on land or at sea.
Reconnaissance Strike Control and Reconnaissance (SCAR). An aerial mission to conduct reconnaissance strike control and reconnaissance.
Search. An air reconnaissance by one or more aircraft dispatched to locate an object or objects known or suspected to be in a specific area.
Suppression Enemy Air Defense. An aerial mission conducted to neutralize, destroy, or temporarily degrade surface-based enemy air defenses by destructive and/or disruptive means.
Searching Fire. Fire distributed in depth by successive changes in the elevation of the gun.
Security. The measures necessary to achieve protection against espionage, sabotage, subversion, and terrorism, as well as against loss or unauthorized disclosure.
Shadowing. To observe and maintain contact (not necessarily continuously) with a unit or force.
Side Looking Airborne Radar. An aerial mission which focuses on an airborne radar, viewing at right angles to the axis of the vehicle, which produces a presentation of terrain or moving targets.
Side Looking Radar. An aerial mission which focuses on the use of a radar, viewing at right angles to the axis of the vehicle, which produces a presentation of terrain or moving targets.
Support Mission. This mission type includes movement of personnel or equipment other than via tactical airlift, security services missions, UHF relay, etc.

Special Operations Forces. Those active and reserve component forces of the military services designated by the Secretary of Defense and specifically organized, trained, and equipped to conduct and support special operations.

Special Operations. Military activities conducted by specially designated, organized, trained and equipped forces using operational techniques and modes of employment not standard to conventional forces. These activities are conducted across the full range of military operations independently or in coordination with operations of conventional forces to achieve political, military, psychological, and economic objectives. Politico-military considerations may require clandestine, covert, or discrete techniques and the acceptance of a degree of physical and political risk not associated with conventional operations.
Special. An aerial mission which may be further described in a free-text set.
Sensor Implant. An aerial mission, which focuses on operations where aircraft are tasked to airdrop sensors over a given geographic area.
Surface Combat Air Patrol (SUCAP). Combat air patrol flown in support of surface vessels conducting maritime operations.
Support. The action of a force, or portion thereof, which aids, protects, complements, or sustains any other force.

Air Surveillance. The systematic observation of airspace by electronic, visual, or other means, primarily for the purpose of identifying and determining the movements of aircraft and missiles, friendly and enemy, in the airspace under observation.
Fighter Sweep. An aerial offensive mission conducted by fighter aircraft to seek out and destroy enemy aircraft or targets of opportunity in an allotted area of operations.
Tactical Aircraft Coordinator (Airborne). An officer who coordinates, from an aircraft, the actions of other aircraft engaged in air support of ground or sea forces.
Tactical Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on airdrop of troops or cargo into a hostile environment.
Tactical Aeromedical Evacuation. The phase of evacuation which provides airlift for patients from the combat zone to points outside the combat zone and between points within the communication zone.

Theater Airlift. That airlift assigned or attached to a Combatant Commander other than Commander, U.S. Transportation Command, that provides air movement and delivery of personnel and equipment directly into objective areas through air landing, airdrop, extraction, or other delivery techniques; and the air logistic support of all theater forces, including those engaged in combat operations, to meet specific theater objectives and requirements.
Tactical Airland (Assault). An aerial mission, which focuses on cargo and/or passengers delivered by air-landing the aircraft.
Tactical Air Reconnaissance (Maritime). An aerial mission, which focuses on, short range reconnaissance conducted by maritime assets.
Tactical Electronic Reconnaissance. An aerial mission, which focuses on short range collection of data on electronic emitters.

Tactical Air Reconnaissance (Land). The use of air vehicles to obtain information concerning terrain, weather, and the disposition, composition, movement, installations, lines of Communications, electronic and communication emissions of enemy forces.  also included are artillery and naval gunfire adjustment, and systematic and random observation of ground battle areas, targets, and/or sectors of airspace.
Operational Training. Training that develops, maintains or improves the operational readiness of individuals or units.

Television. An aerial mission which focuses on an electronic system of transmitting transient images of fixed or moving objects together with sound over a wire or through space by apparatus that converts light and sound into electrical waves and reconverts them into visible light rays and audible sound.
Utility Flight. An aerial mission in which the aircraft has the capability of performing multiple missions.

Unconventional Warfare. General term used to describe operations conducted for military, political, or economic purposes within an area occupied by the enemy and making use of the local inhabitants and resources.
Very Important Person (VIP) Lift. An aerial mission, which focuses on the air transport of high ranking and/or important individuals.
Visual. An aerial mission which focuses on primarily one of visual observation.
Weather. The mission is primarily for the purpose of collecting weather data.

Weather Reconnaissance (Recce). An aerial mission to obtain, by visual observation or other detection methods, information concerning the meteorological or hydrographic characteristics of a particular area.

Airborne Alert Reconnaissance Strike Control and Reconnaissance (SCAR). A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to conduct reconnaissance Strike Control and Reconnaissance (SCAR) operations.

Airborne Alert Suppression Enemy Air Defense (SEAD). A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform SEAD operations.

Advisory Control. The controlling unit will provide adequate warnings of hazards affecting aircraft safety. The aircraft commander is responsible for the aircraft’s navigation and collision avoidance. For further U.S. implementation guidance, see Repository of USMTF Program Items Document, item 388.

Broadcast Control. The controlling unit will provide adequate warnings of hazards affecting aircraft safety. The aircraft commander is responsible for the aircraft’s navigation and collision avoidance. For further U.S. implementation guidance, see Repository of USMTF Program Items Document, item 388.

Close Control. A form of aircraft mission control in which the aircraft is continuously controlled, for altitude, speed and heading, to a position from which the mission can be accomplished. The controlling unit will advise the aircraft commander of the current tactical picture and will provide further advice if and when available. For further U.S. implementation guidance, see Repository of USMTF Program Items Document, item 388.

Close-Advisory Control. A form of aircraft mission control in which aircraft is continuously controlled, for altitude, speed and heading, to a position from which the mission can be accomplished. The controlling unit will provide adequate warnings of hazards affecting aircraft safety. The aircraft’s commander is responsible for the aircraft’s navigation and collision avoidance. For further U.S. implementation guidance, see Repository of USMTF Program Items Document, item 388.

Close-Positive Control. A form of aircraft mission control in which the aircraft is continuously controlled, for altitude, speed and heading, to a position from which the mission can be accomplished. The controlling unit will advise the aircraft commander of the current tactical picture and will provide further advice if and when available. The controlling unit is responsible for taking actions for collision avoidance, such as ordering the necessary alterations to heading, speed and altitude to maintain separation criteria. For further U.S. implementation guidance, see Repository of USMTF Program Items Document, item 388.

Loose Control. A form of aircraft mission control in which the aircraft commander selects his own speed, altitude, heading and the appropriate tactics required to accomplish the assigned task. The controlling unit will advise the aircraft commander of the current tactical picture and will provide further advice if and when available. For further U.S. implementation guidance, see Repository of USMTF Program Items Document, item 388.

Loose-Advisory Control. A form of aircraft mission control in which the aircraft commander selects his own speed, altitude, heading and the appropriate tactics required to accomplish the assigned task. The controlling unit will advise the aircraft commander of the current tactical picture and will provide further advice if and when available. The controlling unit will provide adequate warnings of hazards affecting aircraft safety. The aircraft commander is responsible for the aircraft’s navigation and collision avoidance. For further U.S. implementation guidance, see Repository of USMTF Program Items Document, item 388.

Loose-Positive Control. A form of aircraft mission control in which the aircraft commander selects his own speed, altitude, heading and the appropriate tactics required to accomplish the assigned task. The controlling unit will advise the aircraft commander of the current tactical picture and will provide further advice if and when available. Beacons. Rotating lights located in the general vicinity of the control tower.

Taxiway Lights. Lights placed on both sides of the taxi route to be followed, or on both sides and down the center of the route.

En Route Onload. En route onload (other than initial onload).

Aerial Refueling. Refueling aircraft in flight, which extends presence, increases range, and serves as a force multiplier. May include bladder drop and refuel operations.
Aeromedical Evacuation. The movement of patients under medical supervision to and between medical treatment facilities by air transportation.
Container Delivery System. An aerial mission, which focuses on the use of a system where containers are airdropped into a forward operating location.

Contingency. An aerial emergency mission involving military force caused by natural disasters, terrorists, subversives, or by required military operations. Due to the uncertainty of the situation, contingencies require plans, rapid response, and special procedures to ensure the safety and readiness of personnel, installations, and equipment.
Distinguished Visitor Support. Air operations where military aircraft are used to transport distinguished visitors.

Exercise. A military maneuver or simulated wartime operation involving planning, preparation, and execution. It is carried out for the purpose of training and evaluation. It may be a combined, joint, or single-service exercise, depending on participating organizations.
Functional Check Flight. A flight conducted to confirm operational readiness of the flight crew or aircraft.

Ground Alert Aerial Refueling. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform aerial refueling operations.

Ground Alert. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order.

Ground Alert Strategic Airlift. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform strategic airlift operations. See strategic airlift.

Ground Alert Theater Airlift. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform theater airlift operations. See theater airlift.
Heavy Equipment Airdrop. An aerial mission to unload heavy equipment from an aircraft in flight.

Joint Airborne Air Transportability Training. Training operations or exercises involving airborne and appropriate troop carrier units. This training includes: a. air delivery of personnel and equipment; b. assault operations by airborne troops and/or air transportable units; c. loading exercises and local orientation fights of short duration; and d. maneuvers and/or exercises as agreed upon by services concerned and/or as authorized by the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Low Altitude Parachute Extraction System. An aerial mission which focuses on the use of self-contained system capable of a low-level delivering, heavy loads into an area where air landing is not feasible from an optimum aircraft wheel altitude of 5 to 10 feet above ground level. One or more platforms may be dropped.
Other. Indicates the mission is something other than any of the missions listed. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Personnel Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on the delivery of personnel from an aircraft in flight.

Special Assignment Airlift Mission. An aerial mission which focuses on specific airlift requirements, that requires special consideration due to the number of passengers involved, weight or size of cargo, urgency of movement, sensitivity, or other valid factors that preclude the use of channel airlift.
Strategic Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on long range airdrop operations, meant to strike an enemy at the sources of its military, economic, or political power.
Strategic Airlift. The carriage of passengers and cargo between theatres by means of: a. scheduled service; b. special flight; c. air logistic support; d. aeromedical evacuation.
Special. An aerial mission which may be further described in a free-text set.
Support. The action of a force, or portion thereof, which aids, protects, complements, or sustains any other force.
Tactical Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on airdrop of troops or cargo into a hostile environment.

Theater Airlift. That airlift assigned or attached to a Combatant Commander other than Commander, US Transportation Command, that provides air movement and delivery of personnel and equipment directly into objective areas through air landing, airdrop, extraction, or other delivery techniques; and the air logistic support of all theater forces, including those engaged in combat operations, to meet specific theater objectives and requirements.
Tactical Airland (Assault). An aerial mission, which focuses on cargo and/or passengers delivered by air-landing the aircraft.
Operational Training. Training that develops, maintains or improves the operational readiness of individuals or units.

Airborne Alert Aerial Refueling. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform aerial refueling operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Combat Air Patrol. An aircraft patrol provided over an objective area, the force protected, the critical area of a combat zone, or in an air defense area, for the purpose of intercepting and destroying hostile aircraft before they reach their targets. (JP 3-52)
Close Air Support Area. Airspace designated for holding orbits and used by rotary- and fixed-wing aircraft that are in close proximity to friendly forces. (JP 3-52)
Drop Zone. A specific area upon which airborne troops, equipment, or supplies are airdropped. (JP 3-52)
Electronic Combat. Airspace established specifically for aircraft engaging in electronic combat. (AJP-3.3.5)
Low-Level Transit Route. A temporary corridor of defined dimensions established in the forward area to minimize risk to friendly aircraft from friendly air defenses or surface forces. (AJP-3.3.5)
Landing Zone. Any specified zone used for the landing of aircraft. (JP 3-52)

Minimum-Risk Route. A temporary corridor of defined dimensions recommended for use by high-speed, fixed-wing aircraft that presents the minimum known hazards to low-flying aircraft transiting the combat zone. (JP 3-52)
Reconnaissance Area. Airspace established specifically for aircraft conducting reconnaissance. (AJP 3.3.5)

Standard Use Army Aircraft Flight Route. Route established below the coordination level to facilitate the movement of Army aviation assets. It is normally located in the corps through brigade rear areas of operation and does not require approval by the airspace control authority. (JP 3-52)
Special Corridor. In air operations, an air corridor established to accommodate the special routing requirements of specific missions. (AJP-3.3.5)
Special Operations Force Area. Airspace of defined dimensions established specifically for special operations forces missions by special operations forces airspace planners. (JP 3-52)
Surface-to-Surface Munitions. Airspace of defined dimensions established specifically for surface-to-surface munitions route of flight and launch and impact points. (JP 3-52)
Surface-to-Surface Missile System. Airspace defined specifically for Army Tactical Missile System and Tomahawk Land Attack Missile route of flight and launch and impact points. (JP 3-52)
Transit Corridor. A bi-directional corridor established in the rear area to route aircraft through air defenses, in the rear area, where appropriate, with minimum risk. (AJP-3.3.5)

Temporary Minimum Risk Route. A temporary route of defined dimensions established to route air traffic between transit routes or the rear boundary of the forward area and their operations area in direct support of ground operations. (AJP-3.3.5).

Transit Route. In air operations, a temporary corridor of defined dimensions established in the forward area to minimize the risks to friendly aircraft from friendly air defenses or surface forces. (AAP-06)

Unmanned Aircraft Area. Airspace of defined dimensions created specifically for unmanned aircraft operations. Generally, this airspace will consist of the area in which unmanned aircraft missions are conducted, not en route airspace. (JP 3-52)

Amphibious/Marines. A military force associated with naval forces of a country intended for land warfare through landing type operations.
