Army. The Army is the largest administrative and tactical organization capable of independent operations. It consists of two or more Corps, service and support units, and may include other separate tactical organizations including divisions and combat units. (In the zone of the interior an army area may be administered by a numbered army headquarters, which is charged primarily with recruiting, equipping, and training reserve personnel and units.)

Army Group. The army group is organized to direct the strategic and tactical operations of two or more field armies and supporting units. May consist of field armies as well as separate corps and/or divisions.

Brigade. An army unit usually smaller than a division to which are attached groups, regiments, and/or battalions and smaller units tailored to meet anticipated requirements. Equates to the combat command of an armored division.

Battalion. A tactical and administrative unit consisting of two or more companies or batteries, normally subordinate to a group, regiment, or brigade, but may be employed separately, operating as an independent unit.

Border District Headquarters. A territorial command or headquarters of the former USSR organized along the frontier and under the control of the main directorate of border troops or the Committee of State Security.
Battery. A tactical and administrative artillery unit usually equating to a company or similar unit.

Command. A regional or area command (as a Military District Command) which is configured and manned in accordance with an official authorization or directive. May also be an organizational or unit Command (as a logistics Command) which is part of a superior organization.
Company. The basic administrative and tactical unit in most army ground forces, on a command level below a battalion and above a platoon. It is usually equivalent to a battery of artillery.

Corps. A unit organized to operate tactically as part of a field army, or tactically and administratively as a separate or independent Corps. Consists of two or more divisions, service and support units, and may include other separate tactical organizations (such as separate brigades, armored cavalry regiments, etc.). (in the zone of the interior of a corps area, which is usually part of an army area, may be administered by a corps headquarters which is charged primarily with recruiting, equipping, and training reserve personnel and units.)
Detachment. Part of a unit separated from its main organization for duty elsewhere--may be any independent unit so designated.

Division. In the U.S. Army the division is the basic self-contained tactical and administrative ground combat unit. Usually the subordinate echelon of a Corps, it consists of two or more regiments plus service and supporting units.
Front. Used in conjunction with ground forces of the former USSR.
Group. An administrative and tactical unit consisting of two or more battalions. Usually smaller than a regiment or brigade and may be subordinate to either.
Group of Forces. Used in conjunction with ground forces of the former USSR.
Group of Fronts. Used in conjunction with ground forces of the former USSR.
Komendatura. A tactical unit of the former USSR with a strength varying from 200- 500 men. Subordinate to the Otryad.
Major Fleet. Permanent organization of ships, aircraft, marines, and shore-based support activities under a single command exercising both operational and administrative control.
Naval Detachment. A part of a naval organization that is separated from its main organization for special duty elsewhere.
Naval Division. A number of naval ships (two or more) of similar type grouped together for operational and administrative control.

Naval Force. A major subdivision or task force of a numbered fleet, consisting of ships, marines, aircraft, or a combination thereof. Naval forces do not ordinarily have their own shore establishments.

Naval Group. A flexible administrative or tactical organization composed of two or more squadrons of ships, but not necessarily ships of the same type. A naval group may be a subdivision of a naval force.
Naval Section. A tactical subdivision of a naval division of ships. It is normally one-half of a division of ships.
Naval Squadron. An organizational element consisting of two or more divisions of ships and assigned tenders. It is normally, but not necessarily, composed of ships of the same type.
National Defense Headquarters. The highest echelon in a national government exercising command control over a nation's military establishment.

Numbered Fleet. A major tactical command immediately subordinate to a major fleet Command and comprised of various task forces, groups, and support elements for the purpose of prosecuting specific naval operations.
Otryad. A regimental-size unit of the former USSR directly subordinate to the Border District Headquarters.
Platoon. A tactical unit usually subordinate to a company or battery.

Patrol. A tactical unit designed for a specific mission or purpose, and sometimes organized officially by an authorized table of organization. May be subordinate to a platoon, company, or battalion. The size varies with the mission or purpose for which organized.
Regiment. An administrative and tactical unit on a level of command that is usually below a division or brigade and above a battalion.
Section. A tactical unit usually smaller than a platoon and larger than a squad. In some organizations the section, rather than the squad, is the basic tactical unit.
Squadron. A tactical and administrative unit usually equating to a battalion, and composed of two or more troops (units).
Squad. A small, basic, tactical unit usually subordinate to a platoon.

Theater Army. A Theater Army is the senior army headquarters in a theater of operations. In a theater where the forces of a single nation comprise the theater command, the Theater Army is the senior headquarters and is charged with the command and control of all army elements in the theater. When the theater is organized as a combined command, the Theater Army of a nation becomes the senior administrative headquarters in the theater for that nation's forces only.
Troop. A subordinate tactical and administrative unit of a cavalry squadron, equivalent to a company or battery.
Task Element. A component of a task group organized to accomplish a specific task.
Task Force. A component of a fleet organization by the commander of a task fleet or higher authority for accomplishment of a specific task or tasks.
Task Group. A component of a naval task force organized by the Commander of a task force or higher authority.
Task Unit. A component of a task element.
Zastrova. Basic operational unit of the former USSR border troops, with a strength from 30-65 men, subordinate to the Komendatura.
Antiair Warfare. A unit organized for antiair warfare.
Airborne Commando. A commando unit with an airmobile capability.
Air Defense. A unit of artillery anti-aircraft artillery weapons and fire control equipment employed in engaging air targets from the ground.
Air Cavalry. A cavalry unit specially equipped to combine movement by air with reconnaissance in depth. (Also see Cavalry, below.)
Amphibious. An infantry assault unit organized, equipped, and trained for amphibious operations.
Amphibious Tank. A unit of heavily-armored vehicles designed to carry out a combat mission on land or water.
Armored Cavalry. An armored cavalry unit.
Armor. A unit of combat tanks and armored motor vehicles heavily protected with metal plates.
Army Aviation. A ground unit of organic aviation limited to fixed and rotary-wing, light aircraft, such as liaison and observation types, which are dedicated to ground support.
Anti-Tank. A unit trained and equipped for operations against armored vehicles.
Biological Ordnance Capable Unit. A unit capable of delivering biological ordnance on a target.
Cavalry. A unit moving in lightly armored vehicles and structured primarily to perform ground reconnaissance and security missions. (Also see Air Cavalry, above.)
Chemical. A unit employing chemical and/or biological agents to prosecute warfare. Performs massive decontamination functions as required by the tactical situation.
Combat Service Support. A combat service support unit.
Composite Warfare Commander. The command directing Naval warfare areas in a naval task force.
Dismounted Cavalry. A cavalry unit that fights as foot infantry.
Engineer. A unit that accomplishes major construction, demolition, and extensive camouflage projects.
Electronic Support Measures. A unit capable of performing electronic support measures.
Electronic Warfare. A unit having multiple/general electronic warfare capability.
EW Coordinator. The command directing electronic warfare in a Naval task force.
Field Artillery. A unit or artillery mounted on carriages and mobile enough to accompany infantry or armored units in the field.
Frog SSM Unit. A unit equipped with Frog SSM.
Gun-Howitzer. An artillery unit having gun-howitzers as principal weapons. Usually part of tube artillery units of regimental size.

Infantry. A unit consisting primarily of foot soldiers. The basic infantry mission is to close with and destroy the opposition by fire, maneuver, and shock effect. Mobility may be increased by the use of motorized or mechanized equipment for transport.
Infantry On Foot. An infantry unit moving primarily on foot, and equipped with a minimum of vehicles.
Medical Air Evac Unit. Treatment and/or medical evacuation unit.
Medical. A unit that provides medical treatment and/or medical evacuation services.
Mining. A unit organized for mine laying or mine clearing.
Mortar. An artillery unit having mortars as principal weapons. May be organic part of larger infantry or artillery unit.
Military Police. A military police unit.
Motorized Rifle Troops. An infantry unit whose organic motorized vehicles and armor facilitate attack from march column.
Nuclear Ordnance Capable Unit. A unit capable of delivering nuclear ordnance on a target.
Ordnance. A unit responsible for the supply and maintenance of weapons, weapon system components, ammunition, and related equipment.
Picket. A ship or ships accomplishing picket duty.
Ranger. Similar to Commando unit in training but usually employed in hit-run raids.
Surface-to-Air Missile. A unit organized and equipped to perform air defense missions by employing surface-launched missiles against hostile aircraft and missiles.
Sapper (Mine). A unit responsible for infiltration operations involving use of satchel charges, mines, and small arms.
Scud SSM Unit. A unit equipped with Scud SSM.

Signal/Electronic. A unit that provides communication electronic support for forces in the field. Constructs communication lines and terminals. Installs and maintains early warning and target acquisition radar.

Special Forces. A unit organized into small multipurpose detachments designed to organize, train, supply, direct, and control indigenous forces in guerrilla and counter-insurgency operations, and to conduct unconventional warfare operations.

Supply. A unit that procures, stores, and distributes supplies and equipment necessary for the maintenance and operations of military organizations. It usually handles two or more classes of supplies.
Surveillance. A unit organized for surveillance.
Service. A unit providing supply, maintenance, transport, evacuation, medical, and other services.
Tactical Missiles. A unit organized primarily to launch independent tactical (short-range) missile attacks or to furnish nuclear fires in support of ground operations.

Damage Avoidance Area. An area in which undesirable materiel damage or personnel casualties produced by the effects of friendly nuclear weapons are to be avoided.
Fire Coordination Area. An area with specified restraints into which fires in excess of those restraints will not be delivered without approval of the authority establishing the restraints.

Forward Edge of the Battle Area. The foremost limits of a series of areas in which ground combat units are deployed, excluding the areas in which the covering forces are operating, designated to coordinate fire support, the positioning of forces or the maneuver of units.
Free Fire Area. Message used to delineate a specific, designated area into which any weapon system may fire without additional coordination from the establishing HQ. (US only)
Forward Line of Own Troops. A line which indicates the most forward positions of the friendly forces in any kind of military operation at a specific time.
Fire Support Area (Naval). A sea area assigned to a fire support unit or individual fire support ship in which to operate when executing fire support missions.

Fire Support Coordination Line. Message used to designate a line beyond which all targets may be attacked by any weapon system (including aircraft and special weapons), without endangering or requiring additional coordination with establishing headquarters. (NATO/US use)
Fire Support Station (Naval). A point within a fire support area where a fire support ship would be stopped for conduct of Naval Surface Fire (NSF).
Line of Departure. A line parallel with the beach (off-shore) which marks the beginning of the boat lanes for an amphibious assault.
Mined Area. An area declared dangerous due to the presence of mines.
Minefield. In land warfare, an area of ground containing mines laid with or without a pattern. in naval warfare, an area of water containing mines laid with or without a pattern.
No Fire Area. Message used to delineate an area into which no fire or effects of fire are allowed. (US only)

No Fire Line. A line short of which artillery or ships do not fire except on request or approval of the supported commander, but beyond which they may fire at any time without danger to friendly troops. (NATO only)

Restrictive Fire Area. Message used to delineate an area in which specific restrictions are imposed and into which fires that exceed those restrictions will not be delivered without coordination with establishing HQ. (US only)

Restrictive Fire Line. Message used to define a line established between converging friendly forces, one or both may be moving, that prohibits fires or effects from fires across the line without coordination with the affected force. (US only)
Target Area. An area designated and numbered for future firing.
Zone of Fire. An area within which a designated ground unit or fire support ship delivers, or is prepared to deliver, fire support. Fire may or may not be observed.
Boulder. A detached, rounded rock, 256 mm or more in diameter.
Clay. An aggregate of unconsolidated, flat, and extremely fine particles of mineral matter less than 0.005 mm in diameter. Commonly sticky and slippery when wet.
Cobble. Rounded rocks ranging from 76 to 256 mm in diameter.
Coral. The calcareous skeletons of various forms of marine life.
Gravel. An aggregate of loose pieces of rock ranging from 5 to 76 mm in diameter.
Mud. A fine grained, fluid to plastic mixture of clay and/or silt and water which forms a wet, soft, sticky earth. Sometimes contains sand and/or organic materials.
Pebbles. Usually smooth and rounded small stones ranging from 5 to 76 mm in diameter.
Rock. A consolidated, coherent and relatively hard, naturally formed mass of mineral matter. Also an aggregate of angular pieces of stone larger than 76 mm in diameter.

Sand. A soil which is loose and single-grained, with individual grains ranging in size from 0.07 to 5 mm. Individual grains can readily be seen or felt. Squeezed when dry, the soil will fall apart. Squeezed when moist, the soil will form a cast, but the cast, but the cast will crumble when touched.
Shell. A hard ridged outer covering of an invertebrate marine animal.
Shingle. Larger and coarser than gravel. The space between fragments is not filled with finer materials.
Silt. A loose, fine sediment of natural mineral grains ranging from 0.005 to 0.07 mm in diameter, which lacks plasticity and has little or no cohesion when dry.
Volcanic Ash. Fine particles of lava (sand size) resembling ash which are ejected from volcanoes. Particles range from 0.25 to 5 mm in diameter.
Irregular. A beach whose contour is uneven and may be a combination of straight, convex, and/or concave contours.

Plunging. The wave crest advances so much faster at the base of the wave that it calls almost into the trough with a violent action. The resulting foam appears almost instantly over the complete front. At times, air is caught in the breaker as it tumbles forward, creating a type of explosion.
Spilling. The waves becomes unstable at the crest and forms white water at the crest. The white water (foam) expands slowly down the front face of the breaker. Breaking action is mild.

Surging. The wave crest tends to advance faster than the base of the wave, suggesting the information of a plunging breaker. However, just before breaking completely, the wave base advances faster than the crest and the plunging is arrested. These are generally found at a steep gradient.

Arch Bridge. A structure supported by an arch or series of arches, with the roadway passing through or over the arch. A fixed arch type is constructed without hinges (i.e., the ends are rigidly anchored at the abutments).  A hinged arch type has in its design one or more hinges permitting movement through the joint.

Beam Bridge. A short span bridge, always deck type, with steel, concrete, or timberbeams extending between abutments or piers. Since this type of construction is under the deck of the bridge and cannot be seen from overhead imagery, it is grouped with girder types(i.e., beam/girder).
Cable Bridge. One in which planking can be easily emplaced or removed from a close series of cables spanning a depression or obstacle.
Cantilever Bridge. A structure of which one portion acts as an anchorage for sustaining another portion which projects beyond the supporting pier.
Deck Bridge. One in which the floor system is supported on or near the top of the trusses or girders with no more than a guardrail at the sides.
Foot Bridge. One that spans a depression or obstacle, suitable only for human or animal foot traffic.

Girder Bridge. A bridge in which the main support is provided by girders. It may be either through or deck construction, and is usually described in terms of the girder type used (i.e., plate, lattice, etc.)  Since this type construction is under the deck of the bridge and cannot be seen from overhead imagery, it is grouped with girder types (i.e., beam/girder).
Mixed Bridge. Normally a multispan structure consisting of two or more span types.
Movable Bascule Bridge. One which moves in a vertical plane, rotating about a horizontal axis (trunnion type), or rolling back from the opening (rolling-lift type).

Movable Retractable Bridge. One which has a span capable of being retracted to a position normally atop the roadbed of the adjoining fixed span. These are most commonly associated with railroad bridges.

Movable Swing Bridge. One which revolves horizontally and generally consists of two or more plate girders or trusses supported on a pier in such a way that they can be rotated on a circular track or pivot resting on or attached to the pier.
Movable Vert-Lift Bridge. One in which a span can be raised vertically to allow vessels to pass underneath.
Pontoon Bridge. A temporary bridge which is supported by light, flat-bottom boats or floats.
See Remarks. Enter this code when the bridge or ferry is not covered by a type.
Suspension Bridge. One with a roadway suspended from two or more cables passing over towers and securely anchored at the ends.
Tramway. One that has a rail for a tramcar.
Trestle. A beam bridge supported by bents or towers, commonly used with railroads.
Truss Bridge. One in which the roadway loads are transmitted from the floor to the abutments or piers by means of trusses, usually one along each side.

Logistics Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Landing Zone. A specified zone used for the landing of aircraft and/or helicopters.
Mined Area. An area declared dangerous due to the presence of mines.
Minefield. In land warfare, an area of ground containing mines laid with or without a pattern. In naval warfare, an area of water containing mines laid with or without a pattern.
Missile Engagement Zone. A zone that has been designated for missile firings at specific targets.
No Fire Area. Message used to delineate an area into which no fire or effects of fire are allowed. (US only)

Objective. The physical object of the action taken. (For example, a definite terrain feature, the seizure and/or holding of which is essential to the commander's plan, or to the destruction of an enemy force without regard to terrain features.)
Potential Evasion Locale. Country-specified geographical locales which have been surveyed and categorized relative to successful evasion potential during wartime operations.
Pickup Zone. A zone that has been designated for aircraft or helicopters to pick up personnel or other objects.
Restrictive Fire Plan. Airspace established for friendly aircraft, by a restrictive fire plan, that is reasonably safe from friendly surface-delivered nonnuclear fires.

Restrictive Fire Area. Message used to delineate an area in which specific restrictions are imposed and into which fires that exceed those restrictions will not be delivered without coordination with establishing HQ. (US only)
Restricted Fire Plan. An area through which an aircraft can fly and avoid artillery.
Selected Area for Evasion. A designated area in hostile territory that offers the evader or escapee a reasonable chance of avoiding capture and of surviving until evacuated.
Search and Rescue Area. An area established for search and rescue missions.
Sector. An area designated by boundaries within which a unit operates and for which it is responsible.
Staging Area. An area designated for use by a unit for resupply, assembly of forces, etc.
Target Area. An area designated and numbered for future firing.
Exercise Area. An area established for use during an operational exercise.
Zone of Fire. An area within which a designated ground unit or fire support ship delivers, or is prepared to deliver, fire support. Fire may or may not be observed.

Visually Estimated Above 1600 Meters. Visual estimate is that base of lowest cloud is above 1600 meters.
No Clouds. The sky is clear.
Searchlight or Laser Estimated Above 1600 Meters. The base of the lowest cloud observed by searchlight or laser is above 1600 meters.
Unreliable Searchlight or Laser Observation. Searchlight or laser observations are unreliable.
Searchlight or Laser No Cloud. No cloud has been detected by searchlight or laser.
Balloon Loss Above 1600 Meters. The height of the base of the lowest cloud in which a balloon was lost was above 1600 meters.
Unreliable Balloon Observation. Balloon observations are unreliable.
Altocumulus. A fleecy cloud formation consisting of large whitish globular cloudlets with shaded portions.
Altostratus. A cloud formation similar to cirrostratus but darker and at a lower level.
Cumulonimbus. A cumulus cloud spread out in the shape of an anvil extending to great heights.
Cirrocumulus. A cloud form of small rounded masses at high altitude usually in regular groupings forming a mackerel sky.
Cirrus. A small white cloud of minute ice crystals formed at altitudes of 20,000 to 40,000 ft.
Cirrostratus. A uniform layer of high stratus cloud form.
Cumulus. A massive cloud form having a flat base and rounded outlines.
Nimbostratus. A low dark gray rainy cloud layer.
Stratocumulus. Rolls of dark cloud which often cover the whole sky especially in winter.
Stratus. A cloud form of greater horizontal extension and comparatively lower altitude (2000 to 7000 ft) than the cumulostratus or cirrostratus.
Circle. Each pair of grid ref define the center of a circle (first point) and one point on the radius of this circle (second point).
Corridor. A series of points with an equal width either side of center line.
Area Reference System Grid. An area reference system grid, for example, Global Area Reference System (GARS).
Line. Sequence of grid ref describes a line from rear to front and from left to right facing the front.
Orbit. The orbit is maintained with either left or right turns to stay within the space allotted.
Point. Each grid ref is displayed as a dot.

Polyarc. The first point is the point of origin followed by a radius with a beginning and ending radial measured in true bearing. This forms the arc. The polygon portion is drawn with a sequence of points that are to be plotted clockwise.
Polygon. A polygon contains at least three sides and drawn clockwise. The first point and the last point are the same. The last point may be omitted but is understood to enclose the polygon.
Radarc. The first point is the point of origin followed by an inner radius (may be equal to "0") and an outer radius. The beginning and ending radials are measured in true bearing.
Track. Similar to a corridor except the width can vary on either side of center line and each leg can have a separate altitude/altitude block.

Control of Aircraft in the Specified Mission and the Network Enabled Weapons (NEW) On Board the Aircraft. The tasked control agency has responsibility for controlling both the aircraft and the Network Enabled Weapons (NEW) onboard the aircraft for the assigned mission being controlled.

Airspace Coordination Area. A Fire Support Coordination Measure that defines a three-dimensional block of airspace in a target area, established by the appropriate ground commander, in which friendly aircraft are reasonably safe from friendly surface fires. (JP 3-52)
Air Control Point. An Air Reference Measure that identifies a point that is defined and used for navigation, command and control, and communications. (AJP-3.3.5)

Air Defense Identification Zone. An Air Defense Measure that defines an airspace of defined dimensions within which the ready identification, location, and control of airborne vehicles are required. (JP 3-52)
Advisory Route. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines a designated route along which air traffic advisory services is available. (AJP-3.3.5)

Amphibious Defense Zone. A Maritime Defense Measure that defines the area encompassing the amphibious objective area and the adjoining airspace required by accompanying naval forces for the purpose of air defense. (JP 3-52)

Air Corridor. An Airspace Coordinating Measure that defines a restricted air route of travel specified for use by friendly aircraft established for the purpose of preventing friendly aircraft from being fired upon by friendly forces. (JP 3-52)

Alert Area. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines an airspace that may contain a high volume of pilot training activities or an unusual type of aerial activity, neither of which is hazardous to aircraft. (JP 3-52)
Altitude Reservation. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines a block of altitude reserved for aircraft to transit or loiter. (AJP-3.3.5)

Amphibious Objective Area. A Maneuver Control Measure that defines a geographical area (delineated for command and control purposes in the initiating directive) within which is located the objective(s) to be secured by the amphibious force. This area must be of sufficient size to ensure accomplishment of the amphibious force’s mission and must provide sufficient area for conducting necessary sea, air, and land operations. (JP 3-52)
Approach Corridor. A Maritime Defense Measure that defines an airspace established for the safe passage of land based aircraft joining or departing a maritime force. (AJP-3.3.5)
Airway. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines a control area or portion thereof established in the form of a corridor equipped with radio navigational aids. (AAP-06)

Base Defense Zone. An Air Defense Measure that defines an air defense zone established around an air base and limited to the engagement envelope of short-range air defense weapons systems defending that base. Base defense zones have specific entry, exit, and identification, friend or foe procedures established. (JP 3-52)

Boundary. A Maneuver Control Measure that defines a line that delineates surface areas for the purpose of facilitating coordination and deconfliction of operations between adjacent units, formations, or areas. (JP 3-52)
Bullseye. An Air Reference Measure that defines an established reference point from which the position of an object can be referenced. (JP 3-52)
Buffer Zone. An Air Reference Measure that defines an airspace designed specifically to provide a buffer between various airspace coordinating measures. (JP 3-52)
Coordinating Altitude. An Airspace Coordinating Measure that uses altitude to separate users and as the transition between different airspace control elements. (JP 3-52)

Coordinated Air Defense Area. An Air Defense Measure that identifies a mutually defined block of airspace between a land-based air commander and a naval commander when their forces are operating in close proximity to one another. (JP 3-52)

Carrier Control Zone. A Maritime Defense Measure that defines the airspace within a circular limit defined by five miles horizontal radius from the carrier, extending upward from the surface to and including 2,500 feet unless otherwise designated for special operations, and is under the cognizance of an air officer during visual meteorological conditions. (JP 3-52) An area around a ship operating fixed-/rotary-wing aircraft. (AJP-3.3.5)
Conditional Route. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines a non-permanent air traffic service route or portion thereof that can be planned and used only under certain conditions. (AJP-3.3.5)

Controlled Firing Area. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines airspace wherein activities are conducted under conditions so controlled as to eliminate hazards to nonparticipating aircraft and to ensure the safety of persons and property on the ground. (FAAO JO 7110.10)

Coordinated Fire Line. A Fire Support Coordination Measure that defines a line beyond which conventional surface-to-surface direct fire and indirect fire support means may fire at any time within the boundaries of the establishing headquarters without additional coordination. (JP 3-52) A line beyond which conventional or improved indirect fire means, such as mortars, field artillery, and naval gunfire, may fire without additional coordination (AJP-3.3.5)

Coordination Level. An Airspace Coordinating Measure that defines a procedural method to separate fixed- and rotary-wing aircraft by determining an altitude below which fixed-wing aircraft normally will not fly. (JP 3-52)

Class A Airspace. An Air Traffic Control Measure that generally defines airspace from 18,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) up to and including flight level 600, including airspace overlying the waters within 12 nautical miles of the congruous states and Alaska. Visual flight rules (VFR) operations are not permitted in CLSA. (JP 3-52)

Class B Airspace. An Air Traffic Control Measure that generally defines airspace from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL surrounding the nations busiest airports in terms of airport operations or passenger enplanements. Air Traffic Control (ATC) provides separation between all aircraft inside CLSB. (JP 3-52)

Class C Airspace. An Air Traffic Control Measure that generally defines airspace from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation (charted in MSL) surrounding those airports that have an operational control tower, are serviced by radar approach control, and have a certain number of instrument flight rules (IFR) operations or passenger enplanements. ATC provides separation between VFR and IFR inside CLSC. (JP 3-52)

Class D Airspace. An Air Traffic Control Measure that generally defines airspace from the surface to 2,500 feet above the airport elevation (charted in MSL) surrounding those airports having an operational control tower. The configuration of each CLSD is individually tailored and when instrument procedures are published, the airspace will normally be designated to contain the procedures. Prior to entering CLSD airspace, two-way radio communication must be established and maintained with the ATC facility providing air traffic service. (JP 3-52)
Class E Airspace. An Air Traffic Control Measure used to define controlled airspace that has not been defined as Class A, B, C, or D. Also includes federal airways. (JP 3-52)

Class F Airspace. An Air Traffic Control Measure that generally defines airspace in which IFR and VFR flights are permitted; all participating flights receive an air traffic advisory service, and all flights receive flight information service, if requested. (JP 3-52)
Class G Airspace. An Air Traffic Control Measure used to define uncontrolled airspace that has not been defined as Class A, B, C, D, or E. (JP 3-52)
Control Zone. An Air Defense Measure that defines a controlled airspace extending upward from the surface of the earth to a specified upper limit. (JP 3-52)

Crossover Zone. A maritime defense that defines a Maritime Control Measure which overlaps a missile engagement zone and a fighter engagement zone. (JP 3-52) Airspace beyond the missile engagement zone into which fighters may pursue targets to complete interception. (AJP-3.3.5)
Contact Point. When referenced to air operations, is an Air Reference Measure that defines the position of which a mission leader makes radio contact with an air control agency. (JP 3-52)
Danger Area. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines an airspace of defined dimensions within which activities dangerous to the flight of aircraft may exist at specified times. (AAP-06)

Fleet Air Defense Identification Zone. A Maritime Defense Measure that defines a specified area established for identification and flight following of aircraft in the vicinity of a fleet-defended area. (JP 3-52)

Fighter Engagement Zone. When referenced to air defense, is an Air Defense Measure that defines an airspace of defined dimensions within which the responsibility for engagement of air threats normally rests with fighter aircraft. (JP 3-52)

Free Fire Area. A Fire Support Coordination Measure that defines a specific designated area into which any weapons system may fire without additional coordination with the establishing headquarters. (JP 3-52)
Flight Information Region. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines an airspace within which flight information service and alerting service are provided. (JP 3-52)

Fire-Power Umbrella. A Maritime Defense Measure that defines an area of specified dimensions defining the airspace over a naval force at sea within which the fire of ships antiaircraft weapons can endanger aircraft, and within which special procedures have been established for identification and operations of friendly aircraft. (AAP-06)

Forward Line of Own Troops. A Maneuver Control Measure that defines a line that indicates the most forward positions of friendly forces during linear operations at a specific time. (JP 3-52) A line which indicates the most forward positions of friendly forces in any kind of military operation at a specific time. (AAP-06)

Fire Support Area. A Maneuver Control Measure that defines an appropriate maneuver area assigned to fire support ships by the naval force commander from which they deliver gunfire support to an amphibious operation. (JP 3-52)

Fire Support Coordination Line. A Fire Support Coordination Measure established by the land or amphibious force commander to support common objectives within an area of operations; beyond which all fires must be coordinated with affected commanders prior to engagement, and short of the line, all fires must be coordinated with the establishing commander prior to engagement. (JP 3-52) Within an assigned area of operations, a line established by a land or amphibious force commander to denote coordination requirements for fires by other force elements which may affect the commanders current and planned operations. The fire support coordination line applies to fires of air, ground, or sea weapons using any type of ammunition against surface or ground targets. Note: In the context of this definition, the term surface targets applies to those in littoral or inland waters within the designated area of operations. (AAP-06)

High-Density Airspace Control Zone. An Airspace Coordinating Measure that defines an airspace designated in an Airspace Control Plan (ACP) or Airspace Control Order (ACO), in which there is a concentrated employment of numerous and varied weapons and airspace users. A HIDACZ has defined dimensions, which usually coincide with geographical features or navigational aids. Access to a HIDACZ is normally controlled by the maneuver commander. The maneuver commander can also direct a more restrictive weapons status within the HIDACZ. (JP 3-52) Airspace of defined dimensions, designated by the airspace control authority, in which there is a concentrated employment of numerous and varied weapons/airspace users. (AAP-06)

High-Altitude Missile Engagement Zone. When referenced to air defense, is an Air Defense Measure that defines an airspace of defined dimensions within which the responsibility for engagement of air threats normally rests with high altitude surface-to-air missiles. (JP 3-52)
Identification, Friend or Foe Switch Off Line. An Air Reference Measure that defines the line demarking where friendly aircraft stop emitting an identification, friend or foe (IFF) signal. (JP 3-52)
Identification, Friend or Foe Switch On Line. An Air Reference Measure that defines the line demarking where friendly aircraft start emitting an identification, friend or foe (IFF) signal. (JP 3-52)

Identification Safety Point. A Maritime Defense Measure that defines a point at which aircraft, on joining a maritime force, will attempt to establish two-way communications with the surface forces and commence identification procedures. (AJP-3.3.5)

Identification Safety Range. A Maritime Defense Measure that defines the minimum range to which aircraft may close to a maritime force without having been positively identified as friendly to ensure that the maritime force does not mistake the aircraft for hostile. (AJP-3.3.5)

Joint Engagement Zone. When referenced to air defense, is an Air Defense Measure that defines airspace of defined dimensions within which multiple air defense systems (surface-to-air missiles and aircraft) are simultaneously employed to engage air threats. (JP 3-52)

Joint Operations Area. A Maneuver Control Measure that defines an area of land, sea, and airspace defined by a geographic combatant commanders or subordinate unified commander, in which a joint force commander (usually a joint task force commander) conducts military operations to accomplish a specific mission. (JP 3-52) A temporary area defined by the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, in which a designated joint commander plans and executes a specific mission at the operational level of war. A joint operations area and its defining parameters, such as time, scope of the mission, and geographical area, are contingency- or mission-specific and are normally associated with combined joint task force operations. (AAP-06)

Joint Special Operations Area. A Maneuver Control Measure that defines an area of land, sea, and airspace assigned by a joint force commander to the commander of a joint special operations force to conduct special operations activities. (JP 3-52)

Kill Box. A Fire Support Coordination Measure that defines a three-dimensional permissive fire support coordination measure with an associated airspace coordination measure used to facilitate the integration of Joint fires. (JP 3-52)

Low-Altitude Missile Engagement Zone. When referenced to air defense, is an Air Defense Measure that defines that airspace of defined dimensions within which the responsibility for engagement of air threats normally rests with low-to-medium-altitude surface-to-air missiles. (JP 3-52)

Missile Engagement Zone. When referenced to air defense, is an Air Defense Measure that defines airspace of defined dimensions within which the responsibility for engagement of air threats normally rests with a surface-to-air missile systems. (JP 3-52)

Missile Arc. An Air Defense Measure that defines an area of 10 degrees or as large as ordered by the officer in tactical command, centered on the bearing of the target with a range that extends to the maximum range of the surface-to-air missile. (AJP-3.3.5)

Military Operations Area. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines an airspace designated outside CLSA area to separate or segregate certain nonhazardous military activities from IFR Traffic and to identify for VFR traffic where these activities are conducted. (JP 3-52)
No Fire Area. A Fire Support Coordination Measure that defines an area designated by the appropriate commander into which fires or their effects are prohibited. (JP 3-52)

No Fly Area. An Airspace Coordinating Measure that defines airspace of specific dimensions set aside for a specific purpose in which no aircraft operations are permitted, except as authorized by the appropriate commander and controlling agency. (JP 3-52)
Phase Line. A Maneuver Control Measure that defines a line utilized for control and coordination of military operations, usually an easily identified feature in the operational area. (JP 3-52)

Prohibited Area. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines a specified area within the land areas of a state or its internal waters, archipelagic waters, or territorial sea adjacent thereto over which the flight of aircraft is prohibited. (JP 3-52) An airspace of defined dimensions, above the land areas or territorial waters of a state within which the flight of aircraft is prohibited. (AAP-06)

Restricted Area. When referenced to air, is an Air Traffic Control Measure that defines designated areas established by appropriate authority over which flight of aircraft is restricted. Return To Force. A Maritime Defense Measure that defines planned route profiles for use by friendly aircraft returning to an aviation-capable ship. (JP 3-52)
Safety Sector. A Maritime Defense Measure that is established to route friendly aircraft to maritime forces with minimum risk. (AJP-3.3.5)
Search And Rescue Point. An Air Reference Measure that defines a pre-designated specific location, relative to which isolated personnel provide their position to recovery forces. (JP 3-52)

Ship Control Zone. A Maritime Defense Measure that defines an area activated around a ship operating aircraft, which is not to be entered by friendly aircraft without permission, in order to prevent friendly interference. (AJP-3.3.5)

Short-Range Air Defense Engagement Zone. When referenced to air defense, is an Air Defense Measure that defines airspace of defined dimensions within which the responsibility for engagement of air threats normally rests with short-range air defense weapons and may be established within a low- or high-altitude missile engagement zone. (JP 3-52)

Safe Lane. An Air Defense Measure that defines a bi-directional lane connecting an airbase, landing site and/or base defense zone to adjacent routes/corridors. Safe lanes may also be used to connect adjacent activated routes/corridors. (AJP-3.3.5)

Temporary Flight Restriction. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines regulatory action issued by the FAA via the U.S. NOTAM System, under the authority of Title 49, United States Code. TFRs are issued within the sovereign airspace of the U.S. and its territories to restrict certain aircraft from operating within a defined area on a temporary basis to protect persons or property in the air or on the ground. (JP 3-52)

Traverse Level. An Air Defense Measure that defines vertical displacement above low-level air defense systems, expressed both as a height and an altitude, at which aircraft can cross that area. (AAP-06)

Warning Area. An Air Traffic Control Measure that defines airspace of defined dimensions extending from three nautical miles outward from the coast of the U.S. that contains activity that may be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft. (JP 3-52)

Weapons Free Zone. An Air Defense Measure that defines an air defense zone established for the protection of key assets or facilities, other than air bases, where weapons systems may be fired at any target not positively recognized as friendly. (JP 3-52)
Zone of Fire. A Fire Support Coordination Measure that defines an area into which a designated ground unit or fire support ship delivers, or is prepared to deliver, fire support. (JP 3-52)

Airspace Coordinating Measure. A measure employed to facilitate the efficient use of airspace to accomplish missions and simultaneously provide safeguards for friendly forces. ACMs are approved by the Airspace Control Authority (ACA) and promulgated via the Airspace Control Order (ACO). Transit of an ACM requires coordination with the owning airspace control element. (JP 3-52)

Air Defense Measure. A measure planned, coordinated, and employed to facilitate responsibilities for identification, detection, and tracking to engage enemy air and missile threats as directed by the Area Air Defense Commander (AADC). ADMs are restrictive. (JP 3-52)

Air Reference Measure. A measure used for command and control purposes that defines a point over the ground or a volume of airspace. ARMs do not require coordination to pass over or through. (JP 3-52)

Air Traffic Control Measure. A measure established by civilian (including host nation) or military air traffic control for the purpose of expeditious and safe movements of aircraft. ATCMs are directive and restrictive and are established in conjunction with the civil and military airspace control authorities and International Civil Aviation Organization (as appropriate). (JP 3-52)

Fire Support Coordination Measure. A measure employed by commanders to facilitate the rapid engagement of targets and simultaneously provide safeguards for friendly forces. FSCMs may be permissive or restrictive. (JP 3-52)

Maneuver Control Measure. A measure established by the supported/supporting commander on the surface to define lines of responsibility in support of movement and maneuver of friendly forces. (JP 3-52)
Maritime Defense Measure. A measure planned, coordinated, and employed by maritime commander to facilitate maritime offensive and defensive actions. MDMs may be restrictive or permissive. (JP 3-52)

Gas Detection. Gas detectors come in two basic types, combustion-type and thermal -conductivity type. The most commonly used combustion type employs a self-heated "hot wire" detector, usually platinum, which serves as a combustion catalyst. After the combustion process is started, a temperature sensor, such as a thermocouple, may detect the temperature rise which is a measure of the concentration of gas. Different gases vary considerably in their ability to conduct heat. These variations make it possible to determine the concentrations of a number of gases, the basis for a thermal-conductivity type gas detector.

Image Intensification, Including Night Vision Devices other than Strictly Optical. This device consists of: (1) a input, photoelectron-emitting photocathode, which converts the image scene photons into an electron image; (2) a drift space with an electrostatic field to accelerate the electrons (providing the amplification energy) and to image the accelerated electrons onto the output surface (i.e., also performs an electron optic function); and (3) a phosphor that converts these high-energy electrons into visible light. Therefore, this device simply provides optical gain, or amplification.

Infrared. Radiant energy within the wavelength range 1 to 100 micrometer (10**-6 meter) is considered infrared energy. In general, unlike ultraviolet energy, infrared energy is not evaluated on a wavelength basis but rather in terms of all of such energy incident upon a surface. An infrared sensor would normally consist of a device for converting an invisible infrared image into a visible image. This device would consist of an infrared-sensitive, semi-transparent photocathode on one end of an evacuated envelope and a phosphor screen on the other, with an electrostatic lens system between the two.

Low Light Level Television (LLLTV). Very low light level. Operation can be obtained by coupling an image intensifier (optical amplifier) tube with a camera tube. The image intensifier tube is used as the prime sensor and its output is coupled to the photocathode of the camera tube. Low light level television has many advantages for night military operations by enhancing battlefield surveillance and reconnaissance for both defense and attack.

Battery. A tactical and administrative artillery unit usually equating to a company or similar unit.

Command. A regional or area command (as a military district command) which is configured and manned in accordance with an official authorization or directive. May also be an organizational or unit command (as a logistics command) which is part of a superior organization.
Company. The basic administrative and tactical unit in most army ground forces, on a command level below a battalion and above a platoon. It is usually equivalent to a battery of artillery.

Corps. A unit organized to operate tactically as part of a field army, or tactically and administratively as a separate or independent corps. Consists of two or more Divisions, service and support units, and may include other separate tactical organizations (such as separate brigades, armored cavalry regiments, etc.). (in the zone of the interior of a corps area, which is usually part of an army area, may be administered by a corps headquarters which is charged primarily with recruiting, equipping, and training reserve personnel and units.)
Detachment. Part of a unit separated from its main organization for duty elsewhere, may be any independent unit so designated.

Division. In the U.S. Army the Division is the basic self-contained tactical and administrative ground combat unit. Usually the subordinate echelon of a corps, it consists of two or more regiments plus service and supporting units.
Front. Used in conjunction with ground forces of the former USSR.
Group. An administrative and tactical unit consisting of two or more battalions. Usually smaller than a regiment or brigade and may be subordinate to either.
Group of Forces. Used in conjunction with ground forces of the former USSR.
Group of Fronts. Used in conjunction with ground forces of the former USSR.
Komendatura. A tactical unit of the former USSR with a strength varying from 200- 500 men. Subordinate to the Otryad.
Major Fleet. Permanent organization of ships, aircraft, marines, and shore-based support activities under a single command exercising both operational and administrative control.
Naval Detachment. A part of a naval organization that is separated from its main organization for special duty elsewhere.
Naval Division. A number of naval ships (two or more) of similar type grouped together for operational and administrative control.

Naval Force. A major subdivision or task force of a numbered fleet, consisting of ships, marines, aircraft, or a combination thereof. Naval forces do not ordinarily have their own shore establishments.

Naval Group. A flexible administrative or tactical organization composed of two or more squadrons of ships, but not necessarily ships of the same type. A Naval group may be a subdivision of a Naval force.
Naval Section. A tactical subdivision of a naval division of ships. It is normally one-half of a division of ships.
Naval Squadron. An organizational element consisting of two or more divisions of ships and assigned tenders. It is normally, but not necessarily, composed of ships of the same type.
National Defense Headquarters. The highest echelon in a national government exercising command control over a nation's military establishment.

Numbered Fleet. A major tactical command immediately subordinate to a major fleet command and comprised of various task forces, groups, and support elements for the purpose of prosecuting specific Naval operations.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Otryad. A regimental-size unit of the former USSR directly subordinate to the Border District Headquarters.
Platoon. A tactical unit usually subordinate to a company or battery.

Patrol. A tactical unit designed for a specific mission or purpose, and sometimes organized officially by an authorized table of organization. May be subordinate to a platoon, company, or battalion. The size varies with the mission or purpose for which organized.
Regiment. An administrative and tactical unit on a level of command that is usually below a division or brigade and above a battalion.
Section. A tactical unit usually smaller than a platoon and larger than a squad. In some organizations the section, rather than the squad, is the basic tactical unit.
Squadron. A tactical and administrative unit usually equating to a battalion, and composed of two or more troops (units).
Squad. A small, basic, tactical unit usually subordinate to a platoon.
Administration, Republic. Former Soviet Union only.
Task Element, Abbreviated. The short title data code of a task element.
Task Force, Abbreviated. The short title data code of a task force.
Task Group, Abbreviated. The short title data code of a task group.

Theater Army. A Theater Army is the senior army headquarters in a theater of operations. In a theater where the forces of a single nation comprise the theater command, the Theater Army is the senior headquarters and is charged with the command and control of all army elements in the theater. When the theater is organized as a combined command, the theater army of a nation becomes the senior administrative headquarters in the theater for that nation's forces only.
Troop. A subordinate tactical and administrative unit of a cavalry squadron, equivalent to a company or battery.
Task Element. A component of a task group organized to accomplish a specific task.
Task Force. A component of a fleet organization by the commander of a task fleet or higher authority for accomplishment of a specific task or tasks.
Task Group. A component of a naval task force organized by the commander of a task force or higher authority.
Task Unit. A component of a task element.
Task Unit, Abbreviated. The short title data code of a task unit.

The first element is a pair of letters representing the 15-degree quadrilateral; the first letter of the pair allows the letters A to Z, omitting I and O; the second letter of the pair allows the letters A to M, omitting I and O. The second element is a pair of letters representing a 1-degree quadrilateral within the 15-degree quadrilateral and allows the letter values A to H, J to N, P or Q. The third element is a 2-digit number representing the easting coordinate to the closest one minute, in values from 00 to 59. The fourth element is a 2-digit number representing one of the 100 equal parts of a minute of angle, in values from 00 to 99. The fifth element is a 2-digit number representing the northing coordinate to the closet one minute, in values from 00 to 59. The sixth element is a 2-digit number representing one of the 100 equal parts of a minute of angle, in values from 00 to 99.

The areas described by GARS are coincident with even WGS-84 degree and minute lines. The areas are read right (west to east, 001-720) then up (south to north, AA-QZ). The 30 minute by 30 minute areas are subdivided by quadrant into 15 minute by 15 minute areas (1-4), then further subdivided by a keypad division into 5 minute by 5 minute areas (1-9).

Archipelago. A sea studded with islands, or the islands themselves, considered collectively.

Bar. An elongated offshore ridge or mound composed of unconsolidated material such as sand, gravel, or shells. Bars are usually submerged, parallel to and a short distance from the coastline, often at the mouth of a river or estuary.

Barrier Reef. An elongated ridge of rock or coral near and roughly parallel to the coast.  It is separated from the shore by the deep water of a lagoon, and is cut through at intervals by channels or passes.
Beach Swale. An elongated, sometimes marshy depression, between two ridges on the beach backshore (or on a sandspit) generally paralleling a shoreline.

Breakwater. A long, solid, structure, sometimes attached to the shore, built to protect a shore area harbor, anchorage, or basin from the impact of waves.  A breakwater is usually made of stone, concrete blocks, rubble, or other material.  Breakwaters are usually associated with harbors and anchorages exposed to the open sea.
Building. A fixed construction, covering a space on land (or in the immediate nearshore) usually covered with a roof, enclosed by walls, and designed to stand more or less permanently.

Buoy. A floating object, anchored in a river or ocean bottom and used as a navigation aid to mark a channel or hazard. The buoy may be attached by a line or cable to an anchor or weight lying on the bottom.
Cabana. A beach shelter, such as a cabin, hut, or bathhouse.
Coral. A stony, solidified mass of calcareous skeletons from various forms of marine life.
Fence. A barrier, usually marking a boundary consisting of wooden or metal pickets, or else supporting wire or rail.

Fishnet. A fish-catching device which is a fabric made from such materials as string and cord, woven in an open-work pattern.  It may be suspended over water and attached to poles or the fishnet may lie on the bottom.
Fishstake. Bamboo like material used to channel fish into a funnel-like trap.
Groin. A shore protective structure (built usually perpendicular to the shore to trap littoral drift or retard erosion of the shore).
Headland. A comparatively high, steep-faced promontory, which projects into a body of water.
Inlet. A narrow arm of the sea, which may extend a considerable distance inland - a shore channel connecting a bay to a lagoon or a lagoon with the sea - a narrow strip between islands.
Island. A land mass completely surrounded by water.
Islet. A very small island, which is a land mass exposed during all tidal conditions, and its longest axis is 100 meters or less.

Jetty. Usually constructed in pairs at the mouth of a river, inlet, or a harbor entrance. This is to prevent deposition of sand in the channel; regulate, restrain, and divert currents; and protect vessels.
Military. Any man-made device (except mines) or passive defense works such as a barrier which is designed to stop, impede, or divert movement of amphibious landing forces to or on the beach or shore.

Mine. An encased explosive or other material (e.g., chemicals) designed to destroy material or to wound, kill, or otherwise incapacitate personnel. Mines are laid on or below the surface of the ground and/or in inland waterways or the sea approach area, so as to stop, delay, or divert amphibious landing or ground force movement. In the sea approach, the fixed mine is either bottomlaid or moored by a cable to an anchor or weight in the water.

Mole. A massive, solid fill structure projecting at an angle from the shore.  A mole may serve as a pier or breakwater or both. It is usually quayed on one or more sides. Its broad surface may support buildings, cargo handling equipment, rail spurs, and roads.
Mudflat. A muddy or sandy coated strip usually submerged by high tide.
None. There is no amphibious landing obstruction on the beach or shore or its approach.

Pier. A long, narrow structure which provides berthing for ships.  It extends into a body of water at an angle to the shore and is made of piles, stone, or concrete.  A pier may be straight, T-beachd, or L-beachd, with berthing along both sides and at its ends. It may support storage facilities, cargo handling equipment, and railroad tracks.

Piling. Wood, metal, or reinforced concrete poles driven into the land or sea bottom, singly, or in clusters (dolphins).  Pilings extend above water to serve as supports, as for a pier, protection for moorings, or to resist lateral pressure.
Pipeline. A line of pipes, including pumping machinery, servicing, and supporting structures, used for conveying liquids, gases, or finely crushed solids (e.g., slurry).
Point. A small promontory which projects into a body of water.

Reef. A low coastal ridge of rock or coral which is offshore (barrier reef) or closely attached to the shore (fringing reef). Most reefs extend upward from the sea floor and lie at or near the water surface at a depth which makes them a danger to surface vessels. Most reefs are submerged, especially at high tide.

River. A natural stream of water which flows permanently or seasonally. A river has greater volume than a creek or rivulet, flows in a more or less permanent bed or channel between defined banks or walls.

Rock. A consolidated or coherent and relatively hard, naturally formed mass of mineral matter. Also an aggregate of angular pieces of stone larger than 76 mm (3 inches) in diameter. Rock may occur as an isolated rocky formation or a single large stone. In the sea it may be submerged, uncovered, or alternatively covered and uncovered by the tide.
Ruin. The remains of a cultural feature such as a building, or an object that has been destroyed or has decayed.
Runnel. An elongated trough or depression of the beach on the foreshore or near shore bottom, approximately parallel to the shoreline.
Seawall. A man-made structure, such as rock or concrete wall or embankment, built along a portion of coast.
Seaweed. Underwater plant life such as seagrass and marine algae.
Shoal. Part of a sea bottom below the surface of the sea composed of, or covered by, sand, gravel, or unconsolidated sediments which may endanger surface navigation.
Spit. A low, elongated, exposed deposit of waterborne sediment, such as a reef, shoal, or sandbank, which protrudes from the shore and terminates in the water.

Stake. A length of material, usually metal or wood, pointed at one end for driving into the ground. May be used for such purposes as anchoring a fish trap, as a boundary marker, or as a military obstacle. May be submerged.
Stream. A narrow body of flowing water or other fluid, great or small, occupying a channel on land.
Tidal Flat. A relatively broad, virtually level coastal flatland of sand, mud, or mudsand which is periodically covered and uncovered by the rise and fall of the tide.
Wall. A continuous, vertical structure, such as a concrete or rock wall serving to enclose, divide, support or protect an area on land. Includes seawalls.
Wreck. A hulk or ruin of a wrecked or stranded ship, either submerged or visible, which is attached to or foul on the bottom, or cast up on the shore.

The first element is a 2 digit number representing the UTM zone, in values from 01 to 60; leading zeroes are included. The second element is a single letter representing the band of latitude beginning at 80°S and proceeding northward; the 20 bands are lettered C through X, omitting I and O. The third element is a pair of letters representing one of the 100,000-meter grid squares within the grid zone; the first letter of the pair allows the letters A through Z, omitting I and O; the second letter of the pair allows the letters A through V, omitting I and O. The fourth element is a 10-digit number representing the Easting and Northing values within the 100,000-meter grid square (5-digit Easting, 5-digit Northing).

Air Defense Artillery. A unit of antiaircraft artillery weapons and fire control equipment employed in engaging air targets from the ground.
Antiarmor Missile. A unit organized and equipped to employ missiles against tanks and other armored vehicles.
Antiair Warfare. A unit organized for antiair warfare.
Airborne. A unit trained and equipped for airborne operations.

Airborne Infantry. An infantry unit organized and equipped for parachute and airlanded operations.
Air Defense. A unit of artillery anti-aircraft artillery weapons and fire control equipment employed in engaging air targets from the ground.
Administrative. A unit performing those functions that are primarily of a management or administrative nature.
Air Cavalry. A cavalry unit specially equipped to combine movement by air with reconnaissance in depth. (Also see Cavalry, below.)
Airmobile Infantry. An infantry unit, trained and equipped for airlanded operations.
Airmobile. A unit trained and equipped to move about the battlefield by aircraft to engage in ground combat.
Amphibious Assault. An infantry unit organized, equipped and trained for amphibious operations.
Amphibious Engineers. An engineer unit trained and equipped to operate as part of an amphibious force.

Armored Artillery. A unit equipped with (mobile) armored artillery.
Armored Cavalry. An armored cavalry unit.
Armor. A unit of combat tanks and armored motor vehicles heavily protected with metal plates.
Army Aviation. A ground unit of organic aviation limited to fixed and rotary-wing, light aircraft, such as liaison and observation types, which are dedicated to ground support.
Artillery. An artillery unit of unknown type.
Assault Engineers. A combat engineer unit that may fight as foot infantry.

Anti-Tank. A unit trained and equipped for operations against armored vehicles.
Biological Ordnance Capable Unit. A unit capable of delivering biological ordnance on a target.
Cavalry. A unit moving in lightly armored vehicles and structured primarily to perform ground reconnaissance and security missions. (Also see Air Cavalry, above.)
Chemical. A unit employing chemical and/or biological agents to prosecute warfare. Performs massive decontamination functions as required by the tactical situation.
Combined Arms. A military unit of the former Soviet Union composed of tank and motorized equipment.
Combat Engineers. A unit of engineers who are also trained to fight as infantry when required by the tactical situation.
Commando. A highly mobile unit trained in counterinsurgency and operations behind enemy lines.
Combat Service Support. A combat service support unit.
Composite Warfare Commander. The command directing naval warfare areas in a naval task force.
Dismounted Cavalry. A cavalry unit that fights as foot infantry.
Engineer. A unit that accomplishes major construction, demolition, and extensive camouflage projects.
Electronic Warfare Support. A unit capable of performing electronic warfare support.
Electronic Warfare. A unit having multiple/general electronic warfare capability.
EW Coordinator. The command directing electronic warfare in a naval task force.
Field Artillery. A unit or artillery mounted on carriages and mobile enough to accompany infantry or armored units in the field.
Frog SSM Unit. A unit equipped with Frog SSM.
Fixed Wing. A unit operating fixed wing aircraft.
Gun-Howitzer. An artillery unit having gun-howitzers as principal weapons. Usually part of tube artillery units of regimental size.

Intelligence. A unit that performs analysis and testing of enemy equipment, translates enemy documents, and interrogates enemy personnel.
Mechanized Engineer. An engineer unit equipped with organic machinery/vehicles for increased support.
Mechanized Infantry. An infantry unit equipped with organic armored and/or mechanized vehicles for increased mobility and support.
Medical. A unit that provides medical treatment and/or medical evacuation services.
Mining. A unit organized for mine laying or mine clearing.
Mortar. An artillery unit having mortars as principal weapons. May be organic part of larger infantry or artillery unit.
Military Police. A military police unit.
Motorized Rifle Troops. An infantry unit whose organic motorized vehicles and armor facilitate attack from march column.
Mountain Infantry. An infantry unit specially trained and equipped for warfare in mountainous terrain.
Nuclear, Biological, Chemical. A unit trained and equipped for NBC defense/cleanup operations.
Nuclear Ordnance Capable Unit. A unit capable of delivering nuclear ordnance on a target.
Ordnance. A unit responsible for the supply and maintenance of weapons, weapon system components, ammunition, and related equipment.
Picket. A ship or ships accomplishing picket duty.
Reconnaissance, Armor. An armed information-gathering unit equipped to conduct deep probes, harass, or make diversionary attacks.

Ranger. Similar to commando unit in training but usually employed in hit-run raids.

Sapper (Mine). A unit responsible for infiltration operations involving use of satchel charges, mines, and small arms.

Surveillance. A unit organized for surveillance.
Service. A unit providing supply, maintenance, transport, evacuation, medical, and other services.
