Attack. Any aerial mission meant to disrupt, neutralize, or destroy enemy forces.

Barrier Combat Air Patrol. An aerial mission which use of one or more divisions or elements of fighter aircraft between a force and an objective area as a barrier across the probable direction of enemy attack. It is used as far from the force as control conditions permit, giving added protection against raids that use the most direct routes of approach.

Combat Air Patrol. An aircraft patrol provided over an objective area, the force protected, the critical area of a combat zone, or in an air defense area, for the purpose of intercepting and destroying hostile aircraft before they reach their targets.

Close Air Support. Air action against hostile targets which are in close proximity to friendly forces and which require detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of those forces.
Container Delivery System. An aerial mission, which focuses on the use of a system where containers are airdropped into a forward operating location.
Communication, Intelligence, Collection. An aerial mission which focuses on gathering communication intelligence in order to meet current operational requirements.

Command and Control. An aerial mission in which a properly designated Commander exercises authority and direction over assigned and attached forces in the accomplishment of the task, command and control functions are performed through an arrangement of personnel, equipment, communications, facilities, and procedures employed by a commander in planning, directing, coordinating, and controlling forces and operations in the accomplishment of the mission.

Contingency. An aerial emergency mission involving military force caused by natural disasters, terrorists, subversives, or by required military operations. Due to the uncertainty of the situation, contingencies require plans, rapid response, and special procedures to ensure the safety and readiness of personnel, installations, and equipment.
Communications Relay. Airborne operations where aircraft serve as a communications relay extending existing capabilities.

Combat Search and Rescue. The detection, location, identification and rescue of downed aircrew in hostile territory in time of crisis or war and, when appropriate, isolated military personnel in distress, who are trained and equipped to receive combat search and rescue support.
Courier Flight. An aerial mission conducted to carry mail, information, or supplies.

Defensive Counterair. An aerial mission, which focuses on all defensive measures designed to detect, identify, intercept, and destroy or negate enemy forces attempting to attack or penetrate the friendly air environment.
Distinguished Visitor Support. Air operations where military aircraft are used to transport distinguished visitors.

Electronic Attack. An aerial mission conducted by a division of electronic warfare involving the use of electromagnetic energy, directed energy, or anti-radiation weapons to attack personnel, facilities, or equipment with the intent of degrading, neutralizing, or destroying enemy combat capability and is considered a form of fires.
Electronic. An aerial mission, which is primarily for the purpose of collecting data on electronic emitters.
Electro-Optical. An aerial mission which focuses on the use of imaging sensors that collect imagery in or just beyond the visible spectrum.

Electronic Support. An aerial mission, which provides information, required for decisions involving electronic warfare operations and other tactical actions such as threat avoidance, targeting, and homing.
Escort. Aircraft assigned to protect other aircraft during a mission.

Electronic Warfare. Military action to exploit the electromagnetic spectrum encompassing: the search for, interception and identification of electromagnetic emissions, the employment of electromagnetic energy, included directed energy, to reduce or prevent hostile use of the electromagnetic spectrum, and actions to ensure its effective use by friendly forces.

Electronic Warfare Support (ES). An aerial mission conducted by a division of electronic warfare involving actions tasked by, or under direct control of, an operational Commander to search for, intercept, identify, and locate or localize sources of intentional and unintentional radiated electromagnetic energy for the purpose of immediate threat recognition, targeting, planning and conduct of future operations. Thus, electronic warfare support provides information required for decisions involving electronic warfare operations and other tactical actions such as threat avoidance, targeting, and homing. Electronic warfare support data can be used to produce signals intelligence, provide targeting for electronic or destructive attack, and produce measurement and signature intelligence.

Exercise. A military maneuver or simulated wartime operation involving planning, preparation, and execution. It is carried out for the purpose of training and evaluation. It may be a combined, joint, or single-service exercise, depending on participating organizations.

Forward Air Controller.  A specifically trained and qualified aviation officer, normally an airborne extension of the tactical air control party, who exercises control from the air of aircraft engaged in close air support of ground troops.
Functional Check Flight. A flight conducted to confirm operational readiness of the flight crew or aircraft.

Forward Looking Infrared. An aerial mission, which focuses on an airborne, electro-optical thermal imaging device that detects far-infrared energy, converts the energy into an electronic signal, and provides a visible image for day or night viewing.

Ground Alert Anti-Air Warfare. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform anti-air operations to defend a maritime force.

Ground Alert Airborne Early Warning. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform early warning operations.

Ground Alert Attack Helicopter. The status in which rotary-wing aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform attack operations.

Ground Alert Air Interdiction. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform interdiction operations.

Ground Alert Aeromedical Evacuation. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform aeromedical evacuation operations.

Ground Alert Troop/Cargo Helicopter Operation. The status in which helicopter aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform transportation operations for troops or cargo.

Ground Alert Aerial Refueling. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform aerial refueling operations.

Ground Alert Anti-Submarine Warfare. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform anti-submarine operations.

Ground Alert Attack. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and are ready to employ various weapons to destroy enemy targets.

Ground Alert Barrier Combat Air Patrol. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform barrier combat air patrol operations.

Ground Alert Combat Air Patrol. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform combat air patrol operations.

Ground Alert Close Air Support. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform close air support operations. See close air support.

Ground Alert Communications Relay. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform airborne operations where aircraft serve as a communications relay extending existing capabilities.

Ground Alert Defensive Counterair. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform defensive counterair operations.

Ground Alert Escort. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform escort operations.

Ground Alert Electronic Warfare. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform electronic warfare operations. See electronic warfare.

Ground Alert Forward Air Controller. The status in which a specifically trained and qualified aviation officer, who exercises control from the air of aircraft engaged in close air support of ground troops, in his aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform forward air control operations.

Ground Alert Flare Illumination. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform battlefield illumination by airdropping high-powered flares.

Ground Alert Joint Airborne Communications Control/Command Post. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform joint command and control operations.

Ground Alert Minelaying. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform airdrops of encased explosive over ground or in water and that are set to explode when disturbed.

Ground Alert Minesweeping. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and once airborne will locate minefields and neutralize them by dropping ordnance over the area.

Ground Alert Offensive Counterair. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform offensive counterair operations. See offensive counterair.

Ground Alert Reconnaissance. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform reconnaissance operations. See reconnaissance.

Ground Alert Strategic Attack. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform any long range air operation meant to strike an enemy at the sources of its military, economic, or political power.

Ground Alert Strategic Airlift. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform strategic airlift operations. See strategic airlift.

Ground Alert Search and Rescue. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform search and rescue operations. See search and rescue.

Ground Alert Reconnaissance Strike Control Coordination and Reconnaissance (GSCAR). The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and conduct reconnaissance strike control coordination and reconnaissance operations.

Ground Alert Defense Suppression Enemy Air Defense. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform SEAD operations that will attempt to neutralize, destroy, or temporarily degrade surface-based enemy air defenses by destructive and/or disruptive means.

Ground Alert Security. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform security operations. See security.

Ground Alert Support Mission. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform air missions that include movement of personnel or equipment other than via tactical airlift.

Ground Alert Sensor Implant. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, airdrop sensors.

Ground Alert Surface Combat Air Patrol (SUCAP). The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform a combat air patrol in support of surface vessels conducting maritime operations. ATO mission that represents ground alert variations of five specific AOMSW missions: surface surveillance coordination (SSC), armed reconnaissance (AR)/strike coordination and reconnaissance (SCAR), war-at-sea (WAS) strike, counter-fast attack craft (FAC)/fast inshore attack craft (FIAC), and airborne maritime mining (AMM).

Ground Alert Theater Airlift. The status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time after receipt of a mission order, and perform theater airlift operations. See theater airlift.
Ground Alert Ground Control Radar Bombing.
Heavy Equipment Airdrop. An aerial mission to unload heavy equipment from an aircraft in flight.
Troop/Cargo Helicopter Operation. Helicopter transportation operations airlifting troops or cargo.
Flare Illumination. An aerial mission which focuses on battlefield illumination by airdropping high-powered flares.

Interdiction. Operations conducted to divert, disrupt, delay, or destroy the enemys military surface capability before it can be used effectively against friendly forces, or to achieve enemy objectives.

Intelligence. An aerial mission that's product results from the collection, processing, integration, analysis, evaluation, and interpretation of available information concerning foreign countries or areas or information and knowledge about an adversary obtained through observation, investigation, analysis, or understanding.

Joint Airborne Air Transportability Training. Training operations or exercises involving airborne and appropriate troop carrier units. This training includes: a. air delivery of personnel and equipment; b. assault operations by airborne troops and/or air transportable units; c. loading exercises and local orientation fights of short duration; and d. maneuvers and/or exercises as agreed upon by services concerned and/or as authorized by the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Joint Airborne Communications Center/Command Post (JACC/CP). A suitably equipped aircraft used by the commander for conduct of operations.
Minelaying. An aerial mission which permits airdrops of encased explosive over ground or in water that are set to explode when disturbed.

Minesweeping. The technique of searching for, or clearing mines using mechanical or explosion gear, which physically removes or destroys the mine, or produces, in the area, the influence fields necessary to actuate it.
Observation Flight. The airborne surveillance of aerospace, surface, or subsurface areas, places, persons, or things, by visual, aural, electronic, photographic, or other means.

Offensive Counterair. Offensive operations to destroy, disrupt, or neutralize enemy aircraft, missiles, launch platforms, and their supporting structures and systems both before and after launch, but as close to their source as possible. Offensive counterair operations range throughout enemy territory and are generally conducted at the initiative of friendly forces. These operations include attack operations, fighter sweep, escort, and suppression of enemy air defenses.
Other. Indicates the mission is something other than any of the missions listed. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Personnel Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on the delivery of personnel from an aircraft in flight.
Point CAP. Combat Air Patrol flown in support of a rendezvous or a break-up point.

Pararescue Jumper Combat Rescue Exfiltration. The removal of personnel from areas under enemy control by specially trained personnel qualified to penetrate to the site of an incident by land or parachute, render medical aid, accomplish survival methods, and rescue survivors.

Pararescue Jumper Combat Rescue Infiltration. The movement through or into an area or territory occupied by either friendly or enemy troops or organizations specially trained personnel qualified to penetrate to the site of an incident by land or parachute, render medical aid, accomplish survival methods, and rescue survivors.
Psychological Operations. Planned psychological activities designed to influence attitudes and behavior affecting the achievement of political and military objectives.
Armed Road Recce. An aerial mission with the primary purpose of locating and attacking targets of opportunity such as enemy troop movements along lines of communication.

Reconnaissance. A mission undertaken to obtain, by visual observation or other detection methods, information about the activities and resources of an enemy or potential enemy, or to secure data concerning the meteorological, hydrographic, or geographic characteristics of a particular area.

Special Assignment Airlift Mission. An aerial mission which focuses on specific airlift requirements, that requires special consideration due to the number of passengers involved, weight or size of cargo, urgency of movement, sensitivity, or other valid factors that preclude the use of channel airlift.
Strategic Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on long range airdrop operations, meant to strike an enemy at the sources of its military, economic, or political power.
Strategic Airlift. The carriage of passengers and cargo between theatres by means of: a. scheduled service; b. special flight; c. air logistic support; d. aeromedical evacuation.
Search and Rescue. The use of aircraft, surface craft (land or water), submarines, specialized rescue teams, and equipment to search for and rescue personnel in distress on land or at sea.
Strike Coordination and Reconnaissance (SCAR). An aerial mission to conduct reconnaissance strike coordination and reconnaissance.
Suppression Enemy Air Defense. An aerial mission conducted to neutralize, destroy, or temporarily degrade surface-based enemy air defenses by destructive and/or disruptive means.
Security. The measures necessary to achieve protection against espionage, sabotage, subversion, and terrorism, as well as against loss or unauthorized disclosure.
Support Mission. This mission type includes movement of personnel or equipment other than via tactical airlift, security services missions, UHF relay, etc.
Special. An aerial mission which may be further described in a free-text set.
Sensor Implant. An aerial mission, which focuses on operations where aircraft are tasked to airdrop sensors over a given geographic area.

Surface Combat Air Patrol (SUCAP). Combat air patrol flown in support of surface vessels conducting maritime operations. ATO mission that represents five specific AOMSW missions: surface surveillance coordination (SSC), armed reconnaissance (AR)/strike coordination and reconnaissance (SCAR), war-at-sea (WAS) strike, counter-fast attack craft (FAC)/fast inshore attack craft (FIAC), and airborne maritime mining (AMM).
Fighter Sweep. An aerial offensive mission conducted by fighter aircraft to seek out and destroy enemy aircraft or targets of opportunity in an allotted area of operations.
Tactical Aircraft Coordinator (Airborne). An officer who coordinates, from an aircraft, the actions of other aircraft engaged in air support of ground or sea forces.
Tactical Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on airdrop of troops or cargo into a hostile environment.

Theater Airlift. That airlift assigned or attached to a Combatant Commander other than Commander, US Transportation Command, that provides air movement and delivery of personnel and equipment directly into objective areas through air landing, airdrop, extraction, or other delivery techniques; and the air logistic support of all theater forces, including those engaged in combat operations, to meet specific theater objectives and requirements.
Tactical Airland (Assault). An aerial mission, which focuses on cargo and/or passengers delivered by air-landing the aircraft.

Tactical Air Reconnaissance (Land). The use of air vehicles to obtain information concerning terrain, weather, and the disposition, composition, movement, installations, lines of communications, electronic, and communication emissions of enemy forces.  Also included are artillery and naval gunfire adjustment, and systematic and random observation of ground battle areas, targets, and/or sectors of airspace.
Operational Training. Training that develops, maintains or improves the operational readiness of individuals or units.
Utility Flight. An aerial mission in which the aircraft has the capability of performing multiple missions.
Very Important Person (VIP) Lift. An aerial mission, which focuses on the air transport of high ranking and/or important individuals.

Weather Reconnaissance (Recce). An aerial mission to obtain, by visual observation or other detection methods, information concerning the meteorological or hydrographic characteristics of a particular area.

Airborne Alert Anti-Air Warfare. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform anti-air operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Airborne Early Warning. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform early warning operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Attack Helicopter. A state of aircraft readiness wherein rotary-wing aircraft are airborne and ready to perform attack operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Interdiction. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform interdiction operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.
Armed Reconnaissance (Maritime). A mission with the primary purpose of locating and attacking enemy maritime targets of opportunity.

Airborne Alert Aeromedical Evacuation. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform aeromedical evacuation operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.
Airborne Alert Troop/Cargo Helicopter Operation. A state of aircraft readiness wherein helicopter aircraft are airborne and ready to perform transportation operations for troops or cargo.

Airborne Alert Aerial Refueling. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform aerial refueling operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Anti-Submarine Warfare. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform anti-submarine operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.
Airborne Alert Attack. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to employ various weapons to destroy enemy targets.

Airborne Alert Barrier Combat Air Patrol. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform barrier combat air patrol operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Combat Air Patrol. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform combat air patrol operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Close Air Support. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform close air support operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Communications Relay. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and fitted with communication relay stations for the purpose of increasing the range, flexibility, or physical security of communications systems.

Airborne Alert Defensive Counterair. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform defensive counterair operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.
Airborne Alert Escort. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform escort operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Electronic Warfare. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform electronic warfare operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Forward Air Controller. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform forward air control operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.
Airborne Alert Illumination. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform battlefield illumination by airdropping high-powered flares.
Airborne Alert Joint Communications Center/Command Post. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform joint command and control operations.
Airborne Alert Minelaying. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to airdrop an encased explosive over ground or in water and set to explode when disturbed.
Airborne Alert Minesweeping. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to locate minefields and neutralize them by dropping ordnance over the area.

Airborne Alert Offensive Counterair. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform offensive counterair operations.  It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Reconnaissance. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform reconnaissance operations. It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Strategic Attack. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform any long range air operation meant to strike an enemy at the sources of its military, economic, or political power.

Airborne Alert Search and Rescue. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform search and rescue operations. It is designed to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.

Airborne Alert Suppression Enemy Air Defense. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform activities which neutralizes, destroys, or temporarily degrades enemy air defenses in a specific area by physical attack and/or electronic warfare.
Airborne Alert Sensor Implant. A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to airdrop sensors.

Airborne Alert Surface Combat Air Patrol (SUCAP). A state of aircraft readiness wherein aircraft are airborne and ready to perform a combat air patrol in support of surface vessels conducting maritime operations. ATO mission that represents airborne alert variations of five specific AOMSW missions: surface surveillance coordination (SSC), armed reconnaissance (AR)/strike coordination and reconnaissance (SCAR), war-at-sea (WAS) strike, counter-fast attack craft (FAC)/fast inshore attack craft (FIAC), and airborne maritime mining (AMM).

Abort Complete. The reconnaissance mission is aborted after entering denied airspace or the RRA, or a mission planned outside denied airspace or RRA has completed more than one-half (50%) of the scheduled collection.

Abort Incomplete. The reconnaissance mission is aborted before entering denied airspace or the RRA, or a mission planned outside denied airspace or RRA has completed less than one-half (50%) of the scheduled collection time.

As Scheduled. The reconnaissance mission launched within plus or minus thirty minutes of the scheduled departure time or plus or minus thirty minutes of the scheduled arrival time at the scheduled recovery base.

Deviation. The reconnaissance mission deviates more than thirty minutes from the scheduled departure or arrival times or the mission launches or recovers at any base other than the scheduled recovery base.
Other ASW Operational Tasking. Includes convoy support, barrier ops, investigations, and water sampling. Assigned tgt level or higher trademark, omitting the words case and desig.
Unrestricted Submarine Services. Use last name of submarine.
Coordinated ASW Training Operations. Use last name of the OCE and submarine separated by a hyphen (e.g., CASW-FIFE-GURNARD).
Ice Patrol. Track name or operation name.
Surface Intelligence Collection. Flight tasked against a surface intelligence collection unit. Use last name of unit, or vessel pennant number (e.g., PELENG).
Logistics Support Flight. Use assigned name (e.g., CYNTHIA 14).
Maritime Air Patrol. Designated track/area name.
Restricted Submarine Services. Use last name of submarine.

Former Soviet Submarine Prosecution Program. Prosecution program specifically in response to former Soviet submarine patrols on station. Assigned target level or higher trademark. Omit the words case and desig. Use INVEST if no trademark is assigned.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Peacetime Aerial Reconnaissance Program (PARPRO). Track designator or name.
Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation. Research, development, test, and evaluation support tasking. Use RDTE project code or name.
Relocation Mission. Use last name of vessel or class and hull number (e.g., SVERDLOV 382) or ship pendant number (e.g., MB11).
Reposition. Reason for reposition (e.g., deployment, ice recce, etc.).
Search and Rescue. Use last name of distressed vessel or aircraft, or medevac, when appropriate.
Support Services. Tasked collateral services in support of another command. Use the unit or command for which services are provided.
Special Operations. Use a nickname or brief description of the operation (e.g., SOJOPS).
Surveillance. Used when the objective is observation and information. Use mission objective (e.g., SMRIS), assigned operation or code name (e.g., Team Spirit), or track name.

Unit Training. Use ADVASW, BASASW, WST, or leave blank for miscellaneous training. SOSEX flights will be reported following an ADVASW entry. No other qualification exercises will be reported in this field (e.g., UNIT-ADVASW-SOSEX).
Intermittent or Selective Use of Electronics.
Unrestricted If Line of Sight Only.
Intermittent or Selective Use of Line of Sight Only.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Target Fired Upon. The target has been fired upon (fire mission has been conducted against the target).
Refueling Anchor. The point or set of points that establishes a refueling anchor.
CAP Point. Combat Air Patrol (CAP) point.
Center. The center of a circle.
Commence Search Point. Point at which to start search.

End Point. The point an aircraft should cross to complete a mission track flown while employing special equipment (e.g., dispensers, emitters, sensors). Used in conjunction with initial point (IP) to depict a mission track.
Holding Point. The point an aircraft should orbit at until instructed to proceed on the mission by the appropriate authority.

Initial Point. The point an aircraft should cross when initiating the final phase of the mission. When used in conjunction with End Point (EP), IP refers to the start point of a mission track flown while employing special equipment (e.g., seeder of a chaff corridor).
Orbit Coordinates. The set of points that establishes the area within which an aircraft should orbit.
Survivor Pickup Point. The point established as a survivor pickup point.
Rendezvous Point. The point established as a rendezvous.
Naval Ship Coordinates. The set of points that establishes the location of a ship centrally involved in an air mission.
Search Area. Area to be searched.
Strip Coordinates. The set of points that establishes the strip of area to be reconnoitered.
Target Area Coordinates. The set of points that establishes a target area.
Target Points. The individual points that should be reconnoitered, the points that allow for new pinpoint data coverage, or attack.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Anti-Air Warfare. Measures taken to defend a maritime force against attacks by airborne weapons launched from aircraft, ships, submarines, and land-based sites.

Air Interdiction. Air operations conducted to destroy, neutralize, or delay the enemy's military potential before it can be brought to bear effectively against friendly forces at such distance from friendly forces that detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of friendly forces is not required.  Does not include battlefield interdiction for this usage.

Close Air Support. Air action against hostile targets which are in close proximity to friendly forces and which require detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of those forces.

Command and Control. An aerial mission in which a properly designated commander exercises authority and direction over assigned and attached forces in the accomplishment of the task, command, and control functions are performed through an arrangement of personnel, equipment, communications, facilities, and procedures employed by a commander in planning, directing, coordinating, and controlling forces and operations in the accomplishment of the mission.

Defensive Counterair. An aerial mission, which focuses on all defensive measures designed to detect, identify, intercept, and destroy or negate enemy forces attempting to attack or penetrate the friendly air environment.

Electronic Attack. An aerial mission conducted by a division of electronic warfare involving the use of electromagnetic energy, directed energy, or anti-radiation weapons to attack personnel, facilities, or equipment with the intent of degrading, neutralizing, or destroying enemy combat capability and is considered a form of fires.
Escort. Aircraft assigned to protect other aircraft during a mission.
Forward Air Controller. A qualified individual who, from a forward position on the or in the air, directs the action of combat aircraft engaged in close air support of land forces.

Offensive Counterair. Offensive operations to destroy, disrupt, or neutralize enemy aircraft, missiles, launch platforms, and their supporting structures and systems both before and after launch, but as close to their source as possible. Offensive counterair operations range throughout enemy territory and are generally conducted at the initiative of friendly forces. These operations include attack operations, fighter sweep, escort, and suppression of enemy air defenses.
Other. Indicates the mission is something other than any of the missions listed. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.

Reconnaissance. A mission undertaken to obtain, by visual observation or other detection methods, information about the activities and resources of an enemy or potential enemy, or to secure data concerning the meteorological, hydrographic, or geographic characteristics of a particular area.
Reserve. A force held to counter unforeseen situations or to impact on future events.
Rescue. The use of aircraft, surface craft (land or water), submarines, specialized rescue teams, and equipment to rescue personnel in distress on land or at sea.

Special Operations. Military activities conducted by specially designated, organized, trained, and equipped forces using operational techniques and modes of employment not standard to conventional forces. These activities are conducted across the full range of military operations independently or in coordination with operations of conventional forces to achieve political, military, psychological, and economic objectives. Politico-military considerations may require clandestine, covert, or discrete techniques and the acceptance of a degree of physical and political risk not associated with conventional operations.
Support. The action of a force, or portion thereof, which aids, protects, complements, or sustains any other force.
Tactical Airdrop. An aerial mission, which focuses on airdrop of troops or cargo into a hostile environment.
Tactical Airland (Assault). An aerial mission, which focuses on cargo and/or passengers delivered by air-landing the aircraft.

Unconventional Warfare. General term used to describe operations conducted for military, political, or economic purposes within an area occupied by the enemy and making use of the local inhabitants and resources.
Aerial Refueling. An airborne tanker and another aircraft conducting refueling operations.
Aerial Combat Maneuvers. The aerial maneuvers used to effectively employ fighter aircraft against hostile or simulated hostile aircraft.
Aircraft Refueling. The process of replenishing an aircraft with fuel.
Antisubmarine Warfare, Air. Aerial operations conducted with the intention of denying the enemy the effective use of his submarines.
Aircraft Airborne. A term applied to an aircraft from the instant it becomes entirely sustained by air.
Interdiction. To isolate or seal off an area by any means, i.e., to deny use of a route or approach.
Air Sampling. An operation in which specifically equipped aircraft collect samples of air in the atmosphere.
Aircraft Arrival. The arrival or landing of an aircraft.
Barrier Combat Air Patrol. One or more divisions or elements of fighter aircraft employed between a force and an objective area as a barrier across the probable direction of enemy attack.
Bombing. A term for air operations when using air to ground ordnance to destroy or neutralize enemy forces or installations.

Combat Air Patrol. An aircraft patrol provided over an objective area, over the force protected, over the critical area of a combat zone, or over an air defense area, for the purpose of intercepting and destroying hostile aircraft before they reach their target.
Cargo Transport. Air movement of military supplies and equipment.

Close Air Support. Air attacks against hostile targets which are in close proximity to friendly forces and which require detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of these forces.

Defensive Counterair. A term for air operations conducted to attain and maintain a desired degree of air superiority by the destruction or neutralization of enemy forces, conducted near to or over friendly territory and generally reactive to the initiative of the enemy air forces.
Defense Suppression. An air suppression mission, e.g., Wild Weasel mission.
Aircraft Deployments. The relocation of aircraft to desired areas of operation.
Escort. In air operations, aircraft assigned to protect other aircraft during a mission.

Electronic Warfare. Military action involving the use of electromagnetic energy to determine, exploit, reduce, or prevent hostile use of the electromagnetic spectrum and action which retains friendly use of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Ground Alert. That status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified short period of time (usually 15 minutes) after receipt of a mission order.
Minelaying, Air. The process of placing mines in a minefield by aerial means.
Minesweeping. The technique of searching for, or clearing mines using mechanical or explosion gear, which physically removes or destroys the mine.
Mine Clearing, Engineering. The process of detecting and/or removing mines by manual or mechanical means.

Offensive Counterair. A term for air operations conducted to attain and maintain a desired degree of air superiority by the destruction or neutralization of enemy forces, conducted throughout enemy territory and generally conducted at the initiative of friendly forces.
Offload. In air operations, to remove cargo and/or equipment from an aircraft.
Onload. In air operations, to place cargo and/or equipment in an aircraft.
Orbiting. In air intercept, means circling or circle and search.

Photo Reconnaissance. Aerial photography for use in intelligence.

Reconnaissance. A mission undertaken to obtain, by visual observations or other detection methods, information about the activities and resources of an enemy or potential enemy. A visual observation or detection by other means with the goal of securing data.
Search and Rescue. The use of aircraft, surface craft, submarine, specialized rescue teams and equipment to search for and rescue personnel in distress on land or at sea.
Personnel Shuttling. Repetitive, frequent movements of personnel between two or more locations.
Special Operations. Secondary or supporting operations which may be adjuncts to various other operations and for which no one service is assigned primary responsibility.
Supply. Replenish/refuel to a location ashore.
Aircraft Takeoff. The takeoff or departure of an aircraft.
Target Antisubmarine Patrol. The systematic and continuing investigation of an area or along a line to detect or hamper submarines.
Targeting. The detection, identification and location of a target.
Transport, General. The movement of non-specific personnel and/or cargo.
Weather Collection. The collection of meteorological information.

Duststorm, Heavy. A duststorm is reported as heavy when the prevailing visibility is reduced to less than 5/16 statute mile.
Tornado or Waterspout. A violent, rotating column of air, forming a pendant and touching the ground or water.
Heavy Small Hail and/or Ice Pellets.
Rain, Heavy. Intense precipitation of liquid water particles.  Rain seemingly falls in sheets at a rate greater than 0.30 inches (7.6 mm) per hour.
Snow, Heavy. Intense precipitation of ice crystals falling at a rate greater than 0.30 inches (7.6 mm) per hour.
Sandstorm, Heavy. A sandstorm is reported as heavy when the prevailing visibility is reduced to less than 5/16 statute mile.

Patchy Fog. When fog covers portions of the station and the apparent visibility in the fog or bank is less than 5/8 statute miles and visibility over the uncovered portions of the station is 5/8 statute miles or greater.
Blowing Dust. Dust raised by the wind to a height sufficient to reduce the horizontal visibility to below 7 statute miles.

Blowing Spray. Water droplets torn by the wind from a body of water, generally from the crest of waves, and carried up into the air in such quantities that reduces the horizontal visibility to below 7 statute miles.
Blowing Sand. Sand raised by the wind to a height sufficient to reduce the horizontal visibility to below 7 statute miles.
Blowing Snow. Snow raised by the wind to a height sufficient to reduce the horizontal visibility to below 7 statute miles.

Mist. A visible aggregate of microscopic and more-or-less hygroscopic water droplets suspended in the atmosphere, based at the earth's surface, which reduces prevailing visibility to between 5/8 and 6 statute miles.

Low Drifting Dust. Dust raised by the wind to less than 6 feet above the ground. Visibility is not reduced below 7 statute miles at eye level although obstructions below this level may be veiled or hidden by the particles moving nearly horizontal to the ground.

Low Drifting Sand. Sand raised by the wind to less than 6 feet above the ground. Visibility is not reduced below 7 statute miles at eye level although obstructions below this level may be veiled or hidden by the particles moving nearly horizontal to the ground.

Low Drifting Snow. Snow raised by the wind to less than 6 feet above the ground. Visibility is not reduced below 7 statute miles at eye level although obstructions below this level may be veiled or hidden by the particles moving nearly horizontal to the ground.
Duststorm. An unusual, frequently severe weather condition characterized by strong winds and dust-filled air over an extensive area.
Widespread Dust. Fine particles of dust or sand suspended in the air by a duststorm or sandstorm that may have occurred at or far away from the station.
Drizzle. Fairly uniform precipitation composed exclusively of fine drops (diameter less than 0.02 inch) very close together.
Funnel Cloud. A violent, rotating column of air which does not touch the surface, usually a pendant from a cumulonimbus cloud.

Fog. A visible aggregate of minute water particles (droplets) which are based at the earth's surface. Fog reduces horizontal and vertical visibility, and may extend over a sizeable area. In surface reports, fog is recorded when the depth of the phenomena is greater than 20 feet and reduces prevailing visibility to less than 5/8 statute miles.
Smoke. A suspension of small particles in the air produced by combustion.
Freezing Drizzle. Drizzle which freezes upon impact with the ground or with objects in flight or on the ground.

Freezing Fog. A suspension of numerous minute ice crystals in the air, or water droplets at temperatures below 0 Celsius, based at the earth's surface, which reduces horizontal visibility to less than 7 statute miles.
Freezing Rain. Rain which freezes upon impact with the ground or with objects in flight or on the ground.

Hail. Precipitation in the form of small balls or other pieces of ice (hailstones) falling separately or frozen together in irregular lumps. Hailstones consist of alternate opaque and clear layers of ice in most cases.

Small Hail and/or Ice Pellets. Precipitation of white, opaque grains of ice.  The grains are sometimes round and sometimes conical.  Diameters range from about 0.08 to 0.2 inch.  Snow pellets are brittle and easily crushed; when they fall on hard ground, they bounce and often break up.
Small Hail and/or Ice Pellets, Light.

Haze. A suspension in the air of extremely small, dry particles invisible to the naked eye and sufficiently numerous to give the air an opalescent appearance. This phenomenon resembles a uniform veil over the landscape that subdues all colors.
Ice Crystals. Unbranched ice crystals in the form of needles, columns, or plates.

Shallow Ground Fog. When fog covers the surrounding area and visibility at 6 feet above the ground is (1) 7 statute miles or more and (2) the apparent visibility in the fog layer is less than 5/8 statute miles.

Ice Pellets. Precipitation of transparent or translucent pellets of ice, which are round or irregular, rarely conical, and which have a diameter of 0.2 inch, or less. They may be hard grains of ice consisting of frozen raindrops (sleet) or pellets of snow encased in a thin layer of ice.

Well-Developed Dust/Sand Whirls. An ensemble of particles of dust or sand, sometimes accompanied by small litter, raised from ground in the form of a whirling column of varying height with a small diameter and an approximately vertical axis. Also known as dust devils.

Partial Fog. When fog covers a substantial part of the station and visibility in the fog is less than 5/8 statute miles and visibility over the uncovered parts of the station is 5/8 statute miles or more.

Spray. An ensemble of water droplets torn by the wind from the surface of an extensive body of water, generally from the crest of waves, and carried up a short distance in the air in such quantities as to reduce the horizontal visibility at eye level (6 feet).
Rain. Precipitation of liquid water particles, either in the form of drops larger than 0.02 inch, or smaller drops which, in contrast to drizzle, are widely separated.
Rain, Light. Precipitation of liquid water particles generally falling at a rate of a trace up to 0.10 inches (2.5 mm) per hour.
Sand. Sand raised by the wind to moderate heights above ground.

Snow Grains. Precipitation of very small, white, opaque grains of ice. When the grains hit hard ground, they do not bounce or shatter. They usually fall in small quantities, mostly from stratus type clouds, and never as showers.
Hail Showers. Precipitation of hail that is showery in nature.
Small Hail/Snow Pellet Showers. Small hail/snow pellet events which start and stop abruptly.
Ice Pellet Showers. Precipitation of ice pellets that is showery in nature
Rain Shower. Precipitation of liquid water particles which changes intensity or starts and stops abruptly.
Snow Shower. Precipitation of ice crystals which changes intensity or starts and stops abruptly.
Clear. Reported when 0/8 of the sky is covered.
Snow. Precipitation of snow crystals, mostly branched in the form of six-pointed stars.  At temperatures higher than about -5 degrees Celsius, the crystals are generally clustered to form snowflakes.
Snow, Light. Precipitation of ice crystals, mostly branched in the form of six-pointed stars falling at a rate less than 0.10 inches (2.5 mm) per hour.
Squalls. A strong wind characterized by a sudden onset in which the wind speed increases at least 16 knots and is sustained at 22 knots or more for at least one minute.
Sandstorm. Particles of sand that are carried aloft by strong wind. The sand particles are mostly confined to the lowest ten feet, and rarely rise more than fifty feet above the ground.
Thunderstorm. A local storm produced by a cumulonimbus that is accompanied by lighting and/or thunder, usually with gusty winds, heavy rain, and sometimes, with hail.
Volcanic Ash. Fine particles of rock powder that are blown out from a volcano and that may remain suspended in the atmosphere for long periods.

Airfield. An area prepared for the accommodation (including any buildings, installations, and equipment), landing and take-off of aircraft.

Bar. An elongated offshore ridge or mound composed of unconsolidated material such as sand, gravel, or shells. Bars are usually submerged, parallel to and a short distance from the coastline, often at the mouth of a river or estuary.

Barrier Reef. An elongated ridge or rock or coral and/or coral-like organisms, near and roughly parallel to the coast. It is separated from the shore by the deep water of a lagoon, and is cut through at intervals by channels or passes.
Beach Swale. An elongated, sometimes marshy depression, between two ridges on the beach backshore (or on a sandpit), generally paralleling the shoreline.
Building. A fixed construction, covering a space on land (or in the immediate nearshore), usually covered with a roof, enclosed by walls, or designed to stand more or less permanently.

Breakwater. A long, solid structure, sometimes attached to the shore, built to protect a shore area, harbor, anchorage, or basin from the impact of waves. A breakwater is usually made of stone, concrete blocks, rubble, or other material. Breakwaters are usually associated with harbors and anchorages exposed to open sea.

Barrier System. A coordinated series of obstacles designed or employed to canalize, direct, restrict, delay, or stop the movement of an opposing force, and to impose additional losses in personnel, time, and equipment on the opposing force.
Bunker. A fortified chamber mostly below ground, often built with reinforced concrete and provided with embrasures.

Buoy. A floating object, anchored in a river or ocean bottom and used as a navigation aid to mark a channel, anchorage, or hazard. The buoy may be attached by a line or cable to an anchor or weight lying on the bottom.
Barbed Wire. Twisted wires armed with barbs or sharp points.
Cable. A strong rope, wire, or metal chain used for mooring vessels, buoys, etc., or an electric or communication wire.
Cave. A natural underground chamber open to the surface.
Church (Chapel, Temple). A building for public worship.
Contamination. The deposit and/or absorption of radioactive material, biological or chemical agents on or by structures, areas, personnel, or objects.

Crater. The pit, depression, or cavity formed in the surface of the earth by an explosion. It may range from saucer shape to conical, depending largely on the depth of burst. In the case of a deep underground burst, no rupture of the surface may occur. The resulting cavity is termed a camouflet.
Dam. A barrier preventing the flow of water.
Depression. A hollow in the terrain.
Ditch, Tank. A barrier prepared to stop, impede, or divert movement of hostile tanks.
Emplacement. A prepared position for one or more weapons or pieces of equipment, for protection against hostile fire or bombardment, and from which they can execute their tasks.
Fence. A barrier, usually marking a boundary consisting of wooden or metal pickets, or else supporting wire or rail.
Foxhole. A pit dug usually hastily for individual cover against enemy fire.
Fortification/Structure. Works erected to defend a place or position.

Fishnet. A fish-catching device which is a fabric made from such materials as string and cord, woven in an openwork pattern. It may be suspended over water and attached to poles or the fishnet may lie on the bottom.
Fishstake. Bamboo-like material used to channelize fish into a funnel-like trap.

Groin. A one hundred to several hundred foot long, low, narrow, wall-like man-made protective structure. It is usually perpendicular to and extends from the backshore. It is designed to trap littoral drift or retard erosion. Groins are usually constructed of wood, masonry, steel reinforced concrete, or loosely piled rock and are spaced at intervals along the shore.
Headland. A comparatively high, steep-faced promontory, which projects into a body of water.
Helipad. A prepared landing area designated and used for the takeoff and landing of helicopters (including touchdown and/or hover point).
Hilltop. The highest part of a hill.
Ice Inlet. A narrow arm of sea which may extend a considerable distance inland. A short, narrow channel connecting a bay to a lagoon or a lagoon with the sea. A narrow strip of water between islands.
Island. A land mass exposed during all tidal conditions which is completely surrounded by water, and whose longest axis is greater than 100 meters.

Jetty. A solid, linear, wall-like structure used to improve and stabilize tidal inlets and river mouths. Jetties project at an angle seaward from the shoreline through the normal surf zone. Usually constructed in pairs at the mouth of a river, inlet, or a harbor entrance. This is to prevent deposition of sand (shoaling) in the channel, regulate tides and river discharge, regulate, restrain and divert currents and protect vessels entering the channel against wave action.
Lake. A considerable inland body of standing water.
Landing Strip (Fixed Wing). An unimproved surface which has been adapted for takeoff and landing of fixed wing aircraft, usually having minimum facilities.
Landslide. A mass of rock, earth or artificial fill that has moved down a slope.
Logs. A section of the trunk of a felled tree adrift in the water off a beach or shore or ensnared on the sea bottom.
Marsh (Swamp). A track of soft, wet land.

Medical Facility. A structure or group of structures, permanent or temporary, which has a primary purpose of providing preventative or remedial medical treatment to personnel. Includes hospitals and aid stations.

Mine. An encased explosive or other material (e.g., chemicals) designed to destroy material or to wound, kill or otherwise incapacitate personnel. Mines are laid on or below the surface of the ground and/or in inland waterways or the sea approach area, so as to stop, delay, or divert amphibious landing or ground force movement. In the sea approach, the fixed mine is either bottomlaid or moored by a cable to an anchor or weight in the water.
Military Obstacle. Any man-made device (except mines) or passive defense works such as a barrier which is designed to stop, impede, or divert movement of amphibious or ground forces.
Minefield. An area of ground containing mines laid with or without pattern.

Mole. A massive, solid fill structure projecting at an angle from the shore.  A mole protects a harbor from the force of waves and may serve as a pier or breakwater or both. Usually revetted with masonry or large stone. Its broad surface may support buildings, cargo handling equipment, rail spurs and roads.
None. There is no natural or man-made terrain feature or object which is likely to impede the free movement of forces moving toward an objective.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.

Pier. A long, narrow structure which provides berthing for ships. It extends into a body of water at an angle to the shore and is made of piles, stone, or concrete. A pier may be straight, T-shaped, or L-shaped, with berthing along both sides and at its ends. It may support storage facilities, cargo handling equipment, and railroad tracks.
Pillbox. A small, low fortification that houses machine guns, antitank weapons, etc. A pillbox is usually made of concrete, steel, or filled sandbags.
Pipeline. A line of pipe, including pumping machinery, servicing and supporting structures, used for conveying liquids, gases, or finely crushed solids (e.g., slurry).

Piling. Wood, metal or reinforced concrete poles driven into the land or sea bottom, singly or in clusters (dolphins). Pilings extend above water to serve as supports, as for a pier, protection for moorings, or to resist lateral pressure.
Point. A small promontory which projects into a body of water.
Roadblock. A barrier or obstacle (usually covered by fire) used to block or limit movement of hostile vehicles along a route.
Junction, Road. An intersection of roads.

Reef. A low coastal ridge of rock or coral which is offshore (barrier reef) or closely attached to the shore (fringing reef). Most reefs extend upward from the sea floor and lie at or near the water surface at a depth which makes them a danger to surface vessels. Most reefs are submerged, especially at high tide.
Revetment. An embankment to provide shelter (as against bomb splinters or strafing).
Ridge. An elongated crest or series of crests of hills or mountains.

River. A natural stream of water which flows permanently or seasonally. A river has greater volume than a creek or rivulet, flows in a more or less permanent bed or channel between defined banks or walls.
Runnel. An elongated trough or depression of the beach on the foreshore or nearshore bottom, approximately parallel to the shoreline.
Road. An open way for vehicles, persons, or animals.

Rock. A consolidated or coherent and relatively hard, naturally formed mass of mineral matter. Also an aggregate of angular pieces of stone larger than 76 mm (3 inches) in diameter. Rock may occur as an isolated rocky formation or a single large stone. In the sea it may be submerged, uncovered, or alternatively covered and uncovered by the tide.
Crossing, Railroad. A place where railroad track crosses a highway or street.
Junction, Railroad. An intersection of railroads.
Ruin. The remains of a cultural feature such as a building, or an object that has been destroyed or has decayed.
Crossing, River. A place where a river can be crossed.
Saddle. A ridge connecting two higher elevations.
School. A building used to provide instruction.

Shoal. A submerged ridge, bank or bar which is a detached elevation of the sea bottom. A shoal is composed of, or covered by sand, gravel, mud or other consolidated sediments. It is at or near enough to the water surface to constitute a danger to surface navigation.
Spit. A low, elongated, exposed deposit of waterborne sediment, such as a reef, shoal or sandbank, which protrudes from the shore and terminates in the water.

Stake. A length of material, usually metal or wood, pointed at one end for driving into the ground. May be used for such purposes as anchoring a fish trap, as a boundary marker, or as a military obstacle. May be submerged.
Stream. A narrow body of flowing water or other fluid, great or small, occupying a channel on land.
Seaweed. Underwater plant life such as seagrass and marine algae.
Tidal Flat. A relatively broad, virtually level coastal flatland of sand, mud, or mudsand which is periodically covered and uncovered by the rise and fall of the tide.
Terrain. The physical features of a tract of land.
Tower. A tall, vertical, obstruction, e.g., radio tower.
Railroad (Tracks). The metal rails forming the path for a train.
Trail. A marked path through forest or mountainous region.
Blowdown, Tree. Tree felled by wind.
Trench. A long cut in the ground used for military defense, often with excavated dirt thrown up in front.
Junction, Trail. An intersection of trails.
Tunnel. A horizontal passageway through or under an obstruction.
Valley. An elongated depression of the earth's surface usually between a range of hills or mountains.
Wall. A continuous, vertical structure, such as a concrete or rock wall serving to enclose, divide, support, or protect an area on land. Includes seawalls.

Wreck. A hulk or ruin of a wrecked or stranded ship, either submerged or visible, which is attached to or foul of the bottom, or cast up on the shore. Includes abandoned, incapacitated vehicle hulls or airframes on land.

Drizzle. Fairly uniform precipitation composed exclusively of fine drops (diameter less than 0.02 inch) very close together.

Hail. Precipitation in the form of small balls or other pieces of ice (hailstones) falling separately or frozen together in irregular lumps. Hailstones consist of alternate opaque and clear layers of ice in most cases.

Small Hail and/or Snow Pellets. Precipitation of white, opaque grains of ice. The grains are sometimes round and sometimes conical.  Diameters range from about 0.08 to 0.2 inch.  Snow pellets are brittle and easily crushed; when they fall on hard ground, they bounce and often break up.
Ice Crystals. Unbranched ice crystals in the form of needles, columns, or plates.

Ice Pellets. Precipitation of transparent or translucent pellets of ice, which are round or irregular, rarely conical, and which have a diameter of 0.2 inch, or less.  They may be hard grains of ice consisting of frozen raindrops (sleet) or pellets of snow encased in a thin layer of ice.
Rain. Precipitation of liquid water particles, either in the form of drops larger than 0.02 inch, or smaller drops which, in contrast to drizzle, are widely separated.

Snow Grains. Precipitation of very small, white, opaque grains of ice.  When the grains hit hard ground, they do not bounce or shatter.  They usually fall in small quantities, mostly from stratus type clouds, and never as showers.
Snow. Precipitation of snow crystals, mostly branched in the form of six-pointed stars.  At temperatures higher than about -5 degrees Celsius, the crystals are generally clustered to form snowflakes.

Graving Dock. An elongated basin of masonry or concrete that is fitted with gates or a caisson at the entrance. It is designed so that a ship may be floated in and the water pumped out, leaving the ship's hull exposed for repair, overhaul, etc.

If reporting a ship as the unit, omit the government designation. For example, enter the USS ROBERT G. BRADLEY as the BRADLEY RG.
Bulk. Cargo that will fit on a 463L pallet.
Burn. Target or target elements are burning.
Destruction. Material attacked (or to be attacked) has been (or will be) destroyed.
Flak Suppression. Ordnance delivered (or to be delivered) have suppressed (or will suppress) antiaircraft fire immediately prior to and during an air attack.

Harassment. Ordnance delivered (or to be delivered) have disturbed (or will disturb) the rest, curtailed (or will curtail) the movement, and lowered (or will lower) the morale of enemy troops by threat of casualties or losses in material.
Interdiction. Ordnance delivered (or to be delivered) have denied (or will deny) the enemy the unrestricted use of an area or point.
Illumination. Ordnance delivered (or to be delivered) to provide illumination of an area during hours of darkness.

Neutralization. Ordnance delivered (or to be delivered) have reduced (or will reduce) the combat effectiveness of the enemy by interrupting and hampering the fire of his weapons, by reducing his ability to inflict casualties on friendly forces and by severely reducing his movements within an area.
No Effect. Attack of the target had no significant effect on the target.
Search for. The desired result is to search for the SAR objective(s).
Recover. The desired result is to recover the search and rescue (SAR) objectives.
Smoke. Ordnance delivered (or to be delivered) to mark or obscure the target.
Multiple-Simultaneous Frequencies. Simultaneous operation on two or more discrete frequencies.
Shifting Frequency Operation. Shifting frequency (e.g., switching, sliding, stepping, or sweeping).
Decibel Referenced to 1 Milliwatt. A negative sign is always understood. Used for measurement of received Radio Frequency (RF) power.
Decibel Watts. Used for measurement of transmitted RF energy.
Right Parenthesis. A character that is used to separate two elements within a data chain.
Motor Way. A controlled access road.
Other Roads. All roads except motor ways. explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Natural Earth. Way improved by grading, rolling, or any other artificial means. Unmaintained.
Earth-Surfaced. Way improved by adding, grading, and rolling topsoil, laterite, etc., to stabilize a clay, sand, or mud subgrade. Requires frequent maintenance.
Loose-Surfaced. Way improved with graded and rolled material such as crushed rock, gravel, coral, etc. Requires periodic maintenance.
Surfaced. Way improved by addition of concrete, asphalt, brick, or bound layers of crushed rock, gravel, coral, etc.
Unsurfaced. Way improved by grading and draining the natural earth surface without adding a stabilizing material (crushed rock, topsoil, etc.).
Usual Coastal Route. The route which follows the shape or boundary of a coast.
Great Circle. The route which follows the shortest arc of a great circle between two points.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Q-Route. The code which delineates a Q-Route point.
Rhumb Line. The route that maintains a fixed compass direction, shown on a map as a line crossing all meridians at the same angle.
Standard Route. The route which follows established route patterns.
Variable Track. Any combination of other standard tracks.
End of Mission. The mission will terminate at the specific point.
End of Route. Identifies the end point of a route.
Initial Point. Identifies the initial point of a route or mission flight path.
Land. The aircraft will land at the route point.
Navigation Point. The aircraft will change course, speed, and/or altitude at this point. The ship will change course and/or speed at this point.
Orbit. The aircraft will orbit around the route point.
Rendezvous Point. The point established as a rendezvous.
Refueling Point. The aircraft will aerial refuel at this point.
Release Point. The aircraft will be released at the route point.
Start Point. The aircraft will start at the route point.
Target. The target of the aircraft is at this point.
Takeoff. The aircraft will take off from the route point.
Termination. The aircraft will terminate its mission at this route point.
Turning Point. The aircraft will change direction at this point.
Other Man-Made. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Other Natural. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Bitumen. A coal tar or petroleum product binding, usually with sand and/or gravel.
Clay. A firm, fine-grained earth, plastic when wet, composed chiefly of hydrous aluminum silicate minerals.
Concrete. Stone, sand, cement, and water mixture.
Coral. A hard stony skeleton secreted by certain marine polyps and often deposited in extensive masses forming reefs and atolls in tropical seas.
Earth. Unrefined soil; the soft granular or crumbly part of land.
Grass. Ground covered with grass, i.e., surface covered by plants with typically long, narrow leaves that grow densely.
Gravel. Small pebbles or stones, may be crushed to achieve uniformity. (Spread and rolled, may be graded.)
Ice. Water frozen, with thickness sufficient to bear weight of specific objects.

Laterite. A residual product of rock decay that is red in color and has a high content of oxides of iron and low proportion of silica; a mottled quarriable type of clay which hardens on exposure to air.
Macadam. Crushed stone rolled to form a smooth, hard surface and bound with clay, tar, or asphalt.
Oil. Surface covered with a substance having smooth, greasy consistency.
Snow. Snow naturally compacted and frozen, forming a solid surface. (Weight-bearing capacity more limited than prepared snow.)
Sod. A surface layer of earth containing grass plants with their matted roots.
Turf. A surface layer similar to sod; however, in most cases a harder grass-covered soil.

The third character (alphabetic) is used if there are parallel runways to indicate "R" for right, "L" for left or "C" for center runway, otherwise this character position is not used.
Runway End Identifier Lights (REIL) (Threshold Strobe Lights).
Runway End Identification Light (Not Strobe Light).
Limited Operations. Aircraft launch and recovery operations from a runway are limited. Explain in subsequent free-text set.
Not Operational. The runway is closed to all aircraft launch and recovery operations. Explain in subsequent free-text set.
Operational. The runway is open to all aircraft launch and recovery operations.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.
Reported Not Operational. The runway is reported closed to all aircraft launch and recovery operations but status has not been confirmed. Explain in subsequent free-text set.
Reported Operational. The runway is reported open to all aircraft launch and recovery operations but status has not been confirmed. Explain in subsequent free-text set.
Unknown. Runway operational status is unknown.
Far. The overrun that is at the end of the runway with the highest magnetic bearing.
Near. The overrun that is at the end of the runway with the lowest magnetic bearing.
All Up Weight. Indication for maximum weight bearing capacity irrespective of landing gear configuration.

Single-Wheel Type Landing Gear. A landing gear with one wheel per strut on the aircraft. Runway qualifiers. For further U.S. implementation guidance, see Repository of USMTF Program Items Document, item 100.
Single-Tandem Landing Gear. Runway weight bearing capacity for aircraft with single-tandem landing gear.
Single Wheel Loading. The maximum load per wheel.
Twin-Wheel Type Landing Gear. Includes single tandem.
Twin Delta Tandem. Runway weight-bearing capacity for aircraft with twin delta tandem landing gear.
Twin-Tandem Type Landing Gear. Includes quadricycle.
Control Channel. Used for communications between the on scene commander and the SAR mission coordinator involved in SAR operations.
Homing Channel. Used to locate a distressed craft or person.
Monitor Channel. Guarded by SAR units throughout SAR operations for possible transmission from distressed craft or survivors.
On Scene Channel. Used for communications between a SAR unit and the on scene Commander involved in SAR operations.
Press Channel. Used by news media personnel.
Actual. The event has occurred and/or the data is actual.
Estimated. The data or event is estimated.
Alert Phase. An alert phase exists when a craft or person has difficulty and may need assistance, but is not in immediate danger or in need of immediate response.
Distress Phase. The distress phase exists when a craft or person is threatened by grave or immediate danger requiring immediate response.
Event Submiss. An emergency phase classification that pertains to the initial search stage for a submarine.
Event Subsunk. An emergency phase classification that pertains to the full-scale search for a submarine.
Uncertainty Phase. An uncertainty phase exists when there is knowledge of a situation requiring monitoring or information gathering, but that does not require moving of resources.
Suspending Activity. Message used to report that a search and rescue mission has been suspended.
Initiate/Terminate. The message is being used to indicate that a search and rescue mission has been initiated and terminated within the reporting period.
Initiate. Message used to initiate a search and rescue mission.
Status Report. Message used to report on the status of a search and rescue mission.
Terminate. Message used to terminate a search and rescue mission.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.

Bi-Directional (Plane Undetermined). The bi-directional movement of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Circular and Conical. The circular and conical movement of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Circular or Rotating. The circular or rotating movement of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Circular and Nodding. The circular and nodding movement of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Conical. The conical movement of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Horizontal Sector (Bidirectional). The bi-directional movement in a horizontal plane of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Helical. The helical movement of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Helical and Conical. The combination of helical and conical movement of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Horizontal Sector (Unidirectional). The uni-directional movement in a horizontal plane of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Irregular, Unsteady or Manual. The irregular, unsteady or manual, movement of emitted electromagnetic energy.
Lobe Switching. The switching lobe movement of emitted electromagnetic energy.
