Cross-Over Barrier. Search pattern used when target motion requires drift compensation.

Creeping Line Single-Unit. Search pattern where the commence search point is located one-half track spacing inside the corner of the search area. Distress is generally known to be between two points. Wider than trackline patterns.

Creeping Line Single-Unit Coordinated. Search pattern used when aircraft and either vessels or boats are available. Aircraft track is planned so that advance of successive legs of the search pattern equals that of the marine craft, and the aircraft passes over the vessel on each leg. Results in a more accurate search pattern, and enables quick rescue by marine craft once survivors are located.
Flare Multiunit. Search pattern used only at night which is similar to the PMN pattern.

Flare Single-Unit. Search pattern used only at night and conducted by a single vessel or helicopter with an aircraft dropping flares. Effective mostly for large objects in well-defined search areas on flat land or at sea.
Homing Multiunit No Return. Same as HSA explanation. Electronic positioning used.

Homing Single-Unit Aural. Search pattern used to locate emergency transmitters or other radio or electronic emissions from survivors or distressed craft when the detected signal is too weak for homing equipment to receive or the SRU does not have homing equipment.
Homing Single-Unit Meter. Same as HSA explanation.
Contour Multiunit. Search pattern used in mountainous/hilly terrain by land search teams.
Contour Single-Unit. Search pattern used in mountainous and hilly terrain. Adaptable to underwater SRUs for searching peaks on the ocean floor.
Parallel Drift Compensated. Search pattern used when target motion requires drift compensation.

Parallel Track Multiunit. Same as PS explanation except that two or more SRUs search abeam each other separated by a distance equal to the track spacing. Provides accurate track spacing and fast area coverage, and an increased safety factor for aircraft over water.
Parallel Multiunit Circle. Search pattern used by two or more underwater swimmers for search of small areas, generally less than 25 yards in diameter.

Parallel Track Multiunit Non-Return. Search pattern is similar to the PMR, except that SRUs continue to a destination other than the departure point. Normally used when en route vessels are available and will alter their tracks to provide uniform coverage of the search area.

Parallel Track Multiunit Return. Search pattern used when simultaneous sweep of an area to maximum radius is desired; used for search of long rectangular area where only one track out and back is possible. Provides concentrated coverage of large areas in a minimum time period, and allows the use of aircraft with different speeds in a parallel search pattern.

Parallel Track Single-Unit. Search pattern used for large areas when the position of distress is unknown. Used for searching rectangular areas and is mostly used by fixed-wing aircraft. Search legs are oriented along the major axis, providing longer legs and fewer turns.

Parallel Track Single-Unit LORAN. Same as PS explanation except that SRU uses LORAN lines for greater navigational accuracy on tracks. Pattern must be oriented so legs flown by SRU are parallel to a system of LORAN lines which are selected at the track spacing desired. One of the most accurate search patterns for searching areas covered by LORAN, Omega, or similar navigational systems.
Parallel Single-Unit Spiral. Search pattern used by a single underwater swimmer for search of small areas, generally less than 25 yards in diameter.
Square Multiunit. Same as SS explanation except two SRUs fly at different altitudes on tracks which differ by 45 degrees.
Square Single-Unit. Search pattern used where distress position is known within close limits or search area is not extensive.
Trackline Multiunit Non-Return. Same as TMR explanation except that search terminates at the opposite end of track from the commence search point.
Trackline Multiunit Return. Same as TSR explanation except that two or more SRUs are used in an abeam formation to afford greater width coverage along track.

Trackline Single-Unit Non-Return. Search pattern is along the track or datum line. SRU makes one or more searches along the track, but the search terminates at the opposite end of track from the commence search point.

Trackline Single-Unit Return. Search pattern where the commence search point is offset one-half search track spacing from the trackline or datum. SRU runs up one side and down the other, ending one track space from where it began.
Sector Single-Unit. Search pattern used where distress position is known within close limits or search area is not extensive.

Sector Single-Unit Radar. Same as VS explanation except that a radar-equipped marine craft takes station at the center of the pattern and provides radar navigation assistance to one aircraft completing a sector search pattern.

Record As Target. Record as a target the location on which a mission was fired.
Abandoned. Target/installation appears devoid of all objects, vehicles, and equipment, and is not in condition to be of immediate use.

Camouflage Concealment, and Deception. Target/installations exhibit some form of camouflage, concealment, and deception activity. The Camouflage, Concealment, and Deception CCD status code will take precedence over all other secondary status codes that may apply. Add any amplifying remarks in another set.
Capable of Emergency Launch. Target/installation has reached that point in construction where it is capable of launching its weapons in an emergency situation.
Cloud Covered. Target is completely obscured by clouds.
Coverage Not Available. No imagery of the target is available.
Complete. Target/installation appears to be externally complete. Appears capable of operating but operational status cannot be determined.
Conversion. Target is undergoing basic change from one activity to another (e.g., a missile site converting from an old to a new system).
Deactivated. Targets that are no longer active, or have been dismantled.
Damaged. Target/installation has been damaged to some extent, but it may be restored to a usable status.
Dummy. An installation created solely for deception to look like an operational installation.

Destroyed. Target is so damaged that it cannot function as intended, nor be restored to a useable condition. In the case of buildings, all vertical supports and spanning members are damaged to an extent that nothing is salvageable. In the case of bridges, all spans must be dropped and all piers require replacement.
Exercise. Target/installation is currently involved in an exercise condition.
Missile Loading and Unloading. Missile site is currently in the process of loading or unloading its weapons.
Periodic Maintenance. Target/installation is currently undergoing periodic maintenance.
Negated (Non-Existent). Target/installation does not exist at or near the coordinates given in the requirement.

Not Operational. Essential elements of a target/installation are observed not to be in operation. Equipment essential to the operation of the installation is either missing or observed to be not operational.
Normal. Essential elements of a target/installation are observed with no unusual activity taking place based on a national statement of normal activity for that target.

Occupied. A completed target/installation, and includes some but not all elements, objects, vehicles, and equipment essential for operational status. This term is also used in describing dummy installations that appear to be inhabited and contains some or all of the objects and equipment necessary to the accomplishment of its designed task.

Operational. Essential elements of a target/installation are observed in operation and/or key objects, vehicles, equipment, and other transportable items which are essential to the operation of the target/installation.
Removed. Target/installation has been dismantled or removed.
Transitory. Fleeting targets to include vehicles, equipment and/or personnel in transit as well as targets which appear to be only temporarily situated.
Under Construction. Target/installation is being initially constructed or repaired, or construction action is underway that will structurally modify an established installation.

Unknown. Status of target cannot be determined. Term is used in describing a target/installation which may be interpreted to some degree, although the status/activity cannot be determined because of limiting factors, (e.g., imagery limitations, camouflage, jungle canopy, etc.).
Unoccupied. Target/installation appears devoid of all objects, vehicles, or equipment, but remains in condition to be of immediate use.
Excess Seats/Pallets. Excess seats/pallets due to larger substitute aircraft.
Excess Seats. Excess seats - capability exceeds stated requirement.
Gained. Gained from previous station not using allocation.
Insufficient Cargo On Hand. Insufficient processed/palletized cargo on hand.
Low Port Level. Low port level - insufficient cargo of any type on hand.
Unsuitable Cargo. Unsuitable cargo (hazard or special handling).
Space Block. Space block - space reserved for downline station.
Aircraft Fully Utilized - Passenger. Passenger only = 95%.
Aircraft Fully Utilized - Cargo. Cargo only = 95%.

Guards, Stationary. Guards who are posted to one station.
Guards, Walking. Guards who walk the perimeter and interior of the facility.

Acoustic. Detects the transmission of sound through various media or in various enclosures or conduits, including the effects of reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction, and absorption.
Commandable Acoustic. Controllable by commands from other sources.

Electronic. Detects the output of electron devices, circuits or systems utilizing electron devices, including electron tubes, magnetic amplifiers, transistors, and other devices that do the work of electron tubes.
Electromagnetic. Detects radio (short-wave and ultra short-wave), infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, x-rays, and gamma-rays waves.

Forward Looking Infrared (FLIR). An imaging scanning electro-optical receiver which is mounted in the front of an airplane to cover the forward sector. The FLIR images on the basis of emitted target radiation due to the target's temperature as contrasted with its background. This contrast is the basis of passive imaging used in these FLIR systems.

Frame Photography. Examples of this type of photography are photography taken of one complete coverage of a television picture, or of the rectangular area representing the size of copy handled by a facsimile system.

Gas Detection. Gas detectors come in two basic types, combustion-type and thermal -conductivity type. The most commonly used combustion type employs a self-heated "hot wire" detector, usually platinum, which serves as a combustion catalyst. After the combustion process is started, a temperature sensor, such as a thermocouple, may detect the temperature rise which is a measure of the concentration of gas. Different gases vary considerably in their ability to conduct heat. These variations make it possible to determine the concentrations of a number of gases, the basis for a thermal-conductivity type gas detector.

Image Intensification, Including Night Vision Devices other than Strictly Optical. This device consists of: (1) a input, photoelectron-emitting photocathode, which converts the image scene photons into an electron image; (2) a drift space with an electrostatic field to accelerate the electrons (providing the amplification energy) and to image the accelerated electrons onto the output surface (i.e., also performs an electron optic function); and (3) a phosphor that converts these high-energy electrons into visible light. Therefore, this device simply provides optical gain, or amplification.

Infrared. Radiant energy within the wavelength range 1 to 100 micrometer (10**-6 meter) is considered infrared energy. in general, unlike ultraviolet energy, infrared energy is not evaluated on a wavelength basis but rather in terms of all of such energy incident upon a surface. An infrared sensor would normally consist of a device for converting an invisible infrared image into a visible image. This device would consist of an infrared-sensitive, semi-transparent photocathode on one end of an evacuated envelope and a phosphor screen on the other, with an electrostatic lens system between the two.

Low Light Level Television (LLLTV). Very low light level. Operation can be obtained by coupling an image intensifier (optical amplifier) tube with a camera tube. The image intensifier tube is used as the prime sensor and its output is coupled to the photocathode of the camera tube. Low light level television has many advantages for night military operations by enhancing battlefield surveillance and reconnaissance for both defense and attack.

LASER. An acronym for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. The device is identical in theory of operation to the MASER except it operates in the optical region of the electromagnetic spectrum, rather than in the microwave. This device provides amplification in the optical region.
Magnetic. Senses the number of magnetic lines of force that are striking the detecting element.

Optical. Uses the measurement of the intensity, spectral distribution, polarization, or other characteristics of light or of infrared or ultraviolet radiation, emitted by or reflected from an object or passing through some medium, to perform range measurements, surveillances, and other measures.
Seismic Acoustic. Acoustic or low frequency signal to determine earth movements.
Seismic. Measures or detects earth movements.

Side Looking Airborne Radar (SLAR). High-resolution airborne radar having antennas aimed to the side of the flight path; used to provide high-resolution strip maps with photograph-like detail, to map unfriendly territory while flying along its perimeter, and to detect submarine wake against a background of sea clutter.
Seismic Magnetic. Disturbances in the earth's magnetic field used to detect earth movements.
Television. The transmission of still or motion scenes, by electrical means, for instantaneous viewing.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.

Recoverable. The sensors in the subject string are recoverable.
Update. Change to previously submitted report.
Tamper. Device self-deactivated when compromised by external force.
Emplacement Report. Report of the actual emplacement of remote sensors.
Monitor Change Report. Report indication that sensor monitoring responsibility is transferred from one monitoring element to another.

Notification Report. Initial report of the planned emplacement of remote sensors.
Removal Report. Report indicating that remote sensors have been removed and monitoring is terminated. A monitoring report is not required when a removal report is used.

Army Forces. A term used to describe the armies of a nation. (The military organization intended for land offensive or defensive warfare on the ground.)

Auxiliary Type Ship, General. General designator for all naval auxiliary ship types.
Auxiliary Rescue Craft. Vessel designed for local rescue operations inshore or offshore.
Assault Vehicle, Amphibious. Tracked or wheeled vehicle designed to carry assault troops in amphibious operations.
Depot Ship/Tender. Usually a large ship designed to provide support and depot facilities to other vessels of a specific type.
Buoy Tender. Ship 40 meters or more employed for the placing and tending of buoys and aids to navigation in coastal and adjoining waters.
Buoy Tender, Heavy Lift. Same as for ABU but with heavy lift capability.
Destroyer Tender. Ships of any size but usually large, employed primarily to furnish facilities and services for the support and repair of destroyer type ships.
Deperming Ship. Ship designed for deperming operations.
Ammunition Ship. Ship about 120 meters or more capable of transporting 5000 or more tons of ammunition and capable of providing underway replenishment of ammunition.
Ammunition Ship, Small. Same as for AE but between 40-120 meters handling less than 5000 tons of ammunition.
Missile Support Ship. Ship larger than 40 meters employed primarily to transport missiles.
Ammunition Ship, Transport. Ship capable of transporting 5000 or more tons of ammunition but lacking sophisticated underway replenishment capabilities.
Ammunition Ship, Transport, Small. Same as for AET but handling less than 5000 tons of ammunition.
Stores Ship. Ship 60 meters or more capable of underway replenishment of ships with refrigerated and dry provisions. May carry ammunition and POL but main emphasis is on dry provisions.
Large Auxiliary Floating Drydock. Floating dock capable of docking ships of all sizes.
Small Auxiliary Floating Drydock. Floating dock capable of docking small ships.
Medium Auxiliary Floating Drydock. Floating dock capable of docking small ships.
Stores Ship, Small. Same as for AF but under 60 meters.

Combat Stores Ship (Naval). Large ship, usually over 165 meters capable of underway alongside replenishment of ships with refrigerated and dry provisions, technical spares, ammunition, and general stores.  May carry POL but main emphasis is on mixed replenishment.
Stores Ship, Transport. Same as for AET but used for transporting refrigerated and dry provisions, technical spares, and general stores.
Miscellaneous Auxiliary. Ship 40 meters or more employed in general or multi-purpose functions of support, training, R&D, or a testing nature.
Icebreaker. Armed ship in size range 70 meters or more used primarily for icebreaking duties.
Icebreaker, Small. Same as for AGB but under 70 meters.
Icebreaker, Nuclear Powered. Same as for AGB but with nuclear power.
Communications Ship, Small. Small auxiliary optimized for communications duties.
Deep Submergence Support Ship. Ship with special facilities to support deep submergence diving operations.
Research Ship. Ship 49 meters or more used to conduct tests, experiments, and/or research.
Auxiliary Flag or Command Ship. Ship 55 meters or more used to provide afloat communications facilities and accommodation for a force commander and his operations staff.
Instrumentation Ship, Hydroacoustic Range. Ship specially fitted with instrumentation for hydroacoustic range operations.
Intelligence Collector. Ship specially fitted for and primarily employed in the collection of electronic intelligence.
Missile Range Instrumentation Ship. Ship employed at sea to provide telemetry and recover missiles.
Support Ship, Missile Range. Ship employed in missile range support operations.
Oceanographic Research Ship, Polar. Same as for AGOR but specially fitted for ice operations. Must have icebreaker bow.
Oceanographic Research Ship. Ship which conducts multi-discipline research at sea in oceanographic radiomagnetics, meteorology, and oceanography.
Patrol/Torpedo Boat Support Ship, Tender. Ship of any size employed primarily to furnish facilities and services for the support and repair of small patrol craft, the primary function being support.
Radar Picket Ship, Unarmed. Unarmed surface ship employed for radar picket duty. Any armed ship so employed would be typed DDR, FFR, or PPR.
Survey Ship. Ship 40 meters or more employed to conduct hydrographic and limited oceanographic surveys.
Survey Ship, Polar. Ship used for surveying Arctic/Antarctic areas.
Survey Ship, Coastal. Same as for AGS but only in coastal and inshore waters.
Launching Ship, Satellite. Ship employed in monitoring satellite launching operations.
Service Ship, Target. Ship employed in servicing surface targets.
Service Ship, Torpedo-Target. Ship employed in servicing torpedoes and sub-surface targets.

Hospital Ship. Ship of at least 40 meters which provides 3rd line medical and surgical care.  Declared to and protected by the ICRC (Int. Committee of the Red Cross/Red Crescent (TU ships only)) and marked accordingly.
Cargo Ship, Naval. Ship at least 80 meters employed to transport general cargo and provisions.  No underway replenishment facilities.
Cargo Ship, Light, Naval. Same as for AK but in size range 40-80 meters.
Cargo Ship, RO/RO, Naval. Ship at least 40 meters overall designed to transport vehicles, guns, and tanks in a non-combatant situation.  Must have roll-on/roll-off capability for vehicles.
Stores Ship, Issue, Naval. Ship 40 meters or more used to provide supplies and services.
Stores Ship, Issue, Small, Naval. Same as for AKS but less than 40 meters.
Aircraft Ferry/Cargo Ship. Same as for AK but employed to transport aircraft and aircraft spares.
Light Ship. Ship actually moored or anchored in a fixed position showing navigational aiding light(s).
Cable, Net Laying Ship. Ship equipped for cable or net laying.
Cable/Net Laying Ship, Small. Same as for AN but smaller.
Oiler/Tanker, General. General designator for oilers.

Combat Support Ship, Fast (Naval). Large ship over 230 meters, capable of speeds of 25 knots or more and/or providing rapid and simultaneous underway replenishment of ships at sea with POL, ammunition, refrigerated and dry provisions, spare parts, and general stores.  Primary emphasis is on POL replenishment.
Oiler, Small, Naval. Ship in size range 60-100 meters capable of furnishing underway replenishment of POL products.
Oiler Replenishment (Naval). Ship of at least 140 meters capable of providing rapid replenishment of POL and solid store products.
Oiler, Replenishment, Small, Naval. Same as for AOR but in size range 40-140 meters.
Special Liquid Ship. Ship 40 meters or more designed to transport a special kind of propellant or other non-nuclear associated liquid cargo.
Radiological Liquid Ship. Ship 40 meters or more designed to transport radioactive liquids.
Oiler-Transport. Ship usually exceeding 120 meters capable of transporting POL products but not specially fitted to provide underway replenishment.
Oiler, Transport, Small. Same as for AOT but in size range 40-120 meters.
Personnel Transport. Ship of at least 120 meters employed to transport troops, their supplies and equipment.
Barracks Ship. Self-propelled ship of any size employed as a mobile base facility and support ship for the crews of other vessels (usually small craft).  Has no repair facilities.

Primary Casualty Receiving Ship. Ship of at least 40 meters whose primary purpose is to provide 3rd line medical and surgical care.  Not declared by ICRC/Red Crescent (TU ships only). May be armed and carrying secure communications.

Casualty Transport Ship. Ship of at least 40 meters whose primary purpose is sustaining post operative casualties during transport out of theatre.  Not declared by ICRC/Red Crescent (TU ships only).  May be armed and carrying secure communications.
Barracks Craft. Same as for AP but also with capability of providing barrack facilities.

Repair Ship. Ship of at least 120 meters or more employed as a mobile repair facility providing limited support to various types of ships. Not a lifting ship. Repair primary function, support secondary.
Repair Ship, Battle Damage. Same as for AR but optimized for repair of battle damage.
Repair Ship, Cable. Ship 40 meters or more employed to lay, retrieve, and maintain submarine cables.
Auxiliary Repair Dock. Dry dock with repair facilities for all ship sizes.
Drydock, Auxiliary, Repair, Medium. Same as for AR but for medium and small ships.
Repair Ship, Heavy Hull. Same as for AR but optimized for extensive repairs to ships hulls.
Repair Ship, Small. Ship 40-120 meters capable of providing mobile repair facilities and possible limited support to smaller boats.
Repair Ship, Radiological. Ship optimized to provide mobile repairs to radiological installations and facilities.
Salvage Ship. Ship at least 40 meters used to provide mobile salvage, repairs, diving, and rescue services.
Salvage Ship, Lifting. Same as for ARS but must have heavy lifting capability.
Aircraft Repair Ship. Ship of any size used to repair helicopters, aircraft and aircraft engines.
Submarine Tender. Ship of at least 120 meters or more which provides mobile base facilities and support for submarines.
Submarine Tender, Small. Same as for AS but between 40-120 meters.
Submarine Rescue Ship. Any ship equipped to rescue personnel entrapped in a sunken submarine.
Space Vehicle Recovery Ship. Any ship equipped to recover space capsules following space flights.
Tug, Ocean Going. General designator for tugs capable of operating in open ocean waters.
Tug, Oceangoing, Auxiliary. Seagoing tug employed to tow navy ships and craft, usually about 40-50 meters.
Tug, Oceangoing, Fleet. Same as for ATA but equipped to operate with fleets.
Tug, Oceangoing, Rescue. Same as for ATA or ATF but extensively equipped for fire fighting and rescue operations.
Tug, Oceangoing, or Ship Salvage/Rescue. Ship which can provide salvage, repair, diving and rescue services, and tow ships and craft.
Fishing Vessel, Trawler or Junk, General.
Seaplane Tender. General designator for vessels which have repair and support facilities for aircraft.
Aviation Logistic Support Ship. Large ship equipped to provide aviation logistic support.
Aviation Tender Guided Missile Supply Ship. Ship with supply and support facilities for airborne guided missiles.
Aircraft Rescue Vessel. Any ship equipped to rescue personnel trapped in a sunken aircraft.  May also have facilities to salvage sunken aircraft.
Aviation Supply Ship. Ship equipped to carry and supply aviation stores.
Auxiliary Aircraft Landing Training Ship. Training carrier for command and fleet carrier qualification requirements.
Water Tender, Naval. Ship used primarily for transporting potable water.
Distilling Ship, Naval. Ship capable of distilling and transporting potable water.
Training Ship, Naval. Large oceangoing ship designed to serve as a training ship.
Training Ship, Small, Naval. Same as for AX but not oceangoing.
Training Ship, Sail, Naval. Naval sail training ship.
Battleship, General. Capital surface ship designed for surface action with a reasonable compromise between speed, protection, and armament which may include guided missiles.
Cruiser, Gun. Cruiser with guns 15 cm (6 inch) or larger as its main armament and with no missile systems.
Catamaran. A racing sailboat with two parallel hulls.
Catboat. A single-masted sailing vessel with only a mainsail.
Cruiser, General. General designator for all cruiser type ships of 140 meters or more.
Guided Missile Cruiser. Cruiser with one or more force guided missile systems as its main armament.
Cruiser, Helo Capability, Guided Missile. Same as for CG but fitted with a flight deck with a primary mission of operating and maintaining helicopters.
Cruiser, Guided Missile, Helo Capable, Nuclear Powered. Same as for CGH but with nuclear power.
Cruiser, Guided Missile, Nuclear Powered. Cruiser with one or more force guided missile systems as its main armament with nuclear power.
Cruiser, Helicopter. Same as for CC but fitted with a flight deck with a primary mission of operating and maintaining helicopters.
Cutter. A single-masted yacht or sailboat carrying two head sails under normal wind conditions.
Aircraft Carrier, General. 1. General designator for aircraft carriers. 2. Designator for multi-role aircraft carriers.
Aircraft Carrier, Guided Missile. Same as for CV but fitted with one or more force guided missile systems.
Aircraft Carrier, Guided Missile, Nuclear Powered. Same as for CVG but with nuclear power.
Helicopter/VSTOL Aircraft Carrier. Aircraft carrier without arrest gear/catapult operating VSTOL aircraft and/or helicopters which is not an amphibious or minewarfare ship.
Aircraft Carrier, VSTOL, Guided Missile. Same as for CVH but fitted with one or more force guided missile systems.
Aircraft Carrier, VSTOL, Guided Missile, Nuclear Powered. Same as for CVHG but with nuclear power.
Aircraft Carrier, VSTOL, Nuclear Powered. Same as for CVH but with nuclear power.
Aircraft Carrier, Light, Guided Missile. Same as for CVL but fitted with one or more force guided missile systems.
Aircraft Carrier, Light, Guided Missile, Nuclear Powered.
Aircraft Carrier, Nuclear Powered. Same as for CV but with nuclear power.
Aircraft Carrier, ASW. Carrier capable of operating VSTOL and/or helicopters in sustained ASW area operations and escort duties.
Aircraft Carrier, Training. Same as for CV but used primarily in a training role.

Destroyer, General. General designator for destroyer type ships.  Major surface combatant in range of about 95 to 140 meters whole general mission is to conduct operations with strike, ASW, and amphibious forces, and to perform screening and convoy duties. May have helicopters not especially fitted for ASW.
Destroyer, Guided Missile. Same as for DD but fitted with one more force guided missile systems.
Destroyer, Helo, Guided Missile. Same as for DDG and DDH.
Destroyer, Helo Capable. Same as for DDG.
Destroyer, Aviation, Guided Missile, Nuclear Powered.
Destroyer, Training. Same as for DD but used primarily in a training role.
Destroyer Escort. Same as for DD but optimized for escort duties.
Dhow. Sailing vessel, usually associated with Middle Eastern countries of specific design. May be powered by engine or sails, usually used for transportation purposes.
Deep Submergence Rescue Vehicle. Submersible designed for submarine rescue operations at great depth (more than 300 meters).
Deep Submergence Vehicle, Commercial. Submersible designed to operate at great depth (more than 300 meters).
Frigate, General. General designator for frigate.  A surface combatant in size range of about 75-150 meters.  Fitted primarily to fulfill an AWS role.  Generally has lighter surface armament than DD.
Frigate, Guided Missile. Same as for FF but fitted with one or more force guided missile systems.
Frigate, Aviation, Guided Missile. Same as for FFG and FFH.
Frigate, Aviation. Same as for FF but fitted with a flight deck with a primary mission of operating and maintaining helicopters.
Frigate, Guided Missile, Aviation, Nuclear Powered.
Frigate, Aviation, Nuclear Powered. Same as for FFG and FFH, nuclear.
Frigate, Small or Corvette. Same as for FF but smaller. Classification determined by armament or capability.
Corvette, Guided Missile. Same as for FFL but fitted with one or more force guided missile systems.
Frigate, Training. Same as for FF but used primarily in a training role.
Corvette. Small escort in size range 60 to 100 meters.
Hovercraft, Air Cushion/Ground Effect Machine, General.
Houseboat. A flat-bottomed boat with a superstructure resembling a house.
Unclassified Miscellaneous Unit. Ship, vessel or craft whose designation has not been classified.
Ketch. A small, two-masted sailing vessel rigged fore and aft, with the mizzenmast (aftermast) located forward of the rudderpost.
Lighter, Amphibious, Re-Supply, Cargo. A lighter designed to carry cargo for the re-supply of landing forces.
Lighter, Amphibious, Re-Supply, Vehicle. A lighter designed to carry cargo and vehicles for the re-supply of landing forces.
Landing Craft. General desig. For amphibious landing craft.
Landing Craft, Air Cushion. High speed (40 knots) assault landing craft capable of travelling over land and water from over-the-horizon distances (12-200 nm) using air cushion/gas turbine propulsion.
Amphibious Command Ship. Command ship for amphibious task force and landing operations.  May carry a limited number of troops and supplies for the headquarters element of the landing force.
Landing Craft, Fire Support. Landing craft optimized to provide fire support with guns or rockets during amphibious assaults.  Probably does not carry troops.
Landing Craft, Mechanized. Landing craft in size range 15-25 meters capable of carrying 1 tank or 50-200 troops.  Must have landing ramp.
Landing Craft, Medium, Air Cushion. Same as for LCM but is an air cushion or surface effect design.
Landing Craft, Personnel. Landing craft in size range 7.5-30 meters overall suitable only for carrying personnel.  May be fast and/or ramped.
Landing Craft, Personnel, Armored. Same as for LCP but armored for protection.
Landing Craft, Personnel, Large. 11 meter landing control boat used primarily to control amphibious seaborn assault waves.
Landing Craft, Tank. Same as for LCM but optimized for carrying and landing tanks and vehicles.
Landing Craft, Utility. All purpose landing craft in size range 25-55 meters and full load of 120-500 tons with landing ramp/other landing facilities used for handling 2-3 tanks or 300-450 troops.
Landing Craft, Utility, Air Cushion. Same as for LCU but is an air cushion or surface effect design.
Landing Craft, Vehicle/Personnel. Similar in size to LCP but capable of carrying a light vehicle in place of troops.  Must have bow ramp.
Landing Craft, Swimmer Support. High speed craft utilized primarily for underwater demolition and/or special warfare operations.
Swimmer Delivery Vehicle. Amphibious ship designed to transport swimmers.
Amphibious Fire Support Ship. Landing ship converted for use in amphibious assaults.  Armament is usually rocket launchers, but may also have bombardment guns.  May or may not carry troops.
Assault Craft, Gun-Equipped. Assault landing craft equipped with guns.

Amphibious Assault Ship, General. A large general purpose ship which embarks and lands elements of an assault force in both organic helicopters and organic landing craft.  Capable of carrying about 1800 assault troops. Must have internal stowage and ramp, and flooded well capability for vehicles or craft.

Amphibious Assault Ship, Multi-Purpose. A large multi-purpose amphibious ship that embarks and lands elements of a landing force by helicopter, landing craft, and amphibious vehicles.  Can also conduct sea control and power projection missions with VSTOL aircraft and ASW helicopters.
Amphibious Cargo Ship. Ship which carries supplies for amphibious assaults and can land the same in its own organic landing craft.
Amphibious Ship, General. General designator for amphibious vessels.
Assault Ship, Beaching. Amphibious ship designed for beaching operations.
Assault Ship, Personnel. Amphibious ship designed specifically to carry personnel.
Assault Ship, Tank. Assault ship optimized for carrying tanks.
Assault Craft, Missile Equipped. Landing craft equipped with other than force guided missiles.

Amphibious Transport, Dock. Ship which carries about 1000 troops. Capable of carrying up to 9 LCM. Primarily a troop ship and armored car carrier, with considerable internal berthing space. Must have permanent helicopter platform.

Amphibious Assault Ship, Helicopter. A large helicopter carrier with the mission of transporting and landing about 1800 assault troops with its organic aircraft.  Employment of organic landing craft not a principal function.
Amphibious Transport, Personnel. A large ship capable of carrying 1300-1500 assault troops and capable of landing them in its own organic landing craft.
Landing Ship, General. General designator for an amphibious landing ship.

Landing Ship, Dock. Primarily a tank and vehicle carrier but capable of transporting 150-400 assault troops and launching them embarked in organic landing craft without off-loading in the landing area.  Need not have a helicopter platform.
Landing Ship, Logistics. Landing ship capable of carrying initial, second and follow-on echelon equipment, vehicles and troops.  Normally ramped, not part of initial assault force.
Landing Ship, Medium. Ship in size range 45-85 meters, capable of beaching to land troops and/or tanks.  Must have bow doors and/or landing ramp.
Landing Ship, Tank. Ship in size range 85-100 meters employed to transport troops, vehicles and tanks for amphibious assault.  Must have bow doors and/or landing ramp.
Landing Ship, Vehicle. Ship in size range 45-60 meters overall, intended primarily to carry vehicles.  Must have bow doors and/or landing ramp.  Not capable of beaching.
Assault Vehicle. Wheeled vehicle designed to carry assault troops.
Mine Countermeasures Vessel, Unspecified. General designator for mine countermeasures vessel with no specification.
Mine Countermeasures Command and Support Ship. An armed combatant fitted for the command and support of MCM vessels and their equipment.
Mine Countermeasures Vessel, Diving. A mine countermeasures vessel specially equipped to carry out and support diving operations.
Mine Countermeasures Vessel, Hovercraft. A mine countermeasures vessel that is air cushion or surface effect design.
Mine Countermeasures Vessel, General. General designator for mine countermeasures vessels.
Mine Countermeasures Support Ship. An armed combatant fitted for the control and support of MCM vessels in combat situations.  Has limited facilities for repair of MCMVS and their equipment.
Mine Countermeasures Ship, Small, General. Same as for MCS but smaller and probably with less capability for support.
Mine Countermeasures Craft, Training. A vessel used primarily in a mine countermeasures training role.
Minehunter, General. Ship equipped with specific equipment to hunt mines.
Minehunter, Auxiliary. Any seagoing ship not designed as a minehunter but converted to such use.
Minehunter, Coastal. Same as for MH but designed to operate in coastal waters.
Minehunter, Coastal With Drone. Same as for MHC but by the use of a drone.
Minehunter, Inshore. Same as for MH but designed for operating in more shallow waters or estuaries.
Minehunter, Ocean. Same as for MH but designed for operating in ocean waters.
Minehunter/Sweeper, General. A minewarfare craft equipped for both hunting and sweeping mines.
Minehunter/Sweeper, Coastal. Same as for MHS but limited to coastal waters.
Minehunter/Sweeper, With Drone. Same as for MHS but by the use of a drone.
Minehunter/Sweeper, Ocean. Same as for MHS but capable of operating in open ocean waters.
Minelayer, General. A ship with a primary mission of laying mines.
Minelayer, Auxiliary. Any fishing or merchant ship having both capability and mission to lay mines.
Minelayer, Coastal. Minelayer in size range 50 - 85 meters overall.
Minelayer, Inshore. Minelayer in size range 25 - 50 meters overall.
Minelayer, Ocean. Large ship over 85 meters used primarily for minelaying.
Minelayer, River. Small minelayer 15 meters or less suitable only for operations on rivers or in protected roadsteads.

Minelayer, Support Ship. A large armed ship (over 90 meters) capable of extensive minelaying, but not capable of speeds over 30 knots, with the facilities for command and control of minewarfare ships and boats in combat environment.  Has limited support capability.
Mine Warfare Vessel, General. General designator for minewarfare vessels.
Minesweeper, Small, General. Ship designed to sweep mines.
Minesweeper, Auxiliary. Any seagoing ship not designed as a minesweeper but converted to such use.
Minesweeper, Boat. Minesweeper less than 12.5 meters.
Minesweeper, Coastal. Non-magnetic minesweeper between 40-70 meters.
Minesweeper, Coastal, With Drone. Coastal minesweeper capable of deploying and/or controlling unmanned remote controlled or towed vehicle(s) used for clearing mines.
Minesweeper, Coastal, Air Cushion. Non-magnetic minesweeper between 40-70 meters, air cushion.
Minesweeper, Coastal, Hydrofoil. Non-magnetic minesweeper between 40-70 meters, hydrofoil.
Minesweeper, Coastal, Special. Same as for MSS but for use within coastal waters.
Minesweeper, Coastal, Training. Same as for MSC but used primarily in a training role.
Minesweeper, Drone. Unmanned remotely controlled or towed vehicle capable of clearing mines.
Minesweeper, Fleet. Minesweeper in size range 46 meters or more which cannot be regarded as being non-magnetic.
Minesweeper, Fleet, Air Cushion. Minesweeper in size range 46 meters or more which cannot be regarded as being non-magnetic, air cushion.
Minesweeper, Fleet, Hydrofoil. Same as for MSF but fitted with hydrofoils.
Minesweeper, Inshore. Minesweeper between 20-40 meters. Intended and equipped for inshore minesweeping.
Minesweeper, Inshore, Air Cushion. Minesweeper between 20-40 meters. Intended and equipped for inshore minesweeping, hydrofoil.
Minesweeping Light. A small vessel designed to sweep mines.
Minesweeper, Ocean. Non-magnetic minesweeper 46 meters or more designed for open ocean operations.

Minesweeper, River. Shallow water minesweeper in size range 12.5 - 25 meters which has been armored to provide protection for crew in close combat situations. In the USN, a converted LCM-6 known as MSM.
Minesweeper, Special Device. A minesweeper fitted with special tow type mine-sweeping devices.
Motor Yacht. Any of various relatively small vessels for pleasure cruises, racing, etc.
Other. Explain the use of other in a subsequent free-text set.

Patrol Boat, General. Coastal patrol unit intended for a basically coastal guarding function. Includes any coastal patrol ship under 45 meters which cannot qualify as a PG in armament. May be unarmed.
Patrol Boat, Fast. Same as for PB but capable of at least 35 knots.
Patrol Boat, Hydrofoil. Same as for PB but fitted with hydrofoils.
Patrol Boat, Offshore. Coastal patrol unit in size 45-60 meters designed for use in offshore waters. May or may not be armed with guns.
Patrol Boat, River/Roadstead. Lightly armed unit generally suitable by design only for operations in sheltered waters, such as rivers and roadsteads.
Submarine Chaser/Escort Craft, General. Vessel in size range 35-55 meters designed and fitted primarily for escort duties in ASW role.

Patrol Craft, Coastal, Escort. Vessel in size range 55-75 meters designed and fitted primarily for ASW role and coastal duty. Improved seakeeping, vice mere large size, distinguishes PCE from PC, and vessels lacking this should be typed as PC.
Patrol Subchaser, Fast. Same as for PC but capable of at least 35 knots.
Patrol Craft, Air Cushion, Fast. Same as for PCF but is either an air cushion or surface effect design.
Patrol Craft, Hydrofoil, Fast. Same as for PCF but fitted with hydrofoils.
Patrol Craft, Hydrofoil. Same as for PC but fitted with hydrofoils.
Submarine Chaser. Patrol craft optimized for the ASW role.
Patrol Craft, Training. Same as for PC but used primarily in a training role.

Patrol Craft, Gun Equipped, General. Patrol, blockade and surveillance ship in range 45-85 meters overall. Designed to operate in other than open ocean areas. Has special mission of attacking hostile ships. Must have at least 76MM main armament.

Patrol Ship, Icebreaker. Any ship designed as an icebreaker but employed primarily in a patrol mission. The icebreaking capability is to facilitate the patrol function through ice, rather than to support the movement of other ships.
Patrol Ship, Fast. Same as for PG but capable of at least 35 knots.
Patrol Combatant, Guided Missile. Same as for PG but fitted with one or more force guided missile systems.
Patrol Combatant, Guided Missile, Air Cushion. Same as for PGG but is either an air cushion or surface effect design.
Patrol Combatant, Guided Missile, Hydrofoil. Same as for PGG but fitted with hydrofoils.
Patrol Combatant, Hydrofoil. Same as for PG but fitted with hydrofoils.
Motor Gunboat. Same as for PG but fitted with guns and other than force guided missile systems.
Patrol Ship, ASW. ASW patrol ship in size range 45 - 85 meters fitted with medium range sonar and ASW weapons.
Patrol Combatant, Hovercraft. A high speed patrol hovercraft which can conduct surveillance screening and special operations and is operated by naval or marine forces.
Patrol Combatant, Hovercraft, Guided Missile. Same as for PHJ but fitted with other than force guided missile systems.
Patrol Combatant, Hovercraft, Minewarfare Capable. A high speed patrol hovercraft which is used primarily in minewarfare.
Patrol Ship, Offshore. Same as for PBO but in size range over 60 meters.
Patrol Craft, Torpedo. High speed (35 knots) anti-surface ship patrol craft in size range 20 - 30 meters fitted with torpedoes.
Attack Boat, Guided Missile. Same as for PT but fitted with a force guided missile system.
Attack Boat, Guided Missile, Air Cushion. Same as for PTG but is an air cushion or surface effect design.
Attack Boat, Guided Missile Hydrofoil. Same as for PTG but fitted with hydrofoils.
Attack Boat, Guided Missile, Training. Same as for PTG but used primarily in a training role.
Torpedo Boat, Air Cushion. Same as for PT but is either an air cushion or surface effect design.
Torpedo Boat, Motor, Hydrofoil. Same as for PT but fitted with hydrofoils.
Torpedo Boat, Small. Same as for PT but smaller.
Torpedo Boat, Small, Hydrofoil. Same as for PTL but fitted with hydrofoils.
Torpedo Boat, Training. Same as for PT but used primarily in a training role.
Junk. Sail/motor powered vessel, usually associated with China, of wooden construction designed with high bow and poop deck area.  Usually used for transportation purposes.
Seaplane. Aircraft designed to take-off/land on water.
Racing Cruiser. A low-profile, high-powered motor boat.
Schooner. A ship with two or more masts, the after mast being the same height or taller than the forward, rigged fore and aft.
Sloop. A fore- and aft-rigged, single-masted sailing vessel with a mainsail and jib.
Speedboat. Small, sleek boat capable of high speeds with or without outboard engines.
Submarine, General. General designator for submarines.
Submarine, Auxiliary. Submarine used mainly in a non-combatant role which has at least a residual combat capability.
Submarine, Auxiliary Nuclear Powered. Same as for SSA but with nuclear power.
Submarine, Ballistic Missile. Submarine armed with ballistic missiles normally deployed on strategic missions.
Submarine, Ballistic Missile, Nuclear. Same as for SSB but with nuclear power.
Submarine, Coastal. Submarine designed primarily for operations in coastal and shallow waters.
Submarine, Attack Missile. Submarine fitted with underwater to surface or surface to surface missiles.
Submarine, Attack, Missile, Nuclear. Same as for SSG but with nuclear power.
Submarine, Patrol. Long range patrol submarine. May have primary anti-surface or anti-submarine role.
Submarine, Attack, Nuclear. Nuclear propelled attack submarine with both anti-submarine and anti-surface capability.
Submarine, Training. Submarine used primarily in a training role but with at least a residual combat capability.
Submarine, MILCAP Unknown. Submarine whose full military capability is unknown or has not been determined.
Submarine, MILCAP Unknown, Nuclear Powered. Same as for SSU but with nuclear power.
Submarine, Midget, Swimmer. Midget submarine or submersible designed primarily for special operations and operated by naval forces.
Special Warfare Craft, Light. A light craft specifically designed for special warfare operations.
Special Warfare Craft, Medium. Same as for SWCL but larger in size.
Hovercraft, General. General designator for non-naval hovercraft.
Hovercraft, Transport/Cargo. Hovercraft capable of carrying vehicles and cargo.  Not fitted to carry passengers.
Hovercraft, Ferry. Hovercraft fitted to carry passengers and/or vehicles.
Hovercraft, Icebreaker. Hovercraft specially fitted to assist in icebreaking.
Hovercraft, Scientific Research/Survey. Non-military hovercraft specially equipped for research or survey duties.
Merchant Ship, General. General designator for non-naval ship designed to transport cargo or passengers.  All merchant ship designators below indicate non-naval ships.
Merchant Ship, Dry Cargo, Break Bulk. Dry cargo carrying ship capable of handling break bulk cargo.
Merchant Ship, Bulk. Ship designed to carry dry cargo in bulk form.
Merchant Ship, Container, Non-Self Sustained. Ship designed to carry cargo in loadable and unloadable containers.  Not equipped to handle the containers with own equipment.
Merchant Ship, Container, Self-Contained. Same as for TMC but with own handling equipment.
Merchant Ship, Dredger. Ship designed to dredge channels in open seas.
Merchant Ship, RO/RO. Ship 40 meters or more having capability for roll-on/roll-off (RO/RO) cargo.
Merchant Ship, Car/Passenger Ferry. Ship or craft designed to run a ferry service of both cars and passengers.
Merchant Ship, Railroad, Car Ferry. Same as for tmf but designed to ferry railroad cars.
Merchant Ship, Icebreaker. Ship used primarily for icebreaking.
Merchant Ship, Scientific Research/Survey. Ship employed to conduct scientific research.
Merchant Ship, Heavy Lift. Ship fitted with heavy duty crane or derrick for heavy lift.
Merchant Ship, Inland Waterway. Ship primarily used to transport cargo via inland waterways.
Merchant Ship, Cable Layer. Ship designed to lay and/or retrieve cables.
Merchant Ship, Lash. Ship equipped with gantry crane, capable of embarking and disembarking pre-loaded standard sized barge (lash lighters).
Merchant Ship, Seabee. Barge carrying ship with a stern elevator, capable of embarking and disembarking barges of non-standard size.
Merchant Ship, Meteorological. Ship designed primarily to monitor meteorological conditions.
Merchant Ship, Tanker. Ship designed to transport liquids (or gases).
Merchant Ship, Replenishment, Oiler, Small. Ship able to provide replenishment to ships at sea of POL and solid store products, less than 120 meters in size.
Merchant Ship, Replenishment, Oiler. Ship able to provide replenishment to ships at sea of POL and solid store products, over 120 meters in size.
Merchant Ship, Special Liquids. Ship 40 meters or more designed to transport a special kind of propellant or other non-nuclear associated liquid cargo.
Merchant Ship, Liquid. Ship designed to transport liquid gas.
Merchant Ship, Passenger. Ship designed primarily to transport passengers.
Merchant Ship, Refrigerated. Ship designed primarily to transport cargo in refrigerated spaces.
Merchant Ship, Space/Missile Associated. Ship designed or converted primarily to support space and missile programs.
Merchant Ship, Tug, Oceangoing. Sea-going tug with horsepower of 1000 or more, length usually over 60 meters.
Merchant Tug, Oceangoing Rescue. Same as for TMT but extensively equipped for fire fighting and rescue operations.
Merchant Tug, Oceangoing Salvage. Sea-going tug which can provide towing, salvage, repair, diving, and rescue services to ships and craft.
Merchant Ship, Water Tender. Ship designed primarily for transporting potable water.
Merchant Ship, Distilling. Ship capable of distilling and transporting potable water.
Merchant Ship, Training. Ship used primarily for training purposes.
Trimaran. A boat similar to a catamaran, but with three parallel hulls.
Submersible, General, Commercial. General designator for non-combatant submersible.
Submersible, Research, Commercial. Submersible with no combat capability used in research role.
Submersible, Rescue, Commercial. Submersible designed specifically for underwater rescue operations.
Fishing Vessel, General. Fishing vessel over 30 meters.
Fishing Vessel Base Ship. Fishing vessel support ship (other than supplying fuel/water only).
Fishing Vessel, Whale Catcher. Fishing vessel equipped to engage in whale hunting.
Fishing Vessel Factory Ship. Fishing vessel equipped to prepare fish or other seafood into commercial products.
Fishing Vessel, Inspection. Any ship other than naval used for inspection of fishing vessels.
Fishing Vessel, Refrigerated. Fishing vessel equipped with refrigerated holds.
Fisheries Research Ship. Vessel equipped to conduct fisheries research.
Fishing Vessel, Training. Vessel used to train personnel in fisheries techniques.
Whale Factory Ship. Vessel equipped to prepare whales into commercial products.
Unknown. Ship, vessel or craft whose designation is unknown.
Patrol Boat, Police. Same as for PB but police operated.
Patrol Craft, Police. Same as for PC but police operated.
Armed Police Gunboat. Armed vessel operated by police. Size may vary.
Police Diving Tender. Same as for YDT but police operated.
Police Launch. Same as for YFL but police operated.
Miscellaneous Auxiliary, Coast Guard. Coast Guard AG.
Icebreaker, Coast Guard. Coast Guard armed ship in size range 70 meters or more used primarily for icebreaking duties.
Buoy Tender, Coast Guard. Coast Guard ABU.
Cargo Ship, Coast Guard. Coast Guard AK.
Cable Repair Ship, Coast Guard. Coast Guard ARC.
Salvage and Rescue Ship, Coast Guard.

Firm at All Times. The surface material is firm at all times consisting of a well-graded mixture of particle sizes. Beach material will support the weight of wheeled vehicles and will allow initial vehicle movement without special equipment aids.

Firm When Dry. The surface material is firm when dry and will support the weight of wheeled vehicles without excessive vehicle settling and/or loss of traction. Beach material will allow initial vehicle movement without special equipment aids.

Firm When Wet. The surface material is firm when wet and will support the weight of wheeled vehicles without excessive vehicle settling and/or loss of traction. Beach material will allow initial vehicle movement without special equipment aids.

Loose. The surface material is generally composed of poorly graded (limited size range) materials which lack fine material to fill the void. Beach material will support the weight of wheeled vehicles, but provides for poor traction. Pebbles and cobbles are examples of poorly graded materials.

Soft at All Times. The surface material is soft at all times. Generally the material is composed of dry sand or sand mixed with silt which will not support the weight of moving wheeled vehicles. Because of poor traction, wheeled vehicles will generally require the assistance of tracked vehicles or mats for initial movement.

Soft When Dry. The surface material is soft when dry, may support the weight of wheeled vehicle, but because of poor traction, wheeled vehicles generally require the assistance of tracked vehicles or mats for initial movement. Soft beach materials are composed of dry sand, or sand mixed with silt.
Soft When Wet. The surface material is soft when wet. Material will not support the weight of moving wheeled vehicles.
Unknown. Surface material and firmness is unknown.
Clay. A firm, fine-grained earth, plastic when wet, composed chiefly of hydrous aluminum silicate minerals.
Coral. A hard stony skeleton secreted by certain marine polyps and often deposited in extensive masses forming reefs and atolls in tropical seas.
Earth. Unrefined soil; the soft granular or crumbly part of land.
Frozen. Frozen material of unknown composition.
Grass. Ground covered with grass, i.e., surface covered by plants with typically long, narrow leaves that grow densely.
Gravel. Small pebbles or stones, may be crushed to achieve uniformity. (Spread and rolled, may be graded.)

Laterite. A residual product of rock decay that is red in color and has a high content of oxides of iron and low proportion of silica; a mottled quarriable type of clay which hardens on exposure to air.

Airfield. An area prepared for the accommodation (including any buildings, installations, and equipment), landing, and takeoff of aircraft.
Arroyo. A water-carved gully or channel in an arid region.
Badlands. A region nearly or completely devoid of vegetation, and where erosion has cut the land into narrow ravines and sharp-ridge crests and pinnacles.

Basin. A broad depression in the land surface surrounded by higher ground. in arid regions, basins commonly include permanent or temporary salt lakes or salt flats. in areas of limestone bedrock, basins may be crossed by streams which emerge from an underground passage at one side and drain out through a continuation of this passage at the opposite end of the basin. This type is also referred to as a valley sink.
Bayou. A minor, slow-moving waterway or estuary creek that is tidal with a slow, imperceptible current.
Bluff, High. An abrupt slope, consisting of unconsolidated materials greater than 15 meters high, commonly borders a stream.
Bluff, Low. An abrupt slope, consisting of unconsolidated materials less than 15 meters high, commonly borders a stream.

Butte. An isolated, flat-topped hill or mountain located in an arid region. It is capped by a layer of hard rock and bounded for most or all of its circumference by an escarpment. It is not to be confused with a mesa.
Canal, Drainage. An artificial water channel designed for drainage. It has uniform depth and drainage width. It is a natural feature which has been improved specially for drainage of an area.

Canal, Irrigation. An artificial water channel designed for irrigation. It has a uniform depth and width, designed for irrigation. It is a natural feature which has been improved specifically for irrigation of an area.
Canal, Navigation. An artificial watercourse cut through land.
Canyon. A deep, narrow valley with steep sides. Canyons often have a stream flowing through it.
Cliff, High. A steep face of rock rising greater than 15 meters above the surrounding land or water.
Cliff, Low. A steep face of rock rising less than 15 meters above surrounding land or water.
Delta. A low, generally triangular, commonly marshy, alluvial deposit at the mouth of a river or a stream. It is often cut by tributaries of the main stream.

Desert. A rocky, sandy area with wide spaces between plants or small groups of plants. Deserts develop as a result of deficient soil moisture associated with meager rainfall. Desert areas normally have a less than 10 inches of annual rainfall in the middle latitudes, and less than 15 inches in the tropics.
Dike. An artificial earth or stone embankment, causeway, or wall designated to contain or hold back water. It prevents flooding or delimiting of an area reclamation.
Dune, High. A mound, ridge, or hill of wind-deposited sand. It is greater than 3 meters high.
Dune, Low. A mound, ridge, or hill of wind-deposited sand. It is less than 3 meters high.
Embankment. An artificial bank or mound built to hold back water or to support a roadway or railroad.
Escarpment. A steep slope or long cliff formed by erosion or faulting and separating two level areas of different elevations.
Fan, Alluvial. A gentle sloping, fan-shaped mass of unconsolidated material deposited by a stream. It is usually located where the stream emerges from a highland, such as the mouth of a canyon.
Fishpond. A small, shallow, and artificially formed body of water used primarily for raising fish.
Fjord. A narrow sea inlet located between cliffs or steep slopes.
Foothills. An area of transition from the higher elevation of a mountain range or higher hills, to adjacent lower terrain.
Glacier. A field of land ice and snow formed by snowfall in excess of melting. It often moves down a mountain slope or across a wide area.
Gorge. A deep, narrow, and extremely steep-sided valley. It is cut by a stream which occupies almost all of the valley floor. See ravine, arroyo, and gully.

Gully. A small, steep-sided, v-shaped natural ditch. It is not occupied by a perennial stream. It is formed in clay or other easily eroded materials by the action of water during and immediately from an arroyo, which has perpendicular sides and a flat floor. See ravine.
Hill. A natural elevation of the terrain with a local relief between 150 and 600 meters.
Hill, High. A natural elevation of the terrain with a local relief greater than 300 meters, but less than 600 meters. It has a surface slope of 30 percent or greater.
Hill, Low. A natural elevation of the terrain with a local relief greater than 150 meters, but less than 300 meters. It has a surface slope of less than 30 percent.

Lagoon. A shallow sound, pond, or lake of salt or brackish water that is partly or completely separated from the sea by a bar, sand dunes, or a similar reef feature. Also, a body of water enclosed by the reefs or islands of an atoll.

Lakebed, Dry. An area occupied by a former lake in which the water has evaporated and/or seeped into porous surface materials. It is usually found in arid regions, and consists of flat to gently undulating deposits of well-sorted, fine textured materials.
Lowland. A small, flat area with a lower elevation than the surrounding or adjacent terrain. It is usually associated with coastal regions.
Marsh. A low area of soft, wet, essentially treeless land. It is periodically inundated with water, and is covered by low rank vegetation such as cattails.

Mesa. A flat-topped, steep-sided hill or mountain smaller than a plateau and situated in an arid region. Although a mesa is generally an isolated feature, the term is also applied to any broad, flat, elevated arid surface which is bound at least on one side by a steep slope or escarpment. Not to be confused with a butte, which is almost entirely surrounded by escarpments.

Military Base. A permanent or semi-permanent military facility located in a fixed or relatively fixed location, with its buildings, building equipment, and subsidiary facilities such as piers, spurs, and access roads. A base is used to perform military functions such as housing military personnel, logistics, or other support functions.
Mountain, High. A natural land elevation with a local relief greater than 900 meters.
Mountain, Low. A natural land elevation with a local relief between 600 and 900 meters.
Mudflats. A deposit of fluid-to-plastic alluvium (commonly clay and silt) which is exposed or partially exposed at low tide along the coast, or in dry periods along inland rivers.
Paddy. An irrigated field used for rice cultivation. It is bound by low ridges or dikes, and is completely covered by slow-moving water for considerable periods of time.
Park. A tract of ground kept in its natural state for game, or improved for recreational purposes.
Petroleum Storage. A facility for the storage of petroleum, oil, and lubricants.
Plain. An extensive, level, treeless region, such as a valley floor or a plateau summit. It has a local relief of less than 150 meters.
Plain, Coastal. An extensive level, rolling, or undulating area that extends from the sea to the nearest elevated land.
Plain, Dissected. A plain cut extensively by watercourses, such as streams, streambeds, or rivers.
Plain, Flat. A plain with a local relief less than 15 meters.
Plain, Flood. An alluvial plain adjacent to a stream or river that is subject to flooding, which deposits soil on the plain.
Plain, Gently Rolling. A plain with a local relief between 45 to 89 meters.
Plain, Rolling. A plain with a local relief between 90 to 150 meters.
Plain, Undulating. A plain with a local relief between 15 to 44 meters.
Plateau. A relatively level, elevated plain or tableland that is miles wide. It has a sharp drop of at least 90 meters on one side.
Playa. A nearly level area located at the bottom of a desert basin. It is sometimes temporarily covered with water.
Plodder. An area of low land reclaimed (usually by dikes or dams) from the sea or another body of water.
Pond. A body of water that is smaller than a lake. It is often constructed artificially.
Quarry. An open pit used for excavating stone by digging, cutting, or blasting.
Ravine. A deep, narrow cleft in the earth's surface. It is often created by the flow of water. Local relief is less than 90 meters.
Reservoir. A natural or artificial lake or pond in which water is collected and stored for use.
River. A large natural surface stream that empties into an ocean, lake, or other body of water.
Saltflat. A level salt-encrusted floor of a dried up lake, lagoon, or arm (bay, harbor, gulf, etc.) of the sea.
Saltpan. A shallow, artificial pond used to naturally evaporate sea water to obtain salt.
Sandhill. A hill or ridge composed of wind-deposited sand. It is stabilized by grass, scrub, or similar vegetation.
Seawall. An artificial structure that is built along part of the coast to prevent erosion by wave action.
Spit. A narrow point of land extending into a body of water.
Stream. A body of water that flows in a channel or bed.
Stream, Intermittent. A stream located in a narrow channel. Its flow of water stops and starts at intervals.
Swamp. A lowland region saturated with water.
Swamp, Mangrove. An inundated tropical or subtropical coastal or riverside swamp that supports a dense growth of mangrove trees.
Terrace. A raised bank of earth with vertical or sloping sides and a flat top.
Tidal Flats. A relatively broad, level flatland of sand, mud, or mud-sand which is periodically covered by the rise and fall of the tide.
Tombolo. Unconsolidated material that is deposited by wave action or currents, such as a sand or gravel bar connecting an island with the mainland or another island.
Tundra. A treeless area located between the arctic ice cap and treeline. It has a permanently frozen subsoil, and it supports low growing vegetation such as lichens, mosses, and stunted shrubs.
Upland. The higher elevation of a region or tract of land.
Valley. An elongated, lowland area located between ranges of mountains, hills, or other uplands. It often has a river stream running along the bottom.
Wadi. A valley, gully, or riverbed that remains dry except during the rainy season (such as in Northern Africa and Southwestern Asia).

Air Operations Center. (U.S.) The principal air operations installation from which aircraft and air warning functions of combat air operations are directed, controlled, and executed. It is the senior agency of the Air Force Component Commander from which command and control of air operations are coordinated with other components and services.
Air Control Center (ACC), Recognized Air Picture Production Center (RPC), Sensor Fusion Post (SFP).

Air Support Operations Center. (U.S.) An agency of a tactical air control system collocated with a corps headquarters or an appropriate land force headquarters, which coordinates and directs close air support and other tactical air support.

Airborne Warning and Control System. (U.S.) The E-3 sentry is an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft that provides all-weather surveillance, command, control, and communications needed by Commanders of U.S. and NATO air defense forces.

Combined Air Operations Center. (U.S.) A facility, staffed by members of more than one nation, established for planning, directing, and executing combined air operations in support of the combined force commander's operation or campaign objectives.
Combined Air Operations Center (CAOC), Air Control Center (ACC), Recognized Air Picture Production Center (RPC), Sensor Fusion Post (SFP).

Combined Joint Operations Center. The CJOC is responsible for the direction and control of current operations. It exercises command and control over joint operations in the Northern Region. It provides the current situation and operations within regional Command North AOR, air, AII and NATO led operations. It monitors and implements the NATO Precautionary System, the military response options, and rules of engagement. It prepares and executes procedures for peacetime, crisis, peace support, and war operations (AIRNORTH).

Control and Reporting Center. (U.S.) The CRC serves as the senior ground radar element of the Theater Air Control System (TACS). Mission is to detect, identify, and verify airborne targets in assigned area. CRC also provides decentralized execution of air defense and airspace control, provides early warning to air and ground elements and manages subordinate radar units.
Direct Air Support Center, Airborne. (U.S.) An airborne aircraft equipped with the necessary staff personnel, communications, and operations facilities to function as a Direct Air Support Center.

Direct Air Support Center. (U.S.) The principal air control agency of the U.S. Marine Air Command and Control System responsible for the direction and control of air operations directly supporting the ground combat element. It processes and coordinates requests for immediate air support and coordinates air missions requiring integration with ground forces and other supporting arms. It normally collocates with the senior fire support coordination center within the ground combat element and is subordinate to the Tactical Air Command Center.

Marine Early Warning/Control Site. (U.S.) U.S. Marine manned site that is subordinate to the Tactical Air Operations Center (TAOC), and provides the TAOC with extended radar coverage and control of anti-air warfare aircraft and surface-to-air weapons.

Forward Air Controller. (U.S.) A member of the Tactical Air Control Party who, from a forward ground or airborne position, controls aircraft in close air support of ground troops. (AAP-06) A qualified individual who, from a forward position on the ground or in the air, directs the action of combat aircraft engaged in close air support of land forces.

Forward Air Controller, Airborne. (U.S.) A specifically trained and qualified aviation officer who exercises control from the air of aircraft engaged in close air support of ground troops. The Forward Air Controller (Airborne) is normally an airborne extension of the Tactical Air Control Party.
Ground Based Air Defense Operations Center.

Joint Air Operations Center. (U.S.) A jointly staffed facility established for planning, directing, and executing joint air operations in support of the Joint Force Commander's operation or campaign objectives.

Marine Air Traffic Control Detachment. (U.S.) Subordinate to the U.S. Marine TACC, the MATC controls local airspace/aircraft in and around a Marine Air Ground Task Force (MAGTF) airfields and provides precision approach control for MAGTF aircraft.
Maritime Coordination Element. The MCE is a Navy liaison element to a CAOC.

Regional Air Operations Center. The RAOC is continuously monitoring and reporting the tactical air defense situation and readiness of the air forces in its AOR. It is monitoring the air activity, relaying, and implementing all phases of the NATO Precautionary System (NPS). It is developing and promulgating crisis management procedures. It is continuously monitoring the status of assigned nuclear forces. It is providing continuity of command and control during crisis and transition to war.

Regional Operations Center. The ROC is responsible for the direction and control of current operations. It exercises command and control over joint operations in the Southern Region. It provides the current situation and operations within regional Command North AOR, air, AII, and NATO led operations. It monitors and implements the NATO Precautionary System, the military response options and rules of engagement. It prepares and executes procedures for peacetime, crisis, peace support, and war operations (AIRSOUTH).

Shape Operations Center. The SOC is to provide SACEUR, and DSACEUR as the EU OPDCR and strategic coordinator, with the means, capabilities, and staff coordination mechanism to exercise command and control over assigned forces in order to meet the requirements of the full spectrum of alliance military missions (Article 5 and non-Article 5) to include NATO support for EU-led operations, with joint and combined force structures. The SOC has to maintain a 24-hours crisis response and crisis management capability.
Tactical Air Coordinator, Airborne. An officer who coordinates, from an aircraft, the action of combat aircraft engaged in close support of ground or sea forces.

Tactical Air Control Center. (OOA) (UK) The tactical air control center (TACACC) provides facilities to exercise tactical control of deployed air defense, offensive support, support helicopter, and other air assets operating out of area.

Marine Tactical Air Command Center. (U.S.) The senior U.S. Marine command and control agency providing centralized command for MAGTF forces, and serves as the command post for the Aviation Combat Element (ACE) Commander.

Marine Tactical Air Direction Center. (U.S.) An air operations installation under the overall control of the Tactical Air Control Center (Afloat) or Tactical Air Command Center, from which aircraft and air warning service functions of tactical air operations in an area of concern are directed.

Marine Tactical Air Operations Center. (U.S.) The principal air control agency of the U.S. Marine Air Command and Control System responsible for airspace control and management. It provides real-time surveillance, direction, positive control, and navigational assistance for friendly aircraft. It performs real-time direction and control of all anti-air warfare operations, to include manned interceptors and surface-to-air weapons. It is subordinate to the Tactical Air Command Center.
Tactical Air Traffic Control Unit. (UK) A TATCU provides a 24 hours visual flight rules (VFR) Air Traffic Control (ATC) service for covert and overt operations in austere and bare base conditions.
