Air-to-Air Refueling. The objective of Air-to-Air Refueling (AAR) operations is to enhance combat effectiveness by extending the range, payload, or endurance of receiver aircraft.

Airborne Command and Control. Airborne Command & Control Communications (ABCCC) aircraft are specially equipped and manned by trained control and coordination personnel. They contribute to the command and control of many different types of air operation.

Airborne Early Warning. Airborne Early Warning & Control (AEW&C) aircraft are specially equipped and manned by trained control and coordination personnel. They contribute to the command and control of many different types of air operation.

Air Interdiction. Air Interdiction (AI) is conducted to destroy, neutralize or delay the enemy's military potential before it can be brought to bear effectively against friendly forces at such distance from friendly forces that detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of friendly forces is not required.
Air Reconnaissance. The collection of information of intelligence interest either by visual observation from the air or through the use of airborne sensors.

Air Surveillance. The systematic observation of airspace by electronic, visual, or other means, primarily for the purpose of identifying and determining the movements of aircraft and missiles, friendly, and enemy, in the air space under observation.

Amphibious Ops Support. Air support for amphibious operations can be provided by both land and sea based air assets depending upon the location of the Amphibious Objective Area (AOA). Air support will normally include the Air Interdiction (AI) and Close Air Support (CAS) roles of air-land operations, but may also require counter-air and supporting air operations.

Airborne Operations. Air delivered combat power can be used to seize ground or installations that are vital to the enemy by delivering land forces directly onto the objective. This may be achieved by parachute insertion (airborne) or Tactical Air Landed Operation (TALO). Ports of entry, airfields, and key installations or structures, all offer potential objectives.

Air Surveillance and Control System. A network of fixed, mobile, and airborne radars, associated communications and facilities that provide for the detection, recognition, reporting, and control of interception and engagement of airborne vehicles within the detection range.

Antisurface Warfare. The aim of Antisurface Warfare (ASUW) is to prevent an adversary from effectively employing his surface forces. Aircraft, submarines, or surface vessels can carry out this task, preferably in a coordinated action. ASUW covers a wide range of operations involving surveillance and reconnaissance missions that may culminate in the targeting and attack of enemy vessels.

Antisubmarine Warfare. The aim of Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) is to deny the adversary effective use of submarines.  Countering the submarine threat demands an extensive range of capabilities and may involve the use of fixed-wing Maritime Patrol Aircraft (MPA), helicopters, friendly submarines, surface ships, or other aircraft.

Air Transport. Air Transport (AT), commonly known as airlift, provides a military commander with the capability to deploy, employ, and redeploy forces and equipment quickly and over considerable distances, sustain those forces and support effective application of their military effort. AT operations are considered in two categories: strategic (inter-theater) and theater (intra-theater).

Close Air Support. Close Air Support (CAS) is defined as air action against hostile targets which are in close proximity to friendly forces and which require detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of those forces.

Combined Air Operations. Combined Air Operations (COMAO) are designed to maximize the impact of a given force by concentrating its effect, whilst at the same time minimizing attrition through mutual support within the attacking force and by saturating defenses en-route, and in the target area. To achieve its aim, a COMAO may need Air-to-Air Refueling (AAR), Air Defense (AD), reconnaissance, surveillance, targeting designation, jamming, and defense suppression aircraft in support.

Combat Search and Rescue. Combat Search and Rescue (CSAR) is a coordinated operation using pre-established procedures for the detection, location, identification, and rescue of downed aircrew in hostile territory in crisis or wartime and, when appropriate, of isolated personnel in distress, who are trained and equipped to be rescued.

Defensive Counter Air. Defensive Counter Air (DCA) involves destruction or neutralization of enemy forces conducted near to, or over, friendly territory and are generally reactive to the initiative of enemy air assets. DCA includes the employment of active air defense weapon systems such as fighters, surface-to-air missiles, and anti-aircraft artillery, complemented by passive defense measures.

Electronic Warfare. Electronic Warfare (EW) is the employment of the full range of modern communications, surveillance, and weapon systems operating across the electromagnetic spectrum, and in an attempt to dominate the spectrum, whilst denying its use to the enemy.

Air Defense Interception. An intercept mission involves the use of an aircraft to intercept enemy or unknown aircraft. Upon completion of the intercept other actions may be ordered e.g. visual identification (interrogation), shadowing, diversion of the target from its intended flight path or mission (intervention) or engagement.

Offensive Counter Air. Offensive Counter Air (OCA) involves destruction or neutralization of enemy forces mostly ranging throughout enemy territory and generally conducted at the initiative of the friendly force. OCA may include fighter sweep, fighter escort, airfield attack, and attacks against missiles and associated systems on the ground, including Suppression of Enemy Air Defenses (SEAD).

Package. Force packaging is used if the requirement is to concentrate a large composite force against a single objective, and particularly if there is a need for combat support forces. The optimum combination of impact and survivability may only be achieved if the force operates as an integrated unit.

Strategic Attack. Strategic Attack is carried out to defeat an adversary's center of gravity or attack other vital target sets including command elements, energy sources, vital war production assets, and key supporting infrastructure to achieve the desired effects. It is normally conducted beyond the range of surface force assets.

Special Air Operations. Special Air Operations (SAO) support special operations and may be conducted during peace, crisis and conflict. SAO activities may include both combat and non-combat tasks involving the deployment, infiltration, support, exfiltration, and withdrawal of special forces.  SAO may be conducted in conjunction with other joint operations or may be autonomous.
Search and Rescue. The use of aircraft, surface craft, submarines, specialized rescue teams and equipment to search for and rescue personnel in distress on land or at sea.
Surface-to-Air Weapons. Surface-to-Air Weapons (SAW), comprising surface-to-air missiles and anti-aircraft artillery, is an integral part of a Defensive Counter Air (DCA) mission.

Unit Tasking. Unit tasking provides the capability to task all missions of one unit in single section of the ATO mission file. This capability also provides multi-role aircraft units a single section of the ATO for their unit mission tasking.

Alert. A taxiway that provides clear and ready access to the runway for alert aircraft to takeoff.
Crossover. A more specific description of a link taxiway that only connects a parallel taxiway to the runway.
Dispersal. A taxiway, not fitting the other definitions, that allows aircraft to be located away from main aprons, parking facilities, and structures during times of emergency.
End Connecting. A taxiway that connects the parallel taxiway to the runway at the end(s) of the runway.
Link. A taxiway that connects runways, taxiways, and parking facilities to each other.
Loop. A taxiway that is normally located at one or both ends of the runway; starting at one end and returning to the runway, forming a loop, with parking facilities commonly located on the loop.
Parallel. A taxiway that parallels a runway or another taxiway, but is normally narrower than a runway. It may be of sufficient length and width to be used as a runway in an emergency.

Perimeter. A taxiway that usually starts at one end of the runway and ends at the other. Perimeter taxiways are normally, but not necessarily, oval in shape. Perimeter taxiways may encompass the entire airfield, allowing access to refueling points, ammunition storage, and service areas.

Turnaround. A taxiway that is normally found at one of both ends of the runway that gives the aircraft the ability to do a u-turn. Aircraft may also be in a holding pattern on the turnaround apron. Unlike loop taxiways, a turnaround will not have a grass or earth center.

Arroyo. The course of an intermittent stream steep-cut in loose earth. Subject to sudden, temporary flooding.
Bald. A high, rounded knob or mountain top. Bare of forest and significant undergrowth.
Bluff, High. An abrupt slope consisting of relatively unconsolidated earth, more than 50 feet high, usually bordering a stream or body of water.
Bluff, Low. An abrupt slope consisting of relatively unconsolidated earth, less than 50 feet high, usually bordering a stream or body of water.
Butte. A steep hill, usually flat-topped, standing alone in a plain, usually consists almost entirely of consolidated rock.
Caldera. A broad, crater-like basin of a volcano, formed by an explosion or collapse of the cone.
Cliff, High. A steep face of rock rising more than 50 feet above the surrounding land or water.
Cliff, Low. A steep face of rock rising to a maximum of 50 feet higher than the surrounding land or water.
Canyon. A deep ravine or gorge with steep sides, usually located in arid or semi-arid area.
Desert. A region rendered barren or partially barren by environmental extremes such as low rainfall, and conforms to lands having discontinuous vegetation.
Defile. A deep, narrow mountain pass.
Dike. An artificial earth or stone embankment or wall constructed to contain or hold back water as a measure to prevent the flooding or delimiting of a reclaimed area.
Dune, High. A mound, ridge, or hill of wind-deposited sand, 10 feet high or higher.
Dune, Low. A mound, ridge, or hill of wind-deposited sand, less than 10 feet high.
Escarpment. A more or less continuous line of cliffs, bluffs, or steep slopes along the margin of a plateau, mesa, terrace, or beach.
Fan, Alluvial. A gentle-sloping, fan-shaped mass of unconsolidated material deposited by a stream, usually at the place where the stream emerges from a highland. As at the mouth of a canyon.
Glacier. A field or mass of ice and snow formed on land by snowfall in excess of melting which moves down a mountain slope or over a wide area.
Hill. A natural elevation of the terrain having local relief of from 150 to 600 meters.

Hill, High-Gentle. A natural elevation of terrain, having local relief of more than 300 meters, but less than 600 meters, and surface slope less than 30 percent (30-meter rise per 100-meter horizontal distance).

Hill, High-Steep. A natural elevation of the terrain having local relief of more than 300 meters, but less than 600 meters, and surface slopes 30 percent or steeper (30-meter rise per 100-meter horizontal distance).
Hill, Low-Gentle. A natural elevation of the terrain, having local relief from 150 to 300 meters, and surface slopes of less than 30 percent (30-meter rise per 100-meter horizontal distance).
Hill, Low-Steep. A natural elevation of the terrain, having local relief from 150 to 300 meters, and surface slopes 30 percent or steeper (30-meter rise per 100-meter horizontal distance).
Icefield. An area of sea ice more than five nautical miles in width.
Jungle. Land densely overgrown with thicket and growth, usually tropical vegetation and trees.
Lake. A considerable inland body of standing water.
Marsh (Swamp). A track of soft, wet land.
Mesa. An area of considerable elevation, usually flat-topped, with steep sides, generally located in an arid or semi-arid area.
Mountain. A natural land elevation having local relief in excess of 600 meters.
Mountain, High. A natural land elevation having local relief in excess of 900 meters.
Mountain, Low. A natural land elevation having local relief from 600 to 900 meters.
Peak. A pointed mountain summit, including the topmost elevation.
Plain. A relatively flat area of land having little or no change in gradient.
Peninsula. A body of land jutting into and nearly surrounded by water, usually connected to a larger body of land by a neck or isthmus.
Precipice. A brink or edge of a high and very steep cliff.
Ridge. The long, narrow top or crest of a hill or mountain.

River. A natural stream of water which flows permanently or seasonally. A river has greater volume than a creek or rivulet and flows in a more or less permanent bed or channel between defined banks or walls.
Scarp. A steep slope, escarpment, or cliff extending along the edge of a plateau or mesa.
Salt Flat. The salt-encrusted, level floor of a dried-up salt lake.
Summit. The highest point or peak of a mountain range (series of peaks).
Snowfield. A large expanse of snow, the duration of which may vary between extended and perpetual coverage.
Valley. A relatively wide, elongated lowland lying between hills, mountains, or other elevated landforms, commonly traversed by a stream.
Volcano. An opening in the earth's crust through which hot lava and ash are ejected. A mountain (usually conical) formed wholly or in part by volcanic action.
Wadi. A ravine or watercourse that is dry except during the rainy season.
Mean. The difference in height between mean high water and mean low water.
Neap. A tide of minimum range between high and low tide occurring each lunar month around the first and third quarters of the moon.

Spring. The average semidiurnal range occurring at the time of spring tides; this is most conveniently computed from the harmonic constants.  it is larger than the mean range where the type of tide is either semidiurnal or mixed, and is of no practical significance where the type of tide is diurnal.

Diurnal. Having a period or cycle of approximately 1 tidal day (24 hrs 48 min).  Thus, the tide is said to be diurnal when only one high water and one low water occur during a tidal day, and the tidal current is said to be diurnal when there is a single flood and single ebb period in the tidal day. A rotary current is diurnal if it changes its direction through all points of the compass once each tidal day.

Mixed. Type of tide with a large inequality in the high and or low water heights, with two high waters and two low waters usually occurring each tidal day. In strictness, all tides are mixed but the name is usually applied to the tides intermediate to those predominantly semidiurnal and those predominantly diurnal.

Semidiurnal. Having a period or cycle of approximately one-half of a tidal day (24 hrs 48 min).  The predominating type of tide throughout the world is semidiurnal, with two high waters and two low waters each tidal day. The tidal current is said to be semidiurnal when there are two flood and two ebb periods each day.

Military Police. A military police unit.
Nuclear, Biological, Chemical. A unit trained and equipped for NBC defense/cleanup operations.
Auxiliary. Refers to a Naval auxiliary vessel.
Replenishment. Refers to a Naval replishment vessel.
Surface-to-Air Missile. A unit organized and equipped to perform air defense missions by employing surface-launched missiles against hostile aircraft and missiles.

Supply. A unit that procures, stores, and distributes supplies and equipment necessary for the maintenance and operations of military organizations. It usually handles two or more classes of supplies.

Army Group. An organization that directs the strategic and tactical employment of two or more armies and supporting units.

Bare of Vegetation. Terrain has no apparent vegetation.
Brambles. Thick bushes or vines with sharp thorns.
Brush. An assemblage of brushes, commonly 15 feet or less in height and including, in places, small trees and woody vines. Does not include brambles.
Coconut Palm Grove. A tropical grove or stand of tall, branchless, pinnate-leaved trees.
Forest, Dense. A large tract of land, covered with trees, with or without underbrush, whose foliage is continuous, or nearly continuous and covers or nearly covers 85 percent or more of the ground.
Forest, Open. Trees growing in groups so that the foliage is not continuous throughout a zone, and covers approximately 35-85 percent of the ground.

Forest, Scattered. Trees so widely scattered that foliage is not continuous throughout a zone, and covers less than 35 percent of the ground. Scattered forest may include widely spaced groups of trees, dense or open.
Grassland, High. Grassland 3 feet or more in height.
Grassland, Short. Grassland with growth less than 3 feet high.
Field Crops, High. Agricultural cultivated vegetation greater than 3 feet in height.
Jungle, Single Canopy. Inland tropical jungle with a single canopy cover.
Field Crops, Low. Agricultural cultivated vegetation 3 feet or less in height.

Mangrove Forest. Tropical trees which grow in dense stands in coastal swamps, typically those near river mouths in brackish water. At high tide, mangrove trees stand above water level on prop roots. At low tide the interlacing roots of the trees, covered with algae and standing in mud constitute a virtually impenetrable barrier.

Nipa Palm Stand. A stand of low, dense palm found in brackish, tropical swamps, typically bordering tidal streams or areas commonly submerged at high tide. Mature trees have feathery leaves 10-15 feet long. In conjunction with their swamp environment, nipa palms impose serious obstacles to movement.
Orchard. An area of cultivated fruit or nut trees characterized by planting of trees in rows, at regular intervals.
Paddy (Wet Rice). Wet rice in an irrigated field bounded by low ridges or dikes. Completely covered by slowly moving shallow water for considerable periods of time.
Palmetto Growth. A growth of low, thick palm with tough vine-like root systems, usually found in tropical, well drained soil.
Pasture. An area, usually of grassland, used for the grazing of livestock.
Plantation. An area of cultivated crops and trees, usually in a tropical or semi-tropical region, such as a sugar or rubber plantation.

Savanna. An area of grassland and scattered trees with grass cover usually 1-4 feet in height, but reaching 12 feet in some tropic areas. Savannas occur in low rainfall areas, especially on plains to the leeward of mountains.
Scrubby Vegetation. Terrain is generally covered with low bushes or shrubs such that personnel traversing would brush against the foliage and be contaminated with liquid chemical agent.
Trees, Scattered. Widely separated trees not considered to be forest.
Sugarcane Field. An area in which a very tall, perennial tropical grass, with jointed stems, is cultivated as a source of sugar.
Cultivation, Terraced. A natural or man-made shelf, that interrupts a rolling or steep slope (sometimes in a series), which is used for growing agricultural crops.
Tundra. Low, dense vegetation consisting of grass, herbs, moss, and lichens covering the nearly level, treeless plains of the arctic.
Vineyard. Land devoted to the cultivation of grapevines.
Wooded Terrain. Terrain is thickly wooded.

Cultivated, Terrace. A natural or man-made shelf that interrupts a rolling or steep slope in a series, which is used for growing agricultural crops.

Forest, Moss. A wet tropical upland forest characterized by the presence of abundant mosses and ferns.
Forest, Open. Trees growing in groups so that the foliage is not continuous throughout a zone, and covers approximately 35 to 85 percent of the ground.

Forest, Rain. A tropical woodland that has an annual rainfall of 2.5 m (8.3 ft), is restricted almost always to certain lowland areas, is characterized by lofty, broad-leaved evergreen trees forming a continuous canopy, and by nearly complete absence of low-growing ground-sooted vegetation.

Forest, Scattered. Trees so widely separated that foliage is not continuous throughout a zone and covers less than 35 percent of the ground. Scattered forest may include widely spaced groups of trees, dense or open.
Forest, Swamp. Wet, spongy terrain that is saturated, and sometimes partially or intermittently covered with water.  Such terrain has natural vegetation predominantly of shrubs and trees.
Grass, High. Grass over 1 m (3.3 ft) high.
Grass, Short. Grass 1 m (3.3 ft) in height or less.
Jungle. Terrain that is impenetrable, with an overgrown, tangled mass of tropical vegetation.  May or may not be inhabited.

Mangrove Trees. A tropical tree which grows in dense stands in coastal swamps, typically those near river mouths in brackish water.  At high tide, mangrove trees stand above water level on prop roots.  At low tide, the interlacing roots of the trees, covered with algae, and standing in mud, constitute a virtually impenetrable barrier.

Nipa Palm. A low palm found in dense stands, in brackish tropical swamps, typically bordering tidal streams or areas commonly submerged at high tide. Mature trees have feathery leaves 3 m (9.8 ft) to 5 m (16 ft) long. In conjunction with their swamp environment, nipa palms impose serious obstacles to movement.
Orchard. An area of cultivated fruit or nut trees characterized by planting trees in rows, at regular intervals.

Paddy (Wet Rice). An irrigated field devoted to rice cultivation by hand methods.  It is bound by low ridges or dikes, and is completely covered by slowly moving shallow water for considerable periods of time.
Pasture. An area, usually of grassland, used for grazing of livestock.
Plantation. An area cultivated crops and trees, usually in a tropical or semi-tropical region, such as a sugar or rubber plantation.

Savanna. An area of grassland and scattered trees with grass cover usually 0.3 to 1.2 m (1 to 4 ft) in height, but reaching 4 m (13.2 ft) in some tropical areas. Savannas occur in low rainfall areas, especially on plains to the leeward of mountains.
Scrub. Land covered with thick growth of short, stunted tree, bush, or shrub, commonly associated with brush and characteristic of cut over land and areas of poor soil.

Air Defense Command and Control Net. A net used by the Area Air Defense Commander (AADC) to disseminate changes to the area air defense plan. The AADC is the net control station of this net.
Chat. The real-time, synchronous, text-based communication via computer.

Data Link Coordination Net. A net used by the Interface Control Officer (ICO) to manage and coordinate the entire multi-TDL interface. The ICO uses this net to direct all changes to the OPTASK LINK, to include entry and exit of units, approving filter used, reconfiguration of the interface, changes to the DLRP, frequencies, or link duties, etc. The ICO is net control station for this net.

Track Supervision Net. A net used by track surveillance personnel for the control and coordination of procedures used to maintain a clear tactical picture and to assist units entering or exiting the interface. The track data controller is net control station for this net.

Voice Product Net. A net used to provide amplifying Signals Intelligence (SIGINT) information to interface units on a timely basis, and is used to coordinate sigint information reported on the interface. The Special Information Systems (SIS) manager is the net control station of this net.

Barrel. A U.S. unit of liquid measure equal to 31 1/2 gallons; or: a unit of measure for petroleum equal to 42 gallons; or: A unit of dry measure (as for fruits and vegetables) equal to 105 dry quarts or about 3.9 bushels.
Anti-Air Warfare. Measures taken to defend a maritime force against attacks by airborne weapons launched from aircraft, ships, submarines, and land-based sites.
Anti-Surface Warfare/Anti-Surface Vessel Operations. Air operations conducted with the intention of denying the enemy the effective use of maritime surface assets.
Anti-Submarine Warfare. Operations conducted with the intention of denying the enemy the effective use of submarines.

Electronic Warfare. Military action to exploit the electromagnetic spectrum encompassing: the search for, interception and identification of electromagnetic emissions, the employment of electromagnetic energy, included directed energy, to reduce or prevent hostile use of the electromagnetic spectrum, and actions to ensure its effective use by friendly forces.

Dust/Snow/Sand. Blowing snow, sand storm, dust storm.
Fog/Haze. Fog, ice fog, or thick haze (visibility less than four km).
Snow. Snow or rain and snow mixed (no showers).
Showers. Showers of rain, snow, rain and snow mixed, or hail.
Thunderstorms. Thunderstorms, with or without precipitation.

Patches. The descriptor used to describe for when it covers portions of the station and the apparent visibility in the fog patch or bank is less than 5/8 SM and visibility over the uncovered portions of the station is 5/8 SM or greater.
Blowing. The descriptor used to further describe the condition of dust, sand, snow, and/or spray which is raised by the wind to a height of 6 feet or more and reduces the prevailing visibility.
Low Drifting. The descriptor used to further describe the condition of dust, sand, or snow which is raised by the wind to a height of less than 6 feet and does not reduce the prevailing visibility.
Freezing. The descriptor used to describe the effect of fog, drizzle, and/or rain which freezes upon contact with exposed surfaces.
Shallow. The descriptor which is used to further describe fog with a vertical extent of less than 6 feet.

Partial. The descriptor used to describe fog when it covers a substantial part of the station and visibility in the fog is less then 5/8 SM and visibility over the uncovered parts of the station is 5/8 SM or more.

Showers. The descriptor used to describe precipitation as characterized by the suddenness with which they start and stop, by the rapid changes in intensity, and usually by rapid changes in the appearance in the sky.
Thunderstorm. A local storm produced by a cumulonimbus that is accompanied by lighting and/or thunder, usually with gusty winds, heavy rain, and sometimes, with hail.
Amber. Forecasted weather conditions indicate caution should be used for identified operations or equipment.
Green. Forecasted weather conditions are favorable for the successful execution of operations or equipment.
Red. Forecasted weather conditions are serious and may prevent the successful execution of operations or equipment.

Mist. A visible aggregate of microscopic and more-or-less hygroscopic water droplets suspended in the atmosphere, based at the earth's surface, which reduces prevailing visibility to between 5/8 and 6 statute miles.
Widespread Dust. Fine particles of dust or sand suspended in the air by a duststorm or sandstorm that may have occurred at or far away from the station.

Fog. A visible aggregate of minute water particles (droplets) which are based at the earth's surface.  Fog reduces horizontal and vertical visibility, and may extend over a sizeable area.  In surface reports, fog is recorded when the depth of the phenomena is greater than 20 feet and reduces prevailing visibility to less than 5/8 statute miles.
Smoke. A suspension of small particles in the air produced by combustion.

Haze. A suspension in the air of extremely small, dry particles invisible to the naked eye and sufficiently numerous to give the air an opalescent appearance.  This phenomenon resembles a uniform veil over the landscape that subdues all colors.

Spray. An ensemble of water droplets torn by the wind from the surface of an extensive body of water, generally from the crest of waves, and carried up a short distance in the air in such quantities as to reduce the horizontal visibility at eye level (6 feet).
Sand. Sand raised by the wind to moderate heights above ground.
Volcanic Ash. Fine particles of rock powder that are blown out from a volcano and that may remain suspended in the atmosphere for long periods.
Distant. Indicates the phenomena is occurring at a distance of greater than 10 statute miles from the station.
Vicinity. Indicates the phenomena is occurring within five (5) to ten (10) statute miles of the observing location.

Weather Advisory. Describes a report issued that states probable weather situations of inconvenience that do not carry the danger of warning criteria, but, if not observed, could lead to hazardous situations.
Weather Warning. Describes a forecast issued when severe weather has developed, is already occurring and reported, or is detected on radar.
Weather Watch. Describes a forecast issued well in advance of a severe weather event to alert the Commander of the possibility of a particular hazard.
